lessons.plain: When a company moves its software into a cloud provider, every database, server and storage bucket has to live somewhere, and how you arrange them matters. Think of a large office building: the whole company is the building, departments are floors, and each application gets its own room with its own locks and its own bill. In Google Cloud the top node is the organization, folders group related work, and projects are the rooms where resources actually live. A good structure makes it easy to answer who can change what, which costs belong to which application, and what gets affected when something breaks. A poor structure makes every later change slow and risky.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has two applications, a ride tracker and a payments service, and each needs a development and a production copy. Before any teaching, sketch how you would group these copies so that a team working on payments cannot accidentally change the ride tracker's production system. What would you group together, and why?
lessons.teach:
The organization is the root node of a Google Cloud estate, normally tied to the company's domain. Below it you can create folders, which are grouping nodes that can nest inside each other. The lowest level is the project, the boundary that holds resources, turns on services, links to a billing account, and carries its own access rules. Every project has exactly one parent, either the organization or a folder, so the whole estate forms a tree.

Why this works: access rules and organization policies attached to a node flow downward to everything beneath it. This is called inheritance. Access grants are additive, so a grant made high in the tree cannot be taken back lower down; you can only add more.

Worked example. Acme has folder ride-tracker containing projects ride-dev and ride-prod, and folder payments containing payments-dev and payments-prod. You grant a group the viewer role on folder ride-tracker. Step 1: the group now sees both ride projects. Step 2: they see nothing in payments, because that folder is a sibling. Step 3: if you later need them to edit ride-dev only, you add a grant on that single project, not on the folder.

Common mistake: granting a broad role at the organization node 'to make things easy'. That reaches every project, including payments-prod.

Consequence: an organization-wide policy that blocks a risky setting applies to every new project automatically, which is the point of organizing well. The structure you choose therefore decides the blast radius of every mistake.

questions.prompt: Brightwell Labs has folder data-platform containing projects etl-dev and etl-live, and folder mobile-apps containing projects app-staging and app-live. An analyst is granted the viewer role on folder data-platform. Step 1: the analyst can see etl-dev and etl-live. Step 2: the analyst sees nothing in app-staging or app-live, because mobile-apps is a sibling folder. Step 3: a new project named etl-archive is created directly under data-platform. Step 4: this is the missing step. What is the analyst's access to etl-archive, and why?
choices: The analyst cannot see etl-archive until someone adds a separate grant on that project, because grants do not reach projects created later.
The analyst can see and also edit etl-archive, because a viewer grant on a folder is automatically upgraded to editor for new projects.
The analyst can see etl-archive, because the viewer grant on the parent folder flows down to every project beneath it, including new ones.
The analyst can see app-live as well, because all folders in one organization share their grants with each other.
questions.why: Access granted on a folder is inherited by every project beneath that folder, and a project created later under the same folder is covered automatically.

questions.prompt: In the resource hierarchy, what is the parent of a project, and what does that rule guarantee about the shape of the estate?
choices: A project has no parent; it sits beside the organization and links to it through its billing account.
A project's parent is always the billing account, so the estate is organised by spending rather than by structure.
A project has exactly one parent, which is either the organization or a folder, so the whole estate forms a tree.
A project may have several parents, so the estate forms a web where any node can be reached from any other.
questions.why: The teaching text states that each project has exactly one parent, either the organization or a folder, which makes the estate a tree.

questions.prompt: Harbor Lane Retail has folder retail containing projects shop-dev and shop-prod, and folder logistics containing route-dev. An organization-wide policy blocks external IP addresses. Next week a team creates a new project shop-test directly under folder retail. Which statement is correct?
choices: The policy applies to shop-test automatically, because it is inherited from the organization node down through every folder and project beneath it.
The policy applies only to projects that already existed when the policy was set, so shop-test is exempt.
The policy does not apply to shop-test until an administrator attaches it to that project by hand.
The policy applies to shop-test automatically, and it applies to route-dev too, because the policy reaches every project in the organization.
questions.why: Policies attached to a node flow down to everything beneath it, so the new project inherits the organization-level block without any extra step.

questions.prompt: A small company grants the editor role at the organization node to one contractor, saying it makes things easy. Which description best names the risk, and why it cannot be reduced lower in the tree?
choices: The contractor can edit every project in the organization, including production projects in unrelated folders, and a lower node cannot take that access back because grants are additive.
The contractor can edit only the project where the grant was typed, because the organization node is only a label with no real effect.
The contractor gains the right to change billing for every project, which is the only effect of an organization-level grant.
The contractor is blocked from production automatically, because production projects always override grants made at higher nodes.
questions.why: Grants at a high node reach every project below it, and since access grants are additive, a lower node can only add access, never remove what was granted above.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we group Google Cloud projects into folders by application rather than by team, and name one limit or tradeoff of that choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: We group by application because the things we need to control together, such as who can deploy, what it costs, and which policies apply, usually belong to one application, not to one team. Each app folder holds its dev and prod projects, so a grant on the folder covers that app's environments and nothing else, and billing reports roll up by application. Separating dev from prod inside the folder keeps a risky test away from live data. The tradeoff is that a team owning several applications has to receive several grants, and shared services used by many apps need their own project and folder, which adds naming and bookkeeping work. Good folder names and a written convention keep that manageable.
rubricPoints: Folders group projects by application so access, billing and policy follow the workload
Projects are the boundary for resources, and each project has one parent in the tree
Access and policies inherit downward, and grants are additive
Tradeoff: multi-app teams need multiple grants and shared services need their own project

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers cloud resource hierarchy, so this objective is best learned from the reading and then checked by explaining it.

lessons.plain: A Google Cloud network is the private road system your applications use to talk to each other and to services. When several teams each have their own project, they often need to share that road system or connect it safely to another one. This objective is about choosing among three ways to do that. Shared VPC lets one team own a network that other teams plug into. VPC Network Peering joins two existing networks directly so their internal addresses can reach each other. Private Service Connect gives you a private door with a local address that leads to one service someone else runs, without merging the networks at all. The skill is picking the simplest option that keeps teams separated where they should be.
lessons.guessPrompt: Three teams each have their own cloud project and their own private network. Team A needs to call a service that Team B runs, but nobody wants Team A's whole network to be able to see Team B's network. Would you first let the two networks talk to each other directly, or give Team A one private address that leads only to that service? Explain your reasoning in a sentence or two.
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A VPC network (virtual private cloud) is a private, isolated network inside Google Cloud. It is divided into subnets, which are blocks of internal IP addresses tied to a region. A project is the unit that holds resources, billing and access. Shared VPC lets a host project own one VPC network and share selected subnets with service projects, so resources in those projects use the host's network while administration stays split between teams. VPC Network Peering is a direct link between two separate VPC networks. Each side must configure its half, and their internal IP ranges must not overlap. Peering is not transitive: if A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B. Private Service Connect creates an endpoint, which is an internal IP address inside your own network that forwards traffic to a published service. The two networks never merge, so their address ranges may even overlap.

Why it works: each option trades visibility for isolation. Shared VPC centralizes network control under one team. Peering joins two networks as equals. Private Service Connect exposes exactly one service.

Worked example. Team Payments has a host project whose network uses the range 10.0.0.0/16. Team Riders' service project is attached to that host and gets a subnet from the shared range, so its virtual machines receive addresses from it. Next, a vendor offers a managed database in its own network, which also uses 10.0.0.0/16. Step one: peering would be rejected because the ranges overlap. Step two: Private Service Connect gives Payments an endpoint with one internal address in its own subnet. Step three: traffic sent to that address is forwarded to the vendor service, and no route to the vendor's whole network is created.

Common mistake: choosing peering for a chain of networks and expecting transitive reach, or peering networks whose ranges overlap.

Consequence: a missing or overlapping route usually causes connections to silently time out, which looks like an application outage. Choosing the narrowest mechanism that meets the need keeps networks isolated and failures easier to trace.

questions.prompt: Team Kite runs its application in network NET-A, which uses the range 10.20.0.0/16. A logging service runs in network NET-B, which uses 10.30.0.0/16. Step one: the team confirms the two ranges do not overlap, so peering is allowed. Step two: the team creates its half of the peering on NET-A's side. Step three is missing. Which step completes the link so that traffic can flow between the two networks?
choices: Move the logging service into a Shared VPC service project
Add a Private Service Connect endpoint in NET-A, since peering cannot be used between any two networks
Configure the peering on NET-B's side too, so that both halves of the link exist
Shrink NET-B's range to a /24 so the two ranges stop overlapping
questions.why: Peering is a link that each network must configure on its own side, so the half on NET-B is the missing step that completes it.

questions.prompt: Team Harbor has network HARBOR-1 peered with HARBOR-2, and HARBOR-2 peered with HARBOR-3. Which statement is true?
choices: HARBOR-1 can reach HARBOR-3 through HARBOR-2 as long as firewall rules allow it
HARBOR-1 cannot reach HARBOR-3 through HARBOR-2, because peering is not transitive
HARBOR-1 can reach HARBOR-3 because peering chains are allowed up to three networks
HARBOR-1 and HARBOR-3 merge automatically into one network
questions.why: Peering is a direct link between two networks only, so a chain of peerings does not give reach from the first network to the last.

questions.prompt: A team needs its application to call one internal API hosted in a vendor-run network. Both networks use the range 172.20.0.0/18. Which mechanism fits best?
choices: Shared VPC with the vendor project attached as a service project
Private Service Connect, which gives one internal endpoint and does not merge the networks, so the overlap is not a blocker
Peering with a route to the whole vendor network, after renumbering the vendor side
VPC Network Peering, because the two ranges must be identical
questions.why: Private Service Connect exposes a single service through an internal endpoint and never merges the networks, so overlapping ranges do not prevent it.

questions.prompt: A host project owns a VPC network and shares one subnet with a service project. Which statement about this arrangement is correct?
choices: Service project resources must sit in a different region from the shared subnet to keep the network isolated
The host project's network is copied into the service project, and the host loses control of it
Resources in the service project use the host's network while each team still administers its own project
Shared VPC requires a peering link between the host and service projects before any subnet can be shared
questions.why: Shared VPC lets service projects use subnets from the host's network while network control and administration stay split between the teams.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose Shared VPC, VPC Network Peering, or Private Service Connect, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking who owns the network and what needs to reach what. If one platform team should own the network and several application projects should plug into it, I would use Shared VPC: the host project owns the subnets, service projects create resources inside them, and the platform team keeps control. If two existing networks owned by different groups need to talk, peering links them directly, but I would first check that their IP ranges do not overlap. I would also remember that peering is not transitive, so A reaching B and B reaching C does not give A access to C. If I only need to reach one service someone else publishes, especially one whose addresses overlap mine, I would use Private Service Connect, which gives me a single internal endpoint and never merges the networks. The tradeoff with peering is that once connected, both sides have broad reach, which is why I would prefer the narrower endpoint when the goal is just one service.
rubricPoints: Shared VPC: host project owns the network and service projects attach subnets, keeping central control.
VPC Network Peering: links two networks directly, needs non-overlapping ranges, and is not transitive.
Private Service Connect: provides one internal endpoint to a single service without merging networks, and tolerates overlapping ranges.
Choosing the narrowest mechanism that meets the need reduces exposure and makes failures easier to trace.

suggested.rationale: Tracing how traffic moves between networks, subnets and endpoints is best practised with the planned virtual network path tracer.

lessons.plain: When a company runs many separate projects, each one produces its own logs and performance numbers, so someone chasing a problem could be searching dozens of places. Designing multi-project monitoring and logging means deciding in advance how those signals get gathered, where they are viewed, and who can see them. You can let each team keep its own view, pull everything into one shared place, or do both by copying the important records into a central store that keeps working if one team's project is deleted. The real work is setting up these routes so that new projects join them automatically, instead of relying on someone remembering to configure each one.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company has twenty projects and a problem appears in only one of them, what would make it hard to notice the problem from one central screen, and what would you change so that every project's errors show up there without anyone configuring each project by hand?
lessons.teach:
Monitoring means collecting measurements over time, such as request counts and error rates, and alerting when they cross a threshold. Logging means recording individual events, each one a line of text or a structured record. On Google Cloud, Cloud Monitoring holds metrics and Cloud Logging holds logs, and each project has its own default stores. A metrics scope is a setting that lets one project, called the scoping project, view the metrics of other projects on a single dashboard. A log sink is a routing rule in the logging router. It copies log entries matching a filter to a destination such as a log bucket in another project, Cloud Storage, BigQuery, or Pub/Sub. An aggregated sink is created at a folder or organization level, so it collects matching logs from every project beneath that level, including projects created later.

Why it works: routing happens at the level where the resource hierarchy already exists, so a new project inherits the collection rules without anyone remembering to configure it. Central copies also survive if a team's project is shut down or cleaned up.

Worked example: a company has a folder called payments containing three projects. The platform team creates one aggregated sink on that folder with a filter for severity ERROR and above, pointing at a log bucket in a central logging project. Step 1: a fourth project is created under payments. Step 2: its ERROR entries match the folder-level sink automatically. Step 3: the central bucket receives them, and the on-call engineer queries one place.

Common mistake: creating sinks project by project, so the next project is silently missed. Another is forgetting that the sink's writer identity needs write permission on the destination. Without it, the export fails, and nobody reading the dashboards sees an error.

Consequence: a missing route means an outage can look quiet in the central view, which is exactly when you most need that view to be complete. Multi-project monitoring should be built on the hierarchy, not on memory.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a folder named freight that holds two projects, route-api and depot-sync. An engineer creates one aggregated sink on the freight folder. The sink filters for severity WARNING and above and sends matching entries to a log bucket in a central project named ops-central. Step 1: the sink is created at the folder level, so it covers every project beneath freight. Step 2: a third project, billing-batch, is created under freight. Step 3: [MISSING STEP]. Step 4: the WARNING entries from billing-batch appear in the ops-central bucket with no per-project setup.
choices: Create a separate sink inside billing-batch so its logs are copied a second time.
Rename the freight folder so the sink picks up the new project name.
Grant the sink's writer identity permission to write into the ops-central bucket.
Enable a metrics scope on ops-central so the bucket can display billing-batch dashboards.
questions.why: Because the sink writes to the destination under its own writer identity, that identity must have write permission on the bucket, and this is the one step that makes the routing actually deliver entries.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is an aggregated sink in Cloud Logging?
choices: A routing rule created at a folder or organization level that copies matching logs from every project beneath it, including projects created later.
A limit that stops a project from sending logs to any destination outside its own folder.
A dashboard that combines metrics from several projects into one chart.
A copy of a project's logs that is stored only inside that project's own default bucket.
questions.why: The teaching text defines an aggregated sink as one created at folder or organization level that collects matching logs from all projects beneath that level, including future ones.

questions.prompt: A retailer has a folder called checkout with four projects, each with its own project-level sinks sending ERROR logs to a central bucket. Next week a fifth project is created under checkout. What happens to its ERROR logs by default?
choices: They are stored in the central bucket only after someone enables a metrics scope.
They are duplicated into every existing project's sink.
They are sent to the central bucket automatically because the folder already has sinks.
They are missed by the central view unless someone creates a sink for that project, since project-by-project sinks do not cover new projects.
questions.why: Sinks created project by project only cover the projects they were created in, so a new project is silently missed; folder-level or organization-level sinks are what cover future projects.

questions.prompt: A team creates a sink with a correct filter that routes ERROR logs to a Pub/Sub topic in another project. Logs stop arriving at the topic, and the team's dashboards show no error. Which cause is most likely?
choices: The metrics scope on the scoping project has expired.
The project that owns the topic was created after the sink, so it cannot receive entries.
The sink's writer identity lacks permission to publish to the destination, so the export fails silently.
The sink's filter is too narrow, so it matches nothing at all.
questions.why: A sink writes to its destination under its writer identity, and without write permission on the destination the export fails without any visible error in the central views, as the teaching text warns.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would collect error logs from every project in a new folder so that projects created later are covered automatically, and name one limit or tradeoff of centralising those logs.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would create one aggregated log sink at the folder level, not one sink per project. The filter would select entries at ERROR severity and above, and the destination would be a log bucket in a central logging project. Because the sink sits on the folder, it covers projects that already exist and any created later under that folder, which is why I would avoid per-project sinks that people forget to add. The tradeoff is cost and access. Copying everything into one place means more ingestion and storage charges, and it concentrates sensitive logs, so the central bucket needs tight read permissions and a sensible retention period. The sink's writer identity also needs permission to write to the destination, or the export fails quietly. I would confirm it with a test entry and a dashboard query before calling it done.
rubricPoints: Uses a folder- or organization-level aggregated sink so that new projects are covered automatically
Names a central destination and explains why central copies survive project-level changes
States a tradeoff such as ingestion cost or concentrated access to sensitive logs
Notes that the sink's writer identity needs write permission on the destination

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers multi-project monitoring, and the core skill here is reasoning through and explaining where collection rules belong and their tradeoffs.

lessons.plain: When many people and machines share one company cloud account, two questions come up constantly: who is allowed to do what, and what rules must every project follow no matter who is working in it. Designing IAM roles and organization-level policies means answering both on purpose. You decide which bundles of permissions to hand out, to whom, and at which level of the company's cloud tree, so access is granted narrowly and guardrails cannot be quietly switched off further down. Think of a building: keycards open specific doors, and building-wide fire rules apply on every floor whatever a tenant prefers.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer on one team needs to read logs in one project, and a colleague suggests giving them the broadest administrator role on the whole company account just to be safe. What is wrong with that idea, and what would you grant instead?
lessons.teach:
Start with the terms. An IAM (Identity and Access Management) policy is a list of bindings attached to a resource. Each binding ties a principal, meaning a user, a group, or a service account (an identity used by software), to a role. A role is a named bundle of permissions, and a permission is one specific action, such as reading a log entry. Google Cloud resources sit in a hierarchy: the organization at the top, then optional folders, then projects, then individual resources. An allow policy set at one level applies to everything beneath it; this is inheritance. Allow grants are additive, so a lower level can add access but cannot remove what a higher level granted. Deny policies are a separate mechanism that block specific permissions and can override allows below them. Organization policies are constraints rather than grants. They set rules such as which regions resources may be created in or whether service account keys may be created, and they also flow downward.

Why it works: because grants flow down, you grant at the narrowest level that covers the need, and you place non-negotiable rules high in the tree where a project owner cannot bypass them.

Worked example: a payments team needs to read logs in the project payments-prod. Step one: find the smallest predefined role that contains log-read permissions. Step two: bind the team's group to that role on that project only. Step three: check that no folder or organization binding gives the group more. The team can now read logs in one project and nothing else.

Common mistake: granting a broad basic role such as Owner or Editor at the organization level. Those roles carry many permissions, and the grant inherits into every project beneath.

Consequence: a single broad grant at the top is a silent blast radius. A leaked credential or one careless change can reach production in every project. A missing organization policy means a rule you assumed held everywhere in fact does not.

questions.prompt: A data science group in a different company's organization needs to upload training files into one Cloud Storage bucket called ml-features-staging, inside the project ds-sandbox. The company also wants service account keys blocked everywhere. Work through it. Step one: choose the smallest predefined role that lets the group write objects, rather than a broad basic role. Step two: bind the group to that role on the single bucket only. Step three is missing from this trace: ______. Finish it using the idea that a rule placed high in the tree cannot be bypassed by a project owner.
choices: Set the service account key constraint on the organization node so it flows down to every folder and project beneath.
Add a deny policy on each project one at a time so the key rule applies where it is needed.
Remove the group's binding from ds-sandbox so no conflicting rules remain in that project.
Grant the security team Owner at the organization level so they can enforce the key rule themselves.
questions.why: Organization policies are constraints that flow downward, so setting the key rule at the organization node means no project owner can bypass it, which is the purpose of placing non-negotiable rules high in the hierarchy.

questions.prompt: A contractor group is granted the Editor basic role on a folder named vendors, which contains three projects. A fourth project is created inside vendors next month. Which resources can the contractor group change?
choices: Only the first project, because the grant was written on the folder and must be re-applied to others.
Every project inside the vendors folder, including the fourth project created later, because the allow grant is inherited downward.
None of them until each project owner accepts the grant in writing.
Only resources carrying a label that matches the folder name.
questions.why: An allow policy set on a folder applies to everything beneath it through inheritance, so new projects created inside the folder receive the grant too.

questions.prompt: An organization grants a developer group a role on the whole organization. A project owner then adds a project-level binding that gives the same group a smaller role, hoping to limit what they can do in that project. Does this remove the organization-wide access in that project?
choices: Only if the developer group is first removed from the organization binding.
No, because allow grants are additive, so a lower level can add access but cannot remove what a higher level granted.
Yes, because the most specific binding always replaces the broader one.
Yes, but only if the project also sets an organization policy.
questions.why: Allow grants combine additively down the hierarchy, so a narrower project-level binding cannot take back access the organization already granted.

questions.prompt: A ledger folder contains several projects. A folder-level allow grant gives an operations group a permission that includes deleting ledger records. The company wants that one permission blocked for everyone beneath the folder, regardless of any allows. Which mechanism fits this need?
choices: Add a narrower allow binding to each project that omits the delete permission.
Set a deny policy on the ledger folder that blocks that specific permission for everything beneath it.
Remove the operations group from the folder and rely on their project bindings instead.
Create an organization policy constraint that lists the delete permission by name.
questions.why: Deny policies block specific permissions and can override allows below them, so a deny at the folder level stops the delete permission for all projects in that folder.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why a team should receive access through a narrow binding on its own project rather than a broad role on the organization, and name one limit or tradeoff of working that way.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would grant the team a predefined role on their own project, because allow grants flow down the hierarchy and a grant at the organization reaches every project under it. The narrow binding keeps the blast radius small: if the account is compromised or someone makes a mistake, only that project is exposed. The tradeoff is administrative effort. Each team and project needs its own binding, and over time these can drift or pile up, so you need a naming convention and periodic review. Also, a predefined role may still include more permissions than the team needs, so sometimes you must create a custom role, which you then have to maintain. For guardrails that must hold everywhere, such as restricting regions, I would use an organization policy rather than trusting every project to set it correctly.
rubricPoints: Explains that allow grants inherit downward, so the grant level sets the blast radius
Recommends the narrowest role and the lowest level that meets the need
Names a real tradeoff such as administrative overhead, drift, or custom-role maintenance
Distinguishes access grants from organization policy guardrails

suggested.rationale: The authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test whether a binding at one hierarchy level grants or blocks a request, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: A service account is an identity that belongs to a program or machine rather than to a person. When your application needs to read a storage bucket or write to a database, it authenticates as a service account, and the permissions granted to that account decide what it may touch. Creating one is like issuing a badge to a robot: you name it, give it only the access its job needs, and attach it to the workload so it can prove who it is. Managing them well means knowing where their credentials live, avoiding long-lived key files where you can, and removing accounts that nothing uses anymore.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app running on a virtual machine needs to read files from a storage bucket. Would you give the app your own personal login, or create a separate identity for the app? Why?
lessons.teach: A service account is a Google Cloud identity meant for an application or automated job. Unlike a user account, it has no password you type in. It authenticates with credentials the workload obtains at run time or, less preferably, with a key file you download. You create one inside a project, give it a name, and the platform assigns it an email-style address such as name@project-id.iam.gserviceaccount.com. That address is what you later place in access policies. Why it works: access is granted by attaching roles to a principal, meaning the identity being given permissions, and a service account is a principal. So you grant the bucket reader role to the app's service account on that bucket, not to a person. When the workload runs as that account, each call it makes is checked against those grants, and audit logs record its activity under its own name. Worked example. Step 1: a team creates an account called positions-reader in the project. Step 2: they grant it read-only access to one bucket. Step 3: they set the virtual machine running the app to run as that account. Step 4: the app obtains short-lived tokens automatically and reads the bucket. Step 5: an attempt to delete a table fails, because the account holds no role that allows it. Common mistake: creating a key file, downloading it, and committing it to source control or copying it onto many machines. A downloaded key is a long-lived secret that works from anywhere until someone disables it. Another frequent mistake is leaving the default compute account in use for everything, since it often carries a very broad role. Consequence: if a key leaks, an attacker holds the application's full access. If an account is deleted while a workload still uses it, that workload loses access and fails at its next call. Keep credentials short-lived and grants narrow.

questions.prompt: A payments company runs a nightly job that writes ledger summaries to a storage bucket. The setup so far: Step 1: the team creates a service account named ledger-summarizer (a Google Cloud identity for automated work, with no password) in the project fin-prod. Step 2: they grant it the object creator role on the summaries bucket only, so it can add files there but not read or delete others. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the job runs at 02:00 and writes its files without anyone supplying credentials by hand. Which missing step completes the setup?
choices: Download a JSON key file for ledger-summarizer and bake it into the job's container image so it can authenticate from any host.
Configure the job to run as ledger-summarizer, so the platform supplies short-lived credentials to it at run time.
Grant ledger-summarizer the Owner role on the whole project so that no future permission request can fail.
Share the ledger-summarizer email address in the team wiki so that the job can look it up when it starts.
questions.why: Step 4 only works if the job runs as the account, which lets the platform hand it short-lived tokens, while the other choices either create a long-lived secret or grant far more access than the job needs.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a service account in Google Cloud?
choices: A human user account created only when someone changes teams and needs a fresh login.
A network firewall rule that limits which virtual machines may open connections to a database.
An identity for an application or automated job, which can be given roles and whose calls are checked against those roles.
A shared username and password that several engineers type in to reach a monitoring dashboard.
questions.why: A service account is a non-human identity for software, and access is controlled by granting it roles that each call is checked against.

questions.prompt: An engineer finds a JSON key file for the service account report-sync-sa, created two days ago in the project retail-analytics, pasted into a public code repository. What is the best immediate response?
choices: Disable or delete that exposed key, issue a replacement, and move the workload to run as the account instead of using a key file.
Rename the repository so search engines stop indexing it, and keep the key since the service still depends on it.
Add report-sync-sa to the Owner role so its permissions cover whatever an attacker might try with the leaked key.
Leave it alone, because a key only works from the machine it was originally created on.
questions.why: A downloaded key is a long-lived secret that works from anywhere until disabled, so the exposed key must be cut off and the workload moved to platform-supplied short-lived credentials.

questions.prompt: A web service on a managed container platform runs as the service account quote-runner. An administrator deletes quote-runner while the service is still serving traffic. What is the most likely result?
choices: The service keeps working because the platform automatically falls back to the project's default account.
The service pauses until someone restores the account from a backup, then resumes where it left off.
Nothing changes until the service is redeployed, because running services keep their credentials indefinitely.
The service loses its access and fails on its next call that needs credentials, because the identity it runs as no longer exists.
questions.why: A workload depends on its service account at each call, so deleting the account cuts off its access and the next call that needs credentials fails.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants to commit a downloaded service account key file into the repository so the build pipeline can deploy. In your own words, explain why that is risky, what you would do instead, and one tradeoff of your alternative.
lessons.modelAnswer: Committing the key file is risky because the key is a long-lived secret. Anyone who can read the repository, clone it, or view its history gets the account's permissions, and the key keeps working until someone finds it and disables it. Git history preserves it even after the file is deleted. I would instead run the pipeline as a service account attached to the build environment, so the platform issues short-lived tokens and there is no file to leak. I would grant that account only the roles deployment needs, scoped to the specific project, and use an organization policy to block key creation where possible. The tradeoff is setup effort: the pipeline must run somewhere that supports attached identity, and the team has to grant roles deliberately instead of reaching for a broad role just to get things working.
rubricPoints: A service account is a non-human identity whose permissions come from role grants.
A downloaded key is a long-lived secret that works from anywhere until it is disabled.
Attaching the account to the workload gives short-lived credentials without a key file.
Grant least-privilege roles to the account and avoid broad defaults.
Name the tradeoff: setup effort against the risk of a leaked key.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between a key file and an attached identity is a reasoning and explanation skill that no current mission practises directly.

lessons.plain: Data residency is about where an organization's data is physically kept and processed. Some laws or contracts say customer records must stay inside a particular country or region, even when the company operates elsewhere. When you build cloud systems, every storage place and service you create lands in some location, so choosing that location is a design decision made up front, not an afterthought. Good design picks the right location first and then adds guardrails so nobody can quietly place data somewhere else later.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company must keep its customers' files inside the European Union. A developer creates a new storage bucket without thinking about location. What do you think should stop that bucket from being created in the United States, and at what level of the company's setup would you put that stop?
lessons.teach:
Data residency is the requirement that certain data stays stored and processed within a chosen geographic boundary, such as one country or one cloud region. In Google Cloud, most resources, such as storage buckets, databases and virtual machines, are created in a named location: a single region like europe-west1, a multi-region like EU, or in some cases a global scope. The location you pick at creation time decides where the data at rest lives, so it is a decision you make before any data arrives.

Why it works: an organization policy is a rule set at the organization, folder or project level that applies to everything beneath it. The resource location restriction constraint lists the only locations where resources may be created and blocks creation anywhere else. A careless choice then fails loudly instead of silently breaking a legal promise. Where a regulated regime applies, Assured Workloads can create a folder with compliance and location controls already set.

Worked example: a company must keep EU customer data in the EU. Step one, create a folder for that data. Step two, set the resource location restriction on that folder to allow only EU locations. Step three, a developer tries to create a bucket in a US location. The request is denied, so the bucket never exists. Step four, the developer creates it in an EU location, which succeeds.

Common mistake: assuming that a multi-region named US, or a global service, keeps data in one country. Check the actual location of each resource and each service, including backups and logs.

Consequence: moving data after the fact means copying it across a boundary, which can break compliance records and take days. Prevention is far cheaper than cleanup.

questions.prompt: A health startup in Canada keeps patient records in a folder called ca-patients. Its resource location restriction allows only Canadian locations. The team works through these steps: (1) create a project inside ca-patients for the records database; (2) the database is created in northamerica-northeast1 (Montreal) and the request succeeds; (3) [MISSING STEP: the team checks the location of the nightly backup bucket and the audit log storage, which are separate resources, and confirms each is also in a Canadian location]; (4) the team records the locations in its compliance file. What does the missing step 3 need to accomplish?
choices: Set the location restriction to allow every region in North America so that backups have more room.
Create a second folder for the backups, since the restriction only applies to the project that holds the database.
Confirm that the backup bucket and audit log storage are also in an allowed Canadian location, because each resource's location is decided separately.
Move the patient database to a multi-region so that the data is copied automatically to a second site.
questions.why: Each resource, including backups and logs, has its own storage location, so the team must verify each one stays inside the allowed boundary.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what decides where a Cloud Storage bucket's data at rest is stored in Google Cloud?
choices: The region of the developer's laptop used to run the create command.
The service account that the application uses to read the bucket later.
The location chosen when the bucket is created, which is a decision made before any data arrives.
The name of the bucket, since names containing a country code are placed there.
questions.why: Storage location is fixed by the location picked at creation time, so it is a decision taken before data is stored.

questions.prompt: A Japanese company sets a resource location restriction on its folder that allows only asia-northeast1 (Tokyo). A developer in a project under that folder tries to create a bucket in asia-northeast2 (Osaka). What happens?
choices: The bucket is created in Tokyo instead, and the request is rewritten automatically.
The request is blocked at creation, so the bucket never exists, because Osaka is not on the allowed list.
The bucket is created, because Osaka is inside Japan and so matches the country.
The bucket is created, and a report later flags it for review.
questions.why: The restriction lists the only permitted locations and blocks creation anywhere else, and Osaka is not listed even though it is in the same country.

questions.prompt: A team stores EU customer records in a bucket located in an EU region. Their nightly backup job writes copies to a bucket in us-central1. Which statement best describes the problem?
choices: There is no problem, because the primary data is in the EU and backups are a separate concern.
The problem is only cost, since cross-region storage is slightly more expensive.
The backups are copies of the data stored outside the EU boundary, so the residency promise is broken even though the primary data is compliant.
The problem is that the bucket name does not include the word EU, so the restriction cannot apply to it.
questions.why: Backups are data at rest too, so a copy in us-central1 sits outside the required boundary and breaks the residency requirement.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make sure a new project stores data only in one approved country, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would create the project under a folder for that regulated data, then set the resource location restriction on that folder so only the approved regions are allowed. Every new resource created under it is checked against that list, so a wrong location fails at creation time. The limit is that the policy only controls where resources are created, not every place data can flow. Services with global scope, backups, logs, and copies made by other teams can still sit outside the boundary, so I would also check the location of each service we use and review exports to other projects. For stricter regimes I would consider Assured Workloads, which bundles location and compliance controls, but it adds setup constraints and narrows which services are available. Residency is a promise we have to verify, not just configure.
rubricPoints: Applies a location restriction at the folder or organization level so new resources are checked automatically
Explains that the policy controls where resources are created, not every data flow
Names a gap such as global services, backups, logs or exports
Notes that stricter regimes may need Assured Workloads with narrower service choices

suggested.rationale: A scenario about where a regulated workload may be placed is best reasoned through, and no current mission or planned engine covers location policy directly.

lessons.plain: Infrastructure as code means describing the cloud resources you want, such as projects, networks, and clusters, in text files instead of clicking through a console. Those files live in version control, so changes can be reviewed, repeated, and reversed. The tools in this lesson differ in where they run, how they remember what already exists, and what kind of thing they manage. Choosing one is less about which tool is best and more about which one fits the layer you are working on: the base of an organization, a Kubernetes application, or a cluster that must keep matching a repository.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team keeps a text file describing a network and a database, and someone edits it. Without looking anything up, what do you think a tool must remember in order to change only what differs, rather than rebuilding everything, and where might it keep that memory?
lessons.teach:
Infrastructure as code is the practice of describing wanted infrastructure in files so a tool can create, change, or remove real resources to match them. The key idea is declarative: you state the end result, not the steps, and the tool works out the difference between that description and what currently exists.

Terraform is a general tool that reads configuration written in its own language and keeps a state file, a record that maps each configuration item to the real resource it created. Infrastructure Manager is Google Cloud's managed service that runs Terraform configurations for you, keeping execution and state inside the cloud instead of on your laptop. Cloud Foundation Toolkit is a set of reusable, tested modules and blueprints that encode Google's recommended layouts for folders, projects, and similar structures; you usually consume it through Terraform. Config Connector is an add-on for a Kubernetes cluster that lets cloud resources be declared as Kubernetes objects, with a controller continuously reconciling them toward that declared state. GitOps is a workflow rather than a single tool: Git holds the desired state, and an agent makes the live system match it, so changes arrive as merged commits. Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes applications. A chart is a templated bundle of manifests, and a release is one installed instance of that chart with its own revision history.

Worked example: a team needs a new project with a network. They write both in Terraform, run a plan that lists what will be created, then apply it. The state file now records both resources. Later they add a subnet, and the next plan shows one addition and no recreation.

Common mistake: editing a resource by hand in the console. The next plan sees drift between the state and reality, and the tool may revert the change or fail.

In a running system, drift means the repository no longer describes production, so a later apply can silently undo a manual fix made during an incident.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain called Crumb and Co wants a Cloud Storage bucket for receipts and a Pub/Sub topic for order events, both declared in Terraform. The engineer writes the configuration, then runs a plan, which lists two resources to add. Next, the engineer takes the step that makes Terraform create those two resources, and the state file then records both. Which step did the engineer take?
choices: Apply the plan so Terraform creates the two resources
Wrap the configuration in a Helm chart before running anything
Delete the state file so the next run starts fresh
Create the resources by hand in the console, then rerun the plan
questions.why: A plan only lists the changes it would make, and applying the plan is what actually creates the resources and writes them into the state file.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes what a Terraform state file does?
choices: It maps each configuration item to the real resource that Terraform created for it
It stores a copy of the cloud billing export for each project
It is a backup of the Git repository's commit history
It holds the container images that a Helm release runs in the cluster
questions.why: The teaching text defines state as a record that maps each configuration item to the real resource it created, which is what lets later plans compare the description with reality.

questions.prompt: A team declares a storage bucket as a Kubernetes object using Config Connector. Later, an engineer changes the bucket's label directly in the cloud console. What is the most likely result?
choices: Nothing happens, because Config Connector only reads the object once at deployment time
The controller ignores console edits because Kubernetes objects cannot be changed outside the cluster
The label change is kept and the cluster automatically commits it to Git
The controller works back toward the declared object and will normally revert the label
questions.why: Config Connector runs a controller that continuously reconciles the live resource toward the declared Kubernetes object, so an out-of-band change is normally reverted.

questions.prompt: A team installs the same Helm chart twice in one cluster, using two different release names. How many releases exist, and how is their history kept?
choices: Zero releases, because a chart is a template and is never installed
One release, with both sets of revisions merged into a single history
One release, because a chart can only be installed once per cluster
Two releases, each with its own revision history
questions.why: A release is one installed instance of a chart with its own revision history, so each separate installation counts as its own release.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks which tool to use for a new organization's base layer versus the Kubernetes applications. In your own words, explain how you would choose between Terraform, Config Connector, and Helm, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: For the base layer, I would use Terraform, or Infrastructure Manager if we want Google to run the execution and hold the state. Projects, folders, IAM, and networks exist before any cluster does, and Terraform lets us review a plan before anything changes. Helm fits the application layer, since it packages workloads for a cluster rather than managing the organization itself. Config Connector is appealing if the team already works in Kubernetes and wants cloud resources managed the same way as other objects. Its tradeoff is that the cluster becomes a dependency: if that cluster is unhealthy, management of the resources it controls can stall, so I would not start the foundation there. Whichever tool we choose, we should keep one source of state for each resource, because two tools managing the same thing will fight and cause drift.
rubricPoints: Matches the layer (organization base, application, or cluster state) to the right tool
Explains that Terraform or Infrastructure Manager uses a plan and state for cloud resources
States a concrete limit of Config Connector, such as its dependence on cluster health
Notes that one resource should have only one owning tool to avoid drift

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers choosing infrastructure-as-code tooling, so explaining the layer-to-tool choice and its tradeoffs is the core skill.

lessons.plain: Making infrastructure changes the recommended way means treating the setup of your cloud resources, such as networks, servers, databases and permissions, like software. Instead of clicking through a console and hoping for the best, you write the desired setup in files, store those files in version control so every change has a history, have a second person review the change, preview exactly what would be altered, and then apply it through an automated path. Google publishes blueprints, which are tested starting templates for common layouts, so you adapt a proven design rather than inventing one from scratch. The goal is changes that are repeatable, reviewable and easy to undo.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a colleague changes a firewall rule directly in the cloud console at 4pm on a Friday and tells nobody. What is the first problem you would worry about, and what would you change about how that change was made?
lessons.teach:
Infrastructure as code means describing cloud resources, such as networks, virtual machines, storage and access permissions, in text files instead of creating them by hand. Those files live in a version control system, a tool that records every edit, who made it and when, so any change can be compared or reverted. The recommended practice rests on a few habits. Each change is proposed as a merge request, a request to combine a branch of edits into the main copy, and another engineer reviews it before it is accepted. Before anything is applied, the tooling produces a plan, a preview listing exactly which resources will be created, changed or deleted. Changes are applied by an automated pipeline, a scripted sequence of steps that runs the same way every time, rather than from one person's laptop. Environments such as development, staging and production are kept separate, and a change is proven in a lower environment first.

A blueprint is a tested starting template that encodes a known good layout, for example a folder structure, a baseline network and a set of security guardrails. You adopt it and adjust parameters for your organization rather than designing every piece yourself.

Worked example: a team needs a new private subnet for a database. Step one, add the subnet to the network definition on a branch. Step two, open a merge request; the reviewer reads the plan, which shows one subnet added and nothing deleted. Step three, the pipeline applies that plan to staging. Step four, after checks pass, the same reviewed change is promoted to production.

Common mistake: editing production by hand in the console. The next pipeline run either reverts the manual fix or fails, because the recorded state no longer matches reality. That mismatch is called drift.

Consequence: a running service can go down when an untracked change is silently overwritten by an automated run. Reviewed, previewed and staged changes are what make infrastructure safe to change.

questions.prompt: A retail company's platform team wants a read-only service account for a nightly reporting job. The steps are listed below, but one is missing. Step 1: the engineer edits the account definition on a new branch. Step 2: the engineer opens a merge request. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: after checks pass, the reviewed change is promoted to production. Which option fills Step 3?
choices: A reviewer reads the plan and confirms it shows one account added and nothing deleted, before the change is approved.
The pipeline is skipped because the change is small.
The engineer deletes the old reporting account so the plan is smaller.
The engineer applies the change directly to production from a laptop.
questions.why: The plan is the preview of exactly what will be created, changed or deleted, and a reviewer checks it before approval, so it belongs between the merge request and the promotion.

questions.prompt: In the sense used in this course, what is drift?
choices: A merge request that a reviewer rejected.
A gap between the recorded state of infrastructure and what actually exists in the cloud.
A slow rise in cloud bills caused by idle virtual machines.
A blueprint's folder layout changing over time.
questions.why: Drift is the mismatch that appears when the recorded state no longer matches reality, typically after someone changes a resource by hand.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's database subnet is defined in its version-controlled files. An engineer changes the subnet's address range by hand in the console and does not touch the files. A pipeline run is scheduled for tonight. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: The version control system automatically merges the console change into the files.
The run reverts the manual change or fails, because the recorded state no longer matches reality.
The run reports success and keeps the manual change because the console is the source of truth.
The reviewer is notified and the change is approved retroactively.
questions.why: Automated runs apply the recorded definitions, so an untracked console edit is either overwritten or causes a mismatch that stops the run.

questions.prompt: A small team of four engineers is setting up a new organization and does not have time to design the folder structure and baseline network from scratch. Which approach matches the recommended practice?
choices: Adopt a tested blueprint, then adjust its parameters for their organization.
Copy a colleague's production project and keep its live resource IDs.
Skip the security guardrails until after the first production release.
Design every folder and network piece from scratch so nothing is inherited.
questions.why: A blueprint is a tested starting template with a known good layout, so adopting it and adjusting parameters is the recommended shortcut over designing everything yourself.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only ever changed cloud resources in the console why we make infrastructure changes through reviewed code and a plan, and name one real limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: We describe our cloud resources in files kept in version control, so every change is written down, reviewed by a second person and can be reverted. Before anything is applied, the tool produces a plan showing what will be created, changed or deleted, so a reviewer can catch a mistake such as an accidental deletion of a database. An automated pipeline applies the reviewed change, and we move it from staging to production rather than typing into the console. The tradeoff is speed: a small fix now needs a branch, a review and a pipeline run, and the code can drift from reality if someone still edits by hand. So we also restrict console write access in production and check for drift regularly.
rubricPoints: Infrastructure is described in version-controlled files so changes are recorded and reversible
A plan previews creates, changes and deletes before anything is applied, and a reviewer checks it
An automated pipeline applies changes and promotes them through staging before production
A real tradeoff is added friction or slower small fixes, and manual edits cause drift

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style change scenario, such as a manual production edit or a surprising plan, adds the most beyond reading the definitions.

lessons.plain: Automating infrastructure tasks with scripting means writing short programs that do the repetitive work of building and checking cloud resources for you, such as creating storage buckets, listing machines, or switching off old resources at night. Instead of clicking through a web console a hundred times, you write the steps once and run them the same way every time. Python and Go are two common languages for this. Python is quick to write and read, while Go produces a single compiled program that is easy to hand to other machines. The real skill is writing scripts that are safe to run more than once.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a script creates 20 test servers and crashes after the 12th one. If you run the same script again from the top, what would you want to happen to the 12 servers already created, and why?
lessons.teach:
A script is a plain text file of instructions that an interpreter runs from top to bottom. Automating infrastructure means letting a script call a cloud provider's API, the programming interface that lets software create, read, change and delete resources. Most scripts reach that API through a client library, a package that wraps the raw calls in ordinary functions for your language. Idempotent means running the same operation again leaves the system in the same final state, with no duplicates and no surprises. A dry run is a mode where the script reports what it would change without changing anything.

This works because cloud resources have a current state. A well-written script reads that state, compares it with the state you want, and makes only the difference. Worked example: a script must give every virtual machine in a project an owner label. Step 1, list all machines. Step 2, for each machine, check whether the owner label exists. Step 3, if it is missing, add it and count the change. Step 4, if an API call fails, log the error, remember that a failure happened, and move on to the next machine. Step 5, print a summary and exit with a nonzero code if anything failed, so whatever called the script knows. Run it a second time and the summary shows zero changes, which shows the script is idempotent.

Common mistake: treating a script as finished because it ran without a visible error. Scripts that ignore failed calls, or that add things without checking whether they already exist, leave half-finished work that looks like success.

Consequence: when a scheduled job runs such a script, a non-idempotent version can create duplicate resources every night, and a script that swallows errors lets the job show green while the environment quietly drifts. Choose Python for quick, readable glue and reporting, and Go when you want a single compiled binary with predictable concurrency and explicit error values. Either language does the job well when the script checks state, supports dry runs and reports failures honestly.

questions.prompt: A team runs a nightly script that makes sure every Cloud Storage bucket in their staging folder has object versioning turned on. The script works like this. Step 1: list all buckets in the folder. Step 2: for each bucket, read whether versioning is already on. Step 3: if it is off, turn it on and count the change. Step 4 is missing from the design. Step 5: print a summary and exit with a nonzero code if any bucket could not be updated. Which Step 4 fits the design?
choices: Stop the whole run at the first bucket that fails and print nothing
Log the failed bucket, remember that a failure happened, and move on to the next bucket
Retry the same bucket without limit until the call succeeds
Turn versioning on for every bucket in the organization before reading any state
questions.why: Step 5 depends on the script remembering failures and continuing, so Step 4 must log the failed bucket, record that a failure occurred, and move on to the next one.

questions.prompt: A script has a dry-run mode and is run against 40 Compute Engine disks. What should a dry run do?
choices: Skip all API calls and exit with code zero without reading any state
Print only the disk names and nothing about what would change
Report the changes it would make without making any of them
Apply every change and print a log of what it changed afterward
questions.why: A dry run reads the current state and reports the changes it would make, but it changes nothing in the environment.

questions.prompt: A script creates one Cloud Storage bucket for each of six teams, and the schedule runs it twice in one day. Which design keeps the second run from creating duplicate buckets?
choices: Before creating each bucket, check whether a bucket with that name already exists, and create it only if missing
Give each bucket a random suffix so that names never collide and the script never has to check anything
Call the create function six times per run so that at least one call is guaranteed to succeed
Always call the create function, then delete any duplicates once a week in a separate cleanup job
questions.why: Checking existing state before each create makes the operation idempotent, so repeated runs end in the same state with no duplicates.

questions.prompt: A script that snapshots VM disks hits a permission error on one disk. It logs nothing, keeps going, and exits with code zero. What is the main risk?
choices: The snapshots will be created twice on the next run
The script will refuse to start until the permission is fixed
The script will run slower because it continues past the error
The job shows green while some snapshots are missing and nobody is told
questions.why: Swallowing the error and exiting with success hides the missing snapshots, so the environment drifts while the job appears to pass.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants to replace a manual checklist with a Python script that deletes unused disks every night. Explain the three things the script must do to be safe to run unattended, and name one limit or tradeoff of scripting this instead of using a managed tool.
lessons.modelAnswer: First, the script should be idempotent: it checks each disk's state before acting, so a second run deletes nothing new and does not fail on disks already gone. Second, it should support a dry run that lists what it would delete, so a person can review the list before any real deletion. Third, it should handle errors honestly: if one API call fails, it logs that failure, keeps going safely, and exits with a nonzero code so the nightly job is marked as failed rather than green. The tradeoff is ownership. A script we wrote is our code to maintain, test and secure, and when the cloud API changes or a permission is missing, we are the ones who debug it, whereas a managed tool carries that maintenance burden for us, though it may offer less control.
rubricPoints: Idempotency: checks current state so reruns are safe
Dry run or review step before destructive actions
Errors are logged and reflected in the exit code
Names a real tradeoff such as maintenance ownership or less control than a managed tool

suggested.rationale: Hardening a config loader with error handling and tests practises the safe, checkable scripting this objective depends on.

lessons.plain: Continuous integration means that every time someone changes the code, an automated system builds it and runs its tests, so problems show up within minutes instead of weeks later. Google Cloud Build is a managed service that does this work. You describe the steps in a file kept alongside your code, and the service runs each step in a fresh container whenever a trigger fires, such as a change landing on a branch. Think of it as an assembly line that starts itself each time a part changes.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team merges a change that passes tests on one developer's laptop, but nobody runs the tests on a shared machine before the change is deployed. What risks does this create, and what would an automatic build on every merge change about when the team finds out about a problem?
lessons.teach:
Continuous integration (CI) is the practice of merging code changes into a shared branch often and having an automated pipeline build and test each change right away. A pipeline is an ordered series of steps that run on each change. In Cloud Build, a build is one run of that pipeline. Each step runs inside its own container, which is a packaged environment holding the tools that step needs. A trigger is a rule that starts a build automatically, for example when a commit lands on the main branch. A commit is a saved snapshot of code changes, and a branch is a named line of commits.

Why it works: every build starts from a clean environment, so the result depends on the code and its declared inputs rather than on whatever happens to be installed on one person's machine. Steps share a workspace, a common folder, so a compile step can hand its output to a packaging step. Successful builds can push their artifacts, such as container images, to a registry where deployment tools pick them up later.

Worked example. A change is merged to main. First, the trigger fires and the service creates a fresh build. Second, step one runs the unit tests in a language-runtime container. If that step fails, the build stops and later steps are skipped. Third, step two builds a container image into the workspace. Fourth, step three pushes that image to the registry, tagged with the commit identifier. The build runs as a service account, an identity that decides what the build may touch, so it should hold only the roles those steps need.

Common mistake: giving the build's service account broad project-wide owner rights so that builds never fail on permissions. This turns any compromised dependency into control of the whole project.

Consequence: if the test step is marked optional or is allowed to fail silently, a broken change still produces an image and gets deployed, so the team learns about the defect in production instead of in the pipeline. A build pipeline is only as trustworthy as its gating steps and its least-privilege identity.

questions.prompt: A payments team has a Cloud Build pipeline for its ledger-sync service. A trigger starts a fresh build when a commit lands on the release branch. Step one builds the container image into the shared workspace, a common folder all steps can read and write. Step two pushes the image to the registry, tagged with the commit identifier. Step three runs the integration tests against the pushed image. The team wants broken changes to never reach the registry. The missing step is one that runs the unit tests between the image build and the push, and stops the whole build if those tests fail. Given that missing step, what does the corrected pipeline do when a commit breaks a unit test?
choices: The unit test step fails, the build stops, and later steps including the push are skipped, so no image reaches the registry.
The build skips the push and the integration tests, then reports success so the release branch stays green.
The image is pushed to the registry anyway, and the integration tests catch the bug later.
The build reruns the image build step in a new workspace until the unit tests happen to pass.
questions.why: A failing step stops the build and skips later steps, so placing the unit test before the push means a broken change never produces a pushed image.

questions.prompt: In Cloud Build, what is the container that each step runs in for?
choices: It stores the finished artifacts so that deployment tools can pull them later.
It is the rule that starts a build automatically when a commit lands on a branch.
It is the identity that decides which projects the build is allowed to change.
It holds the packaged tools that one step needs, so the step runs in its own self-contained environment.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a step's container as a packaged environment holding the tools that step needs, with each step getting its own.

questions.prompt: A team marks its lint step as optional in a build pipeline. A developer merges a change that fails the lint check, and the build still completes and deploys. What is the most direct consequence of this setup?
choices: Cloud Build retries the lint step automatically until the change passes it.
The broken change still produces an image and can be deployed, so the defect is found in production rather than in the pipeline.
The workspace is wiped and the build restarts from the registry copy of the previous image.
The trigger disables itself so no further builds can start on that branch.
questions.why: The teaching text says a step allowed to fail silently lets a broken change still produce an image and get deployed, so the defect surfaces in production.

questions.prompt: A build's service account needs to read source code and push container images to one registry, and nothing else. Which role assignment best follows the least-privilege principle described for Cloud Build?
choices: Only the roles needed to read the source and push images to that one registry.
Project Owner on the project, so that no build fails on a permissions error.
Editor on every project in the organization, so builds can reach any shared resource.
The same identity used by the most senior engineer on the team, for consistency.
questions.why: The teaching text says the build's service account should hold only the roles its steps need, and broad owner rights turn any compromised dependency into control of the whole project.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Cloud Build does in a CI pipeline, and name one limit or tradeoff of running builds in a managed service that uses a shared build identity.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cloud Build is a managed service that runs our build pipeline on every change. The steps live in a config file with the code, each step runs in its own container with the tools it needs, and a trigger starts a run when a commit lands on the branch. If a step fails, the build stops, so a broken change never reaches the registry. The tradeoff is that we do not control the build machines directly, so anything a build needs has to be declared in its steps or granted to its service account. That account is a real risk: if we give it wide project rights just to avoid permission errors, a compromised dependency inherits those rights. So we grant only the roles each step needs and review them whenever pipelines change. Builds are also short-lived, so if we want to audit them later, we have to keep their logs and artifacts on purpose.
rubricPoints: Describes CI as automatically building and testing every change when a commit or merge triggers a run.
Explains that steps run as containers, share a workspace, and stop the build when one fails.
Identifies the build service account as the identity that sets what the build can access, and the risk of over-broad rights.
States a tradeoff of managed, short-lived build environments, such as limited direct control or the need to keep logs and artifacts.

suggested.rationale: Repairing a broken CI pipeline makes the learner read build steps, failure gates and build permissions, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: Continuous delivery means taking a tested build of your software and moving it through a fixed sequence of environments toward real users, in a controlled and repeatable way. Google Cloud's managed service for this is called Cloud Deploy. You describe the path, for example test, then staging, then production. You package one version as a release and promote that release one step at a time, with optional approvals along the way. Two helper tools shape what gets deployed. Kustomize lets you keep one shared set of Kubernetes configuration files and layer small changes on top for each environment. Skaffold automates the build and deploy loop that developers run on their own machines.
lessons.guessPrompt: If the same application runs in test, staging and production, and production needs 5 copies of the app while test needs only 1, would you copy the whole set of deployment files three times, or keep one shared set and record only the differences? Why?
lessons.teach:
A delivery pipeline is the ordered path a release travels. In Cloud Deploy, each stage is called a target, and a target points at a real environment such as a Kubernetes cluster or a Cloud Run service. A release is an immutable snapshot of one version: it fixes the container image and the fully rendered configuration. Creating a release does not change anything live. A rollout is the act of applying a release to a target. Promotion is moving a release from one target to the next, and an approval is an optional human sign-off required before that move.

Kustomize is a tool for customizing plain Kubernetes manifests without templates. You keep a base folder with the common configuration, then write an overlay for each environment that patches only what differs, such as the replica count or the image tag. Skaffold is a developer-side tool that builds images and deploys them on each code change. Cloud Deploy reads a Skaffold configuration to know how to build and render what it will deploy.

Worked example. The base deployment asks for 1 replica. The production overlay changes that to 5. First, a build produces image sha256 abc. Second, Cloud Deploy creates release r-42 by rendering the base plus the staging overlay. Third, the rollout to the test target succeeds. Fourth, promotion to production waits for approval, then renders the production overlay with 5 replicas and applies it. If production misbehaves, rolling back redeploys an earlier good release rather than hand-editing the cluster.
