Common mistake: running kubectl edit against the live cluster during an incident. The running state then matches no release, so the next promotion overwrites the fix or the rollback target is wrong.

In a running system this drift makes rollbacks unreliable exactly when you need them most, so every change must go through a release.

questions.prompt: A team called Ledgerline runs an orders service. Its base Kubernetes deployment asks for 2 replicas, and its dev overlay keeps that at 2. The steps so far are: (1) a build produces image sha256 q9z; (2) Cloud Deploy creates release r-19 by rendering the base plus the dev overlay; (3) the rollout of r-19 to the dev target succeeds. Then the team wants the orders service on the prod target, which should run 6 replicas. The step that is missing from this sequence sits between step 3 and prod being updated. Which step fills that gap?
choices: Rebuild the image as a new tag before promotion so that prod gets a different image than dev.
Create a new release r-20 directly from the dev overlay and roll it out to prod, skipping promotion.
Promote release r-19 from dev to prod after any required approval is given, so Cloud Deploy renders the prod overlay with 6 replicas and applies it.
Edit the prod cluster by hand with kubectl to set the replica count to 6, then leave the release history as it is.
questions.why: Promotion is the act of moving an existing release from one target to the next, with approval if required, and it is the step where the prod overlay is rendered and applied, so it is the step that is missing.

questions.prompt: In Cloud Deploy, what is a release?
choices: A live copy of a running environment that is updated each time someone edits its configuration.
A human sign-off that must be recorded before any change can reach a later stage.
A named stage such as staging or prod that points at a Kubernetes cluster or Cloud Run service.
An immutable snapshot that fixes one container image and the fully rendered configuration, and that changes nothing live when it is created.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a release as an immutable snapshot of one version with the image and rendered configuration fixed, and says creating it does not change anything live.

questions.prompt: A payments team has a live target. After a bad release, an engineer uses kubectl edit on the live cluster to lower a memory limit and says the problem is fixed. The next day a promotion runs from the current release. What is the most likely result?
choices: The memory limit is restored to the value in the release, because the live state no longer matched any release and the promotion overwrites it.
The memory limit stays lowered because Cloud Deploy keeps every manual edit in its release history.
The memory limit is lowered on every target automatically, since edits made to one cluster propagate to all targets.
The promotion fails with an error that asks the engineer to merge the edit into the base folder.
questions.why: A hand edit makes the live state match no release, and the next promotion applies the release's rendered configuration, which overwrites the edit and makes rollbacks unreliable.

questions.prompt: A search team has a Kustomize base with 3 replicas and a canary overlay that is meant to test a new image tag only. What should the canary overlay contain?
choices: A template with placeholder values that a build step fills in at render time.
The replica count and the image tag together, so the canary always matches production size.
A full copy of the base manifests with the image tag changed, so that the overlay stands alone.
A patch that changes only the image tag, letting every other setting come from the base.
questions.why: Kustomize overlays patch only what differs from the base, so a canary overlay that changes just the image tag keeps the base's other settings.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we need a release object at all when we already have a Git commit. Explain what Cloud Deploy adds on top of the commit, and name one limit or tradeoff of promoting releases through approval gates.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Git commit records source code, but it does not say what was actually deployed or where. A Cloud Deploy release is a fixed snapshot that pairs one built image with the fully rendered configuration for that version, so the same artifact can be promoted from target to target without being rebuilt. That makes rollback well defined: we redeploy an earlier release instead of guessing which commit was live. The tradeoff is speed. Each approval gate adds waiting time, and if approvers are slow, a real fix can sit in staging while users are affected. We accept that delay for production, but we keep gates off low-risk targets so the pipeline still moves quickly.
rubricPoints: A release is an immutable snapshot tying an image to rendered configuration, separate from the Git commit
Promotion moves the same release through targets without rebuilding it
Rollback redeploys a known earlier release, which makes it predictable
Approval gates add delay, so they are a tradeoff to place deliberately

suggested.rationale: Choosing which target gets an approval gate and how to roll back is an exam-style situation that benefits from reasoning through a scenario.

lessons.plain: Think of a warehouse where your team keeps the finished, packaged versions of its software before they go out to customers. Each packaged item is an artifact: a container image, a library package, or a build output. Artifact Registry is Google Cloud's managed warehouse for these items, so you do not run your own storage server. You create a repository for one kind of package, choose where it physically lives, and decide who may read or write to it. The build pipeline pushes finished builds in, and servers pull them out. Configuring it means making those choices on purpose, because they decide what you can trust to run and how quickly it arrives.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your build pipeline produces version 2.4.1 of a service and stores it. A week later, someone rebuilds from a different branch and reuses the label 2.4.1. Which would you trust more for a rollback: the label, or something that identifies the exact bytes? Why?
lessons.teach:
A repository is a named container inside Artifact Registry that holds packages of one format, such as container images, Python or Node libraries, or Maven packages. The format is fixed when you create the repository. The location is the Google Cloud region or multi-region where the bytes are stored. That choice affects how far the pulling machines are from the storage, where your data physically sits for residency rules, and what a regional outage can take with it. A mode sets the repository's role. A standard repository stores your own artifacts. A remote repository is a cached proxy in front of an outside public registry. A virtual repository presents several repositories behind one address, so clients need only one setting. Access is controlled with identity and access management roles, usually a reader role for deployers, a writer role for the build pipeline, and an admin role for a few people who run the repository. Cleanup policies delete old versions on rules you set, so storage cost does not grow forever.

Why it works: a pipeline builds once, pushes one artifact, and every later stage pulls that same artifact. An image's digest is a fingerprint of its exact contents, so deploying by digest guarantees that the bytes you tested are the bytes running.

Worked example: CI builds the orders service and pushes it to a standard Docker repository named orders in europe-west1. The push reports a digest, a long hexadecimal fingerprint. The tag 2.4.1 is attached as a readable label. The deploy stage references the image by digest, not by tag. A week later someone rebuilds from a branch and moves the tag 2.4.1 onto new contents. The deployment is unaffected, because it names the digest.

Common mistake: deploying 'latest' or any reusable tag. When a tag is moved, the rollback you thought pointed to the last good release now points to something untested, and the incident runs longer.

Consequence: in a running system, drifting tags make rollbacks unreliable and incident timelines hard to reconstruct. Treat tags as labels and digests as identity, and give the pipeline's identity only the writer role it needs.

questions.prompt: A payments team in asia-northeast1 builds a container image called ledger and pushes it to a standard Docker repository named ledger-images. Step 1 is the build. Step 2 is the push, which returns the digest sha256:9c1f7a0e and lets the team attach the readable tag 3.0.2. Step 3 is the deploy stage, and its notes are missing a line. Which completion correctly fills in step 3?
choices: rebuilds the image from the source branch so the deployed contents match the latest commit
copies the image into a second repository in another region before deploying, for extra safety
reads the tag 3.0.2 and deploys whatever the tag currently points to, since tags are the readable names
references the image by its digest, so the deployed bytes are exactly the bytes that were tested
questions.why: Deploying by digest ties the rollout to the fingerprint of the exact tested contents, whereas a tag such as 3.0.2 can be moved to point at different bytes later.

questions.prompt: Which repository mode should a team choose if they want their clients to fetch public open-source packages through their own cache, rather than reaching the internet every time?
choices: virtual, because it combines several repositories behind one address
standard, because it stores the team's own artifacts
cleanup policy, because it deletes old cached versions on a schedule
remote, because it is a cached proxy in front of an outside public registry
questions.why: A remote repository is defined as a cached proxy in front of an outside public registry, which is exactly the caching role described.

questions.prompt: A platform team keeps a shared internal Python library repository and a separate repository for one product team. They want developers to configure only one package index address. Which mode fits this need?
choices: virtual, because it presents several repositories behind one address so clients need only one setting
standard, because it holds the library packages that the developers will install
remote, because it proxies the packages from the outside world
a reader role on each repository, because that gives developers one address
questions.why: A virtual repository presents several repositories behind one address, which is the stated purpose that solves the one-setting problem.

questions.prompt: A build pipeline only needs to push new images to a repository, but it has been granted the admin role on that repository. What is the problem, and what should change?
choices: It is acceptable as long as cleanup policies are turned off, so the pipeline can keep admin
It grants more rights than a push needs, so the pipeline should be given only the writer role
It lets the pipeline manage repository access, so the deployers should be given the admin role instead
Nothing is wrong, because admin and writer are the same set of permissions
questions.why: The writer role matches what a build pipeline needs, and giving it admin exceeds least privilege, which is the reasoning behind the access guidance.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an Artifact Registry repository is and how you would set one up for a team that ships container images to two regions. Name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: A repository is a named store in Artifact Registry for one package format, such as container images. For a team shipping to two regions, I would create one standard repository per format, located in the region closest to the build pipeline, and let the deploy stages in both regions pull from it. The build pushes each image once, and deployments reference the image by its digest rather than a tag, so both regions run identical bytes. Access is split by identity: the pipeline gets writer, the deployers get reader, and only a couple of people get admin. A cleanup policy keeps storage bounded. The tradeoff is that a single repository in one location means a second region pays cross-region pull latency and depends on that location being available. If that matters, I would accept the extra cost of a multi-region location or replicate the image, and say so in the design notes.
rubricPoints: A repository holds one package format and is created in a chosen location
Access is granted by role to identities, with writers separated from readers
Images are identified by digest, so deploys run the exact tested bytes
Tags are mutable labels and should not be the source of truth for deploys
Location choice trades latency, residency and regional availability against cost

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises repository setup, so reading the configuration concepts is the most direct route.

lessons.plain: Tooling for delivering software is the set of programs that store your work, test it, build it, and put it in front of users. Third-party tools are products from outside the cloud provider, such as Jenkins, Argo CD, Packer and kpt, and Git is the widely used system for storing code and its history. Choosing among them means asking which job each one does: keeping a history of changes, running build and test steps, building machine images, keeping a running system matched to a stored description, or packaging configuration. Most teams use several together. The real decision is where each tool fits and who is allowed to change what, not which one is best.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team stores application code in Git and wants every commit built and tested automatically. Would you choose a setup where a build server pushes changes into production using a stored key, or one where a controller inside the cluster pulls the desired state from Git? Which would you expect to be easier to audit, and why?
lessons.teach:
Git is a version control system: it records every change to files and who made it, and it lets you return to any earlier state. In delivery work it becomes the source of truth, meaning the place where the intended state of your software and infrastructure is written down. Jenkins is a continuous integration server. It runs a pipeline of build and test steps when something triggers it, such as a commit. It is a push tool: after the build, it sends changes out to the target using credentials it holds. Argo CD is a continuous delivery controller for Kubernetes clusters. It runs inside the cluster, watches a Git repository, pulls the desired state in, and continuously compares the live cluster with that state, correcting any drift. This pull model means no outside system needs cluster credentials. Packer builds machine images from a template file, so an image can be recreated the same way every time. kpt packages Kubernetes configuration as versioned bundles that can be fetched, edited and updated from an upstream source.

Worked example: a team builds a web service. A commit to Git triggers Jenkins, which runs unit tests and produces a container image. Jenkins then writes the new image tag into the configuration repository in Git. Argo CD notices that change and applies it to the cluster. If someone edits the live cluster by hand, Argo CD detects the difference and, with self-healing enabled, reverts it to the version in Git.

Common mistake: treating one tool as the whole pipeline, for example using Argo CD to run tests, or giving Jenkins standing admin rights over production. Consequence: a broad credential on a build server becomes a route into every environment it can reach. Keep deployment rights narrow, and let the cluster pull its own changes from a source that is reviewed and recorded.

questions.prompt: A retail data team runs a nightly reporting job on a Kubernetes cluster (a group of machines that run containers, managed as one system). Their setup works like this: (1) an engineer merges a change to the job's configuration file in a Git repository (a version control system that records every change); (2) Argo CD, a continuous delivery controller that runs inside that cluster, notices the new commit; (3) [missing step: ___]; (4) if someone later edits the job's live settings by hand, Argo CD detects the difference and restores the version stored in Git. Which action belongs in the blank at step 3?
choices: Argo CD runs the reporting job's unit tests on the new configuration before anything changes.
Jenkins connects to the cluster using a stored admin token and runs the apply command directly on the job.
An engineer copies the configuration file onto the cluster by hand so Argo CD has a local copy to read.
Argo CD pulls the new state from Git and applies the difference to the cluster.
questions.why: Argo CD's job is to compare the live cluster with the desired state in Git and apply the difference, which is the pull model the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: In delivery work, what is a 'source of truth'?
choices: The build history kept on the Jenkins server, because it records every run.
The template file on an engineer's laptop, because it defines the machine image.
The place where the intended state of software and infrastructure is written down, such as a version-controlled repository.
The live production cluster, because it shows exactly what is running right now.
questions.why: A source of truth is where intended state is recorded; the live cluster shows actual state, which may have drifted, so it is not the source.

questions.prompt: A fintech team gives its Jenkins build server a credential with full administrator rights over its production environment. What is the main risk of that setup?
choices: Argo CD will stop reconciling the cluster because two tools now hold deployment rights.
Git will lose track of which commit produced each build artifact.
If the build server is compromised, the attacker gains a route into every environment that credential can reach.
Jenkins will run its build and test steps more slowly because it has to check permissions each time.
questions.why: A broad credential on a build server becomes a path into every environment it reaches, so deployment rights should be kept narrow.

questions.prompt: A logistics company needs every release to start from the same base virtual machine image, and wants to be able to recreate that image exactly later. Which tool fits this need, and why?
choices: Argo CD, because it watches a Git repository and keeps the cluster matching it.
kpt, because it packages Kubernetes configuration as versioned bundles.
Packer, because it builds machine images from a template file so the same image can be recreated the same way each time.
Jenkins, because it runs the build and test steps that produce the image.
questions.why: Packer's purpose is building machine images from a template so they can be recreated identically, while Jenkins only triggers and runs pipelines and kpt and Argo CD handle Kubernetes configuration.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes using Jenkins to push every Kubernetes change straight into the production cluster, with a long-lived service account key stored in the job. Explain to them, in your own words, how a pull-based approach with Argo CD would differ, and name one limit or tradeoff of the pull approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: The push approach means Jenkins runs at the end of the build and uses a stored key to change production directly. That key is a long-lived secret on a build server, so anyone who compromises the server can reach production, and the cluster has no independent record of what it should look like. A pull approach keeps the desired state in Git and runs a controller inside the cluster, such as Argo CD, that fetches from Git and reconciles the live state to match. No external system needs cluster credentials, and drift is corrected automatically. The tradeoff is that the controller only manages what it has been pointed at, so teams must organize repositories and sync settings carefully, and anything outside its scope needs another path. Jenkins still has a role in building and testing, which the controller does not do.
rubricPoints: Explains that push tools hold credentials and send changes out from the build server, widening the attack surface
Explains that pull controllers such as Argo CD run inside the cluster, read desired state from Git, and correct drift
Names a real limit of the pull approach, such as scope limits or the need for careful repository and sync setup
Notes that build and test work still belongs in a CI tool like Jenkins, so the tools complement each other

suggested.rationale: Choosing between push and pull delivery tools is a judgement that is best shown by explaining the tradeoff back, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this tooling decision directly.

lessons.plain: Securing CI/CD tooling means protecting the automated line that builds, tests and ships your software. That line has real power: it can read source code, pull secrets, and change production. If an attacker or a careless setting gets into it, they can ship their own code under your name. So the job is to give each automated step only the access it needs, keep passwords out of the code, record who did what, and require checks before anything reaches production.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your pipeline needs a password to deploy to production. Where would you put it so that the fewest people and tools can ever read it, and why?
lessons.teach:
A CI/CD pipeline is the automated sequence that builds, tests and deploys software. Each step runs on a runner, which is the machine or service that executes it, and each step talks to cloud resources using an identity. In Google Cloud that identity is usually a service account, meaning an identity for a program rather than a person. Securing this tooling means controlling three things: which identity the pipeline uses, what that identity is allowed to do, and where its credentials are stored.

The core rule is least privilege: grant only the roles a step needs, on only the resources it touches. A secret is any value that proves identity, such as a password, API token or key file. Secrets belong in a dedicated secret store and should be read at run time, never written into source code or build logs. When the CI system runs outside Google Cloud, workload identity federation lets it trade its own short-lived token for temporary cloud credentials, so no long-lived key file has to exist.

Worked example: a pipeline runs on a commit to the main branch. Step 1, the build identity fetches the source and runs tests with no cloud permissions. Step 2, it builds an image and pushes it to a registry, using a write role on that one repository only. Step 3, a separate deploy identity, with rights only on the staging project, rolls the image out after an approval gate. Step 4, every action lands in the audit log, so you can trace which identity changed what.

Common mistake: giving the build identity the project owner role because that was the fastest way to make a failing step pass, or committing a key file to the repository. Either one lets anyone who can influence a build, including a malicious dependency, act with full power.

In a running system, a compromised pipeline is a production incident. The attacker does not need to break your servers when the deploy identity can already change them.

questions.prompt: A team at a freight company runs its CI on a self-hosted runner outside Google Cloud and publishes internal Python packages to one Artifact Registry repository named pkg-internal in the project freight-tools. They want the pipeline to be safe, so they design it in steps. Step 1: the lint job runs on the runner and needs no cloud access, so its identity gets no cloud roles. Step 2: the publish job uploads packages to pkg-internal, so its identity gets a write role on that one repository only, not on the whole project. Step 3: because the runner is outside Google Cloud, the runner trades its own short-lived token for temporary credentials through workload identity federation, so no key file is created. Step 4 is missing: the same pipeline must also roll the package out to the production project, freight-prod. Which choice completes step 4 in line with least privilege?
choices: Reuse the publish job's service account, since it already has write access in freight-tools and so will not need new roles.
Grant the deploy job the Owner role on freight-prod so that a failed rollout cannot block the release.
Create a separate deploy identity with rights only on freight-prod, and have the rollout run after an approval gate.
Store a long-lived JSON key for a deploy account in the repository so that the job can start without federation.
questions.why: Least privilege means the rollout gets its own identity limited to the production project it touches, with an approval gate in front of it, and the other three choices either share or widen privileges in ways the design rules out.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does the principle of least privilege mean for a CI/CD pipeline's service account?
choices: Service accounts get the broadest role available so that no step fails for lack of access.
Pipeline identities are kept as long-lived key files so that they never expire during a long release.
Every step shares one service account so that permissions are easy to review in one place.
Each pipeline step gets the smallest set of roles it needs, on only the resources it touches.
questions.why: Least privilege means granting only the roles and resource scope each step actually needs, which is exactly the first choice, while the others describe shared or excessive access.

questions.prompt: A build step fails with a permission denied error when it tries to push an image to one Artifact Registry repository. An engineer wants the fastest fix. Which change is the safest correct response?
choices: Add the build service account's key file to the repository so the step can authenticate on the next run.
Grant only the write role for that one repository to the build service account, then rerun the step.
Grant the build service account the Owner role on the whole organization so no future step fails for access reasons.
Grant the build service account the Editor role on the project that holds the repository.
questions.why: The narrow fix is to add the one missing role on the one resource the step touches, and the other choices broaden access far beyond what the step needs or put a secret in source code.

questions.prompt: A deployment job needs an API token to call an external service. Where should that token live so the pipeline stays secure?
choices: Printed to the build log at the start of the job so that engineers can check it when a deploy fails.
Written directly into the deployment script so every run has the same value without extra setup.
Kept in a dedicated secret store and read by the job at run time, never written into code or logs.
Stored in the repository as a comment next to the code that uses it, so reviewers can see it.
questions.why: A token is a secret, so it belongs in a dedicated secret store and should be read at run time, while the other three options expose it in code, logs, or repository history.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a CI/CD pipeline should run under its own least-privilege service account instead of a shared admin account, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing it that way.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each pipeline should have its own service account with only the roles it needs, so a compromise is contained to what that pipeline could already do. A shared admin account means one leaked credential covers everything, and the audit log cannot tell which automated job made a change. Separating build and deploy identities also means a test step never holds deploy rights. The tradeoff is operational effort: you have more identities to create, review and rotate, and granting exact roles takes iteration. Early runs often fail with permission errors until the role set is tuned, and teams sometimes widen the role just to get green builds again, which quietly brings back the risk. Narrow roles only stay narrow if someone reviews them.
rubricPoints: Each pipeline step runs under its own identity with only the roles it needs.
A shared admin account lets one compromise reach everything and hides who acted.
Audit logs attribute each action to a specific identity, which supports investigation.
Tradeoff: more identities to manage, and early permission failures while roles are tuned.

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner fix how a deploy authenticates without leaking the secret, which is the core of securing pipeline credentials.

lessons.plain: An ephemeral environment is a complete copy of part of a system that exists only for a short time. A team creates it on purpose, for example when a developer opens a change for review, runs tests against it, and then deletes it automatically once the work is merged or abandoned. Think of a meeting room you book for one afternoon and hand back at five, rather than a permanent office you keep paying for. The skill is making creation and deletion both cheap and repeatable, so nobody is left paying for forgotten copies.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team spins up a full test copy of their app for each code change and deletes it after review. Name two things that could go wrong if nobody ever deletes these copies, and one thing that could go wrong if each copy is filled with a snapshot of live customer data.
lessons.teach:
An ephemeral environment is a short-lived, self-contained copy of part of a system, created for a specific purpose such as testing one change, and destroyed when that purpose ends. Its defining property is that it is disposable. It is built from code, so it can be recreated the same way every time, and it is not treated as a pet that someone maintains by hand.

Why it works: when the description of an environment lives in version-controlled infrastructure-as-code (files that declare resources, such as Terraform or Google Cloud's Infrastructure Manager), creating one becomes a repeatable command rather than days of clicking in a console. Each environment is given a clear owner, a label recording why it exists, and an expiry time. A pipeline step or scheduled job then removes it when the expiry passes or the change closes.

Worked example: a developer opens pull request 412 against a positions service. Step 1: the pipeline creates a new Google Cloud project named for the pull request, applies the same infrastructure code used for staging, and labels the project with owner, purpose, and an expiry of 24 hours. Step 2: integration tests run against it. Step 3: the change is merged. Step 4: the pipeline deletes the project. Deleting a project shuts down its resources and billing, and Google Cloud keeps a deleted project recoverable for a limited window, so a mistake can still be undone.

Common mistake: seeding each environment with a copy of production data. That spreads customer data into many places with weak oversight and makes teardown riskier. Use synthetic or anonymised test data instead.

The consequence in a running system is that environments never torn down keep accruing compute and storage charges, hold quota that blocks other teams, and leave access grants pointing at people who have left. An unowned environment is an orphan, and orphans are how cloud bills surprise a team.

questions.prompt: A reporting team at a retail company is working on a branch that changes how sales totals are rounded. They use an ephemeral environment for it. Step 1: the pipeline creates a new project named for the branch and applies the same infrastructure code used for their staging environment. Step 2: the pipeline labels the project with an owner, a purpose, and an expiry of 48 hours. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: once the change is merged, the pipeline deletes the project. Which choice correctly fills step 3?
choices: Runs the rounding test suite against the project using synthetic sales data, then records the results.
Gives the project to the team lead to use as a permanent staging server.
Creates a second project with no labels so the first one can be kept for later.
Copies the live sales database into the project so the rounding test uses real totals.
questions.why: Step 3 is where the change is verified, and synthetic data tests the logic while keeping real customer records out of a short-lived environment.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines an ephemeral environment?
choices: A short-lived, self-contained copy of part of a system, built from code and destroyed when its purpose ends.
A shared sandbox that stays online indefinitely so any team can use it.
A production system with a backup copy kept in another region.
A staging server that a named engineer maintains by hand between releases.
questions.why: The teaching text defines an ephemeral environment as disposable, created for one purpose, built from code, and destroyed when that purpose ends.

questions.prompt: A team builds its test environments by clicking through the console, and nobody labels them with an owner or an expiry time. Months later, several environments are still running. Which consequence is the most direct result of this practice?
choices: Unowned environments keep accruing charges, hold quota other teams need, and may keep access grants for people who have left.
Google Cloud automatically merges unlabelled environments into production.
The environments run faster because they are isolated from shared traffic.
The pipeline blocks all future deployments until someone deletes the environments by hand.
questions.why: The teaching text lists accruing charges, blocked quota, and stale access grants as the consequences of environments that are never torn down and have no owner.

questions.prompt: A payments team needs a test environment for a new refund feature. Which data should they seed it with?
choices: A full copy of the production payments database, with customer names left in place for realism.
Whatever data the last environment used, carried over so the team does not have to create new data.
A copy of production with only the card numbers removed, since the rest is not sensitive.
Synthetic or anonymised test data, so no real customer records are spread into the environment.
questions.why: Synthetic or anonymised data avoids spreading customer data into many short-lived places, which the teaching text names as the common mistake to avoid.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what makes an environment ephemeral, how a pipeline should create and remove one, and name one limit or tradeoff of running many short-lived environments.
lessons.modelAnswer: An ephemeral environment is a short-lived copy of part of our system, made for one purpose such as testing a single pull request, and deleted when that purpose ends. The key is that it is built from the same infrastructure code every time, so it is repeatable rather than hand-made. The pipeline creates it, labels it with an owner and an expiry, runs the tests, and removes it on merge or when the expiry passes. The tradeoff is cost and time: each environment takes minutes to build, so frequent creation adds up, and an environment can drift from production if its code is not kept in step with the production code. We also cannot fill these environments with real customer data, so test data has to be synthetic, which means our tests are only as realistic as that data.
rubricPoints: Defines an ephemeral environment as short-lived, created for one purpose, and destroyed afterwards
Explains that repeatable infrastructure code is what makes creation and deletion reliable
Describes labelling with an owner and expiry so cleanup can be automated
Names a real tradeoff such as build time and cost, or drift from production, or limits on test data

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a scenario about who creates, labels and removes environments and what happens when cleanup fails adds more than reading alone, and no listed mission covers this objective directly.

lessons.plain: Teams usually run the same application in several places: a development copy for testing, a staging copy that mirrors production, and the real production system. The settings differ between these places, such as how many servers run, which database is called, and which features are switched on. Managing configuration and policy across environments means deciding where those differences live, keeping them written down, making sure each environment matches what was intended, and enforcing the rules that must hold everywhere automatically instead of relying on people to remember them.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team runs development, staging and production copies of the same app. Production forbids public IP addresses, but last week someone opened one in staging by hand. What would you check first, and what would you change so it cannot happen again?
lessons.teach:
Configuration is the set of values that differ between environments, such as server counts, endpoint addresses and feature switches. An environment is a separate copy of a system used at one stage, typically development, staging and production. Policy is a rule that limits what may be created or changed, such as forbidding public IP addresses or restricting which regions may be used. Drift is what happens when the live system no longer matches the written definition, usually because someone changed it by hand.

The approach works because it separates three things: the shared template, the small per-environment values, and the rules that must hold everywhere. The template is written once. Each environment gets a short values file. The build produces one artifact, such as a container image identified by a digest (a fingerprint of its exact contents), and the same artifact moves through development, then staging, then production. Only the values change. Policies are set high in the resource hierarchy so that every folder and project beneath inherits them, and the platform enforces them.

Worked example. A service sets replicas to 1 in development, 2 in staging and 6 in production. The repository holds one template and three values files. Step one: the pipeline builds the image once and records its digest. Step two: it deploys that digest to development with the development values. Step three: after tests pass, it deploys the same digest to staging. Step four: production receives the same digest with production values. Separately, an organization-level policy forbids public IP addresses, so when a staging engineer tries to add one, the platform refuses before it exists.

Common mistake: fixing production by hand in the console during an incident and never copying the fix back to the repository. The written state still says 6 replicas and the old setting, so the next automated deploy quietly reverts the fix, or the drift goes unnoticed for months.

In a running system this can mean an outage that returns the moment a routine release lands, or a security exposure that nobody tracks because the record says it is closed. Keep one source of truth, and treat any change that bypasses it as drift to be reversed or recorded.

questions.prompt: A payments team keeps one deployment template and three small values files: qa with 3 workers, pre-production with 5 workers, and production with 10 workers. A digest is a fingerprint of an image's exact contents. Their pipeline runs these steps. Step 1: build the container image once and record its digest. Step 2: deploy that digest to qa using the qa values file. Step 3: [MISSING]. Step 4: production runs that same digest with 10 workers, using the production values file. Which step fills the gap at Step 3?
choices: Rebuild the image from source for pre-production so it picks up the newest dependencies
Copy the qa values file into pre-production and change only the image tag
Set pre-production to 5 workers by editing the running service in the console
After qa tests pass, deploy the same digest to pre-production using the pre-production values file
questions.why: The same recorded digest must move forward through each environment with only that environment's values changed, so Step 3 is to deploy that digest to pre-production with its own values after qa tests pass.

questions.prompt: A team's production service has 4 replicas in its repository, but the live service runs 7 because an engineer scaled it by hand and never updated the files. Which term describes this gap between the written definition and the live system?
choices: Digest mismatch
Environment promotion
Policy inheritance
Drift
questions.why: Drift is the name for a live system that no longer matches its written definition, usually because someone changed it by hand.

questions.prompt: During a late-night incident, an engineer raises a production service from 6 replicas to 9 in the console to stop errors. The next morning a routine release runs from the repository, whose values file still says 6. What most likely happens?
choices: Production drops back to 6 replicas when the release applies the written values
Production keeps 9 replicas because the release only changes the image
Production stays at 9 and the repository is automatically updated to match
The release fails because the console change blocks deployments
questions.why: Automated deploys apply the written values, so the hand-made fix is quietly reverted unless it is copied back into the repository.

questions.prompt: An organization policy that forbids public IP addresses is set on a top-level folder. A team later creates a new project inside a sub-folder beneath that folder. An engineer in the new project tries to add a public IP address. What happens?
choices: It succeeds once the engineer adds a project-level exception
It is refused, because the policy is inherited by every folder and project beneath it
It succeeds but is logged as a warning only
It succeeds because new projects start with a clean policy
questions.why: Policies set high in the resource hierarchy are inherited by everything below and enforced by the platform, so the request is refused before the address exists.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate suggests keeping separate hand-edited config copies for development, staging and production, changed directly whenever needed. Explain to them why this is risky, what you would do instead, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Separate hand-edited copies are risky because they drift apart. Nobody can be sure which copy reflects what is actually running, and a fix made in production often never reaches the others, so the same bug returns later. I would keep one template for the application and a small values file per environment, so the only differences are the ones we chose on purpose. Each build becomes one immutable artifact that moves through development, staging and production unchanged, and rules such as forbidding public addresses are set as organization-level policy so they are enforced rather than remembered. The tradeoff is up-front effort: someone has to design the template and values, and the pipeline must be trusted as the only path to change. Emergency manual fixes are still possible, but they must be copied back into the repository straight away, or the next deploy will undo them.
rubricPoints: Hand-edited per-environment copies drift apart and make it unclear what is actually running.
One shared template plus small per-environment values keeps differences deliberate and visible.
The same tested artifact should be promoted through environments unchanged.
Policies set high in the hierarchy are inherited and enforced by the platform, not by memory.
A stated limit or tradeoff, such as upfront design effort or the need to back-port emergency manual fixes.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style scenario about where a given setting or rule should live across environments adds the most to this objective.

lessons.plain: When a company runs many Kubernetes clusters, perhaps one per region or per team, managing each one by hand becomes slow and error-prone. Fleet management means grouping those clusters into one logical collection so you can apply shared settings, security rules and configuration sync to all of them from a single place, while each cluster still runs its own workloads. Think of a fleet of delivery vans: every van drives itself, but a dispatcher sets the rules and checks on the group as a whole.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have twelve Kubernetes clusters across three regions and want every one of them to enforce the same security rule. Would you configure each cluster separately, or group them and set the rule once? Why?
lessons.teach:
A cluster is a set of machines that runs containerized applications under Kubernetes, the open-source system that schedules and restarts those containers. A fleet is a named group of clusters that you manage together. The fleet lives inside a fleet host project, which is the Google Cloud project that owns the grouping and its shared settings. Each cluster you add to a fleet is called a membership, and adding it is called registration. Clusters can be Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters or clusters running elsewhere that are attached to the fleet.

Why it works: the fleet is a management layer above the clusters. Clusters keep running their own workloads independently, so the grouping layer does not sit in the request path for applications. What the fleet adds is one place to decide what every member should look like. Features such as a sync agent that pulls configuration from a Git repository, and a policy engine that rejects resources breaking your rules, can be applied across all members.

Worked example: a platform team registers clusters in europe-west and us-east into a fleet called prod-fleet, hosted in a project called platform-host. Step 1: a engineer commits a rule requiring an owner label on every namespace to the Git repository. Step 2: the sync agent on each member pulls that commit. Step 3: each cluster applies the change. Step 4: when someone creates a namespace without the label in us-east, the policy engine rejects it, and the same happens in europe-west.

Common mistake: assuming that registering a cluster automatically applies every policy. Each fleet feature must be enabled and pointed at its configuration, and each member's sync status must be checked separately. Consequence in a running system: if one member's sync fails because of a bad manifest, that cluster silently drifts from the others while the rest update, so sync health must be watched per cluster.

questions.prompt: A payments company runs three clusters: one in asia-south1, one in southamerica-east1, and one in me-central1. It creates a fleet called pay-fleet inside a fleet host project called ledger-host and registers all three clusters as memberships. A team lead commits a rule to the company's Git configuration repository requiring a cost-center label on every Deployment. Step 1 is done: the rule is committed. Step 2 is done: the sync agent on each member pulls that commit. Step 3 is missing. Step 4 is that a Deployment without the cost-center label is rejected by the policy engine in asia-south1. Which choice fills in Step 3?
choices: The policy engine reads the Git repository directly, so no sync step is needed before rejection starts.
The fleet host project copies every Deployment into one central cluster, which then enforces the label rule for all members.
The team lead re-registers each cluster as a new membership, because registration is what loads the rules.
Each member cluster applies the pulled configuration, so its policy engine holds the label rule.
questions.why: Pulling a commit only brings the configuration to the cluster; the cluster must then apply it before its policy engine can enforce the rule.

questions.prompt: In the fleet model, what is a membership?
choices: A Google Cloud project that owns the shared settings for a group of clusters.
The Git repository that stores the fleet's configuration.
A named group of clusters that are managed together.
A cluster that has been registered into a fleet.
questions.why: A membership is the name for a single cluster once it has been added to a fleet through registration.

questions.prompt: A media company has a GKE cluster in us-central1 and a self-managed cluster in its own data centre, both attached to media-fleet in the project media-host. An engineer sees the on-premises cluster listed as a member and assumes its configuration sync is healthy because the other members are. What should she do?
choices: Delete and re-register the on-premises cluster, since registration always sets sync up correctly.
Move the on-premises cluster's workloads into media-host so that sync is shared.
Check that cluster's sync status separately, because each member's sync must be verified on its own.
Trust the fleet-level dashboard entry, since membership implies identical sync status.
questions.why: Being a member does not mean every feature is enabled or healthy, so each member's sync status has to be checked individually.

questions.prompt: A fleet has five memberships. The sync agent on one member fails to apply a commit because the manifest is malformed, while the other four apply it successfully. What is the most likely consequence while nobody intervenes?
choices: All five clusters stop serving application traffic until the manifest is repaired.
The failing cluster drifts from the others without an obvious alert unless each member's sync is watched.
The four healthy clusters roll back to the previous configuration automatically.
The fleet host project blocks further commits until the failing member is removed.
questions.why: Fleet management sits above the clusters, so the failing member keeps running its old configuration while the others update, and the gap is only visible if sync is watched per cluster.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we group our GKE clusters into a fleet instead of keeping each cluster's configuration files in its own folder. Explain what a fleet adds, and name one limit or tradeoff we should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: A fleet gives us one management layer over several clusters. Instead of editing each cluster's configuration by hand, we set shared rules and configuration once, and the fleet's sync and policy features apply them to every registered member. That reduces drift and makes it easier to prove that all production clusters follow the same rules. The tradeoff is that the fleet does not fix configuration by itself. Each feature has to be enabled and configured, and a member whose sync fails can quietly fall behind the others. So we need to check the sync status of every member, not just assume the group is consistent. We also keep the fleet host project's permissions tight, because whoever controls it can change settings across all members.
rubricPoints: A fleet is a named group of clusters managed together, hosted in a fleet host project.
Shared configuration and policy apply to all members from one source of truth.
Clusters keep running workloads independently; the fleet is a management layer, not a runtime dependency.
Features must be enabled per fleet, and per-member sync status must be checked.
Tradeoff: a failing member can drift silently, and control of the host project affects every cluster.

suggested.rationale: Fleet concepts and console or setup steps are reference facts best learned by reading, with no listed mission or planned engine covering them directly.

lessons.plain: Patching means installing fixes and updates on the software your systems run, such as the operating system on a server, the Kubernetes version on a cluster, or the libraries inside a container image. Upgrading means moving a component to a newer version, which can bring bigger changes. Both matter because old software collects known security holes and bugs, but every change can also break something that worked yesterday. Safe practice balances two goals: getting fixes in quickly, and changing things in small, controlled steps with a way back if something goes wrong. This lesson covers how to plan that balance in a cloud project.
lessons.guessPrompt: You run 200 virtual machines, and the operating system vendor has just published an urgent security fix. Would you push the fix to all 200 at the same moment, or in stages? Explain why.
lessons.teach:
Safe patching means changing running software so that a bad change does limited damage. A patch is a small fix to existing software, usually for a security flaw or a bug. An upgrade moves a component to a newer version, sometimes a major one with larger changes. A maintenance window is an agreed time slot when disruptive work is allowed and users have been told to expect it.

Why it works: a bad change is usually discovered by a few machines first, if you let it reach only a few. A staged rollout applies the change to a small group first, which is often called a canary group, then checks health signals such as error rates, restarts and latency. Only when those look normal does the change widen to the rest. Each wave acts as a test that can stop the next wave. Before any wave, you keep a rollback path, meaning a known way to return a machine to its previous state, such as a disk snapshot or the previous machine image. Rollback is then a planned step rather than an improvised scramble.

Worked example. A fleet has 200 virtual machines. Step 1: apply the patch to 10 non-production machines and let them run for a day. Step 2: apply it to 10 production machines, the canary group, and watch error rates for an hour. Step 3: if those look healthy, patch the remaining 180 in waves of 45, pausing between waves. If the second wave shows restarts climbing, stop, roll the affected machines back to their snapshots, and investigate before continuing.

Common mistake: treating a security fix as so urgent that staging is skipped. Urgency argues for starting sooner, not for going everywhere at once. A second mistake is patching without a rollback path, then discovering the old version is no longer available.

Consequence in a running system: an unstaged bad kernel patch can take the whole fleet offline at the same moment. The same patch, staged, takes down only the canary group and halts before it spreads.

questions.prompt: A team runs 48 virtual machines for an internal reporting service and must apply a security patch. Their plan so far: Step 1, patch 4 test machines and let them run for a day. Step 2, patch 6 production machines as the canary group and watch error rates for two hours. Step 3, if those look healthy, patch the other 38 machines in waves of 19, pausing between waves. The plan is missing one step. That step must be completed before any production machine is patched, and it sits between Step 1 and Step 2. What is the missing step?
choices: Patch the 38 remaining machines in a single wave to save time, since the patch is a security fix.
Ask the security team to confirm the patch's severity rating before any machine is changed.
Take a disk snapshot of each of the six canary machines so each one can be returned to its previous state if needed.
Increase the canary group to 20 machines so the canary result is more representative of the fleet.
questions.why: Before any wave, a rollback path such as a snapshot must exist, so the six canary machines need snapshots before they are patched.

questions.prompt: In the context of safe patching, what is a canary group?
choices: A small group that receives a change first, so its health signals can be checked before the change spreads to the rest.
The team members who approve a patch before it is scheduled into a maintenance window.
A backup copy of each machine's disk, kept so that the old version can be restored.
The full set of machines that will receive the change, patched together in one step.
questions.why: A canary group is the small first wave whose health is checked before the change is widened, as defined in the teaching text's account of staged rollout.

questions.prompt: A team with 12 machines applies a kernel patch to all of them at the same moment, with no staging. Shortly after, every machine restarts repeatedly and the service goes offline. Which change to their process would most directly have limited the damage?
choices: Applying the same patch to all 12 machines but at a later time of day.
Patching a small group first, checking health signals such as restarts and error rates, and only then widening the change.
Recording the patch version in a spreadsheet before the change begins.
Skipping the patch entirely until the next major upgrade.
questions.why: Staging limits the first damage to a small group and lets a bad signal halt the rollout before it reaches the rest of the fleet.

questions.prompt: A team plans to upgrade a production database engine from a major version to the next major version. Which statement about this plan is correct?
choices: It needs no rollback path, because a major version change is always reversible automatically.
It should be applied to every database at once, because splitting a major upgrade into waves causes version mismatch.
Because it is an upgrade and not a patch, it can skip staging, since the vendor tested it.
It still needs staging with a canary group and a rollback path, because a major upgrade brings larger changes than a patch.
questions.why: The teaching text notes that a major upgrade has larger changes, so the same staged rollout and rollback path rules apply and are not relaxed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would patch a production fleet safely, and name one tradeoff you accept by working that way.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not patch the whole production fleet in one go. First I would apply the update to a non-production copy and let it run through normal checks. Then I would patch a small canary group in production and watch error rates, restarts and latency for a set period. Only after that would I roll the rest out in waves, inside an agreed maintenance window. Before each wave I would confirm that a snapshot or previous image exists, so a bad change can be reverted. The tradeoff is time: staging means the last machines get the fix later than a patch-everything approach would. For a critical exploit I would shorten the wait between waves rather than remove the waves, and I would document the exposure window we accepted.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes a patch (small fix) from an upgrade (move to a newer version).
Rolls changes out in stages, starting with a small canary group, and checks health between waves.
Uses a maintenance window and keeps a tested rollback path such as a snapshot or prior image.
Names the tradeoff: slower full coverage in exchange for a smaller blast radius.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a wave plan for an urgent patch is an exam-style reasoning task that no current mission covers directly, so a scenario drill adds the most.

lessons.plain: A cloud development environment is a coding workspace that runs on rented servers in the cloud instead of on your laptop. You reach it through a browser or by connecting your editor, and the tools, compilers and credentials you need are already set up. Google Cloud offers two versions of this idea. Cloud Shell is a free, short-lived terminal for quick tasks. Cloud Workstations is a managed, longer-lived machine that a platform team defines once and developers start on demand. Think of Cloud Shell as a loaner laptop you borrow for a quick job, and Cloud Workstations as a standard desk setup that the IT team configured for everyone on the team.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new engineer's laptop has a different Python version from the production servers, so their builds behave differently from everyone else's. Without knowing any product, what would you change so every engineer starts from the same tools, and where would you keep that setup so it stays the same over time?
lessons.teach:
A cloud development environment is a remote machine or container that a developer works in. An ephemeral environment is one that is thrown away and recreated, so nothing important should live only on it. A persistent home directory is storage that survives when the machine stops or is recreated. A workstation configuration is a reusable template that says which machine size to use, which container image (a pre-built package of tools and settings) to boot from, and how long the machine may sit idle before it is stopped.

Why it works: the environment is described by a template instead of by hand-installed software, so every developer who starts from that template gets the same tools. Because the machine runs inside the cloud, it sits close to the resources and identities it needs.

Worked example. A platform engineer creates a workstation configuration that points to an image containing the team's Go toolchain, the gcloud SDK and linters. They set an idle timeout of 30 minutes. A developer starts a workstation from that configuration; it boots from the image in a few minutes. The developer edits code, which is saved to the persistent home directory. They stop the workstation for the night. The next morning they start it again, and their files are still there, with the same tools.

Cloud Shell works differently. Opening it gives a temporary virtual machine with a small persistent home directory. If the session goes idle, the machine is recycled, so anything saved outside the home directory is lost.

Common mistake: keeping work or secrets outside the persistent home directory, or assuming Cloud Shell is a place for long-running jobs. Another is leaving a workstation running after use, which keeps billing for an idle machine.

Consequence: if a build depends on tools one person installed by hand on their laptop, teammates get different results. A shared configuration fixes that, but a bad image change then reaches everyone the next time they start.

questions.prompt: Ana works at a regional bank and her platform team has set up a workstation configuration for the data engineers. The configuration names a container image with Python 3.11 and the bq command-line tool, and sets an idle timeout of 45 minutes, meaning the machine is stopped after 45 minutes without activity. Step 1: Ana starts a workstation from that configuration and writes a reconciliation script, which is saved in her persistent home directory (storage that survives stopping and restarting). Step 2: she runs the script and it produces a report file in the same home directory. Step 3 is missing from her account: before she goes home, she ____. Step 4: the next morning she starts the workstation again and finds the script and report still there, with the same tools. Which completes Step 3 so that the account is correct?
choices: sets the idle timeout to zero so the machine never stops
commits the script to the shared container image so every teammate receives it
stops the workstation rather than leaving it running overnight, since stopping keeps the home directory and avoids billing for an idle machine
copies the script into /tmp so it survives the restart
questions.why: Stopping the workstation keeps the persistent home directory intact while ending the cost of an idle running machine, which is what the next-morning result depends on.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches an ephemeral cloud development environment?
choices: An environment that is discarded and recreated, so nothing important should live only on it
A shared image that each developer must install by hand on a personal laptop
A development machine that keeps every file forever across every restart and recreation
A workstation that is never stopped, so it always stays warm for the next session
questions.why: An ephemeral environment is one that is thrown away and rebuilt, which is why important files belong in persistent storage rather than on the machine itself.

questions.prompt: A data scientist at a retail firm starts a 10-hour model training run in Cloud Shell and leaves the browser tab open overnight. Which outcome is most likely, and why?
choices: The session can go idle and the temporary machine can be recycled, so the job and anything saved outside the home directory can be lost
The job keeps running indefinitely because Cloud Shell is a dedicated virtual machine that never recycles
The job pauses and resumes automatically at the next login with no loss of progress
Only the Python packages are lost, because the output file is always preserved even outside the home directory
questions.why: Cloud Shell is a temporary machine with a small persistent home directory, so long-running jobs on it are at risk when the session goes idle and the machine is recycled.

questions.prompt: A platform team at a logistics company edits its shared workstation configuration so the image no longer includes a linter that developers rely on. Developers already have workstations running from the old image. What happens?
choices: Only the platform team's workstations are affected, because they own the configuration
Every developer who next starts a workstation from that configuration boots the changed image, so the bad change reaches them at their next start
Nothing changes until the configuration's idle timeout expires on each machine
Existing persistent home directories are rewritten to match the new image automatically
questions.why: A configuration is a template, so the image change applies to anyone who starts a new workstation from it, and developers only receive it on their next start.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose Cloud Shell over a Cloud Workstation for a team's development work, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use Cloud Shell for quick, one-off tasks such as checking a resource, running a gcloud command or making a small fix from any browser. It is free for basic use and needs no setup. The tradeoff is that it is temporary: the machine is recycled after inactivity, so only the small home directory survives, and it is not a place for long builds or a shared team setup. For day-to-day development I would pick Cloud Workstations. A platform team defines one configuration with the right tools and a container image, so every engineer starts from the same environment. The tradeoffs are that it costs money while running, so an idle timeout matters, and a bad image change reaches everyone at their next start, so the template needs review like any other code.
rubricPoints: Cloud Shell is a free, temporary terminal suited to quick tasks and loses data outside its small home directory
Cloud Workstations is a managed, reusable environment defined by a configuration template for a whole team
A shared configuration gives consistent tooling but spreads image mistakes to everyone
Running workstations cost money, so idle timeouts and stopping machines matter

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product facts and console or configuration steps that a reading lesson covers better than an existing or planned hands-on engine.

lessons.plain: When a team starts a new project, every engineer needs the same set of programs: a code editor, the command-line tools that talk to the cloud, language runtimes, and checkers that catch mistakes early. Bootstrapping a development environment means setting that up in a repeatable way. A custom image is a saved snapshot of a machine or workstation with those tools already installed and configured, so a new engineer starts from a known state instead of spending a day on setup. The IDE, or integrated development environment, is the code editor and its add-ons. The Cloud SDK is the set of command-line tools for working with cloud resources. Together they make the first day of work predictable and let everyone's machine behave the same way.
lessons.guessPrompt: If ten new engineers each install their own tools by hand on their first day, what is likely to be different between their machines a month later, and how would you prevent that drift?
lessons.teach:
A development environment is the set of tools a person uses to write, test and deploy code: an editor, a command-line interface, language runtimes and helper programs. Bootstrapping means creating that environment from nothing in a repeatable way. A base image is a starting operating system snapshot. A custom image is a base image with your team's tools added and configured, saved under a name and version. The IDE is the integrated development environment, the editor with its plugins. The Cloud SDK is the set of command-line tools, including the gcloud command, that create and inspect cloud resources.

It works because the image is built from a written recipe with pinned tool versions. The same recipe run twice gives the same toolset, so differences between machines come from people, not from setup.

Worked example. Step 1: the team lists the tools and pins versions, for example the Cloud SDK at one exact release, Python at one minor version, and a linter. Step 2: a build starts from the base image and installs those tools. Step 3: a smoke test runs each command with a version flag and fails the build if any is missing. Step 4: the result is saved as a named version, such as a dated release. Step 5: each new engineer's workstation is created from that version, and they sign in to the SDK with their own account.

Common mistake: baking credentials or long-lived service account keys into the image. Every workstation built from it then carries the same secret, and rotating it means rebuilding everything.

In a running system the consequence is serious. A leaked key inside an image persists in every older version and every copy, so the fix is to keep secrets out of images and use per-user sign-in with short-lived tokens.

questions.prompt: A mobile team at another company builds custom images for Android build workstations. Their steps: (1) they pin the Android platform-tools at 35.0.2, Gradle at 8.7, and the Cloud SDK at release 470.0.0. (2) A build starts from their Debian base image and installs those pinned tools. (3) This step is missing. (4) The tested image is saved as android-ws-v3 with a date tag. (5) Each new engineer's workstation is created from android-ws-v3 and signs in to the Cloud SDK with their own account. Which action belongs in the missing step 3?
choices: Run each tool with a version flag and fail the build if any tool is missing or at the wrong version.
Upgrade every pinned tool to the newest release so the image stays current before it is saved.
Publish android-ws-v3 to every engineer immediately and test it later on live workstations.
Copy a shared service account key into the image so builds can reach the registry without prompts.
questions.why: A smoke test run before saving confirms each pinned tool is present at the right version, so a broken build never gets a version name.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches how the teaching text defines a custom image?
choices: A brand-new operating system installed from an installer disk, with no earlier snapshot involved.
A base image with the team's tools added and configured, saved under a name and version.
A running workstation that someone customised by hand and then left switched on for others to use.
A container registry entry that holds only editor plugins and nothing else.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a custom image as a base image with the team's tools added and configured, saved under a name and version.

questions.prompt: A team bakes one long-lived service account key into its workstation image. Version 2 of that image is in use by 30 engineers. What is the main risk?
choices: The key expires automatically after the first workstation boot, so there is no real risk.
The same secret sits on every workstation and in every older image version, so rotating it means rebuilding them all.
Each engineer gets a unique key derived from the image, so a leak would expose only one person.
The Cloud SDK refuses to run on any machine whose image contains a key, so builds simply fail.
questions.why: Every workstation built from the image carries the same baked-in secret, and older versions keep it too, so the fix requires rebuilding everything.

questions.prompt: A new engineer joins and needs to run gcloud commands against the project. Which setup follows the approach in the teaching text?
choices: Sign in to the Cloud SDK with their own account, using short-lived tokens, rather than a shared key.
Ask a colleague to run the commands for them under the colleague's own login.
Store a key in the editor's settings file so the IDE can authenticate on their behalf.
Copy the team's long-lived service account key from the image onto their laptop.
questions.why: The teaching text says to keep secrets out of images and use per-user sign-in with short-lived tokens, which is what the first choice describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would bootstrap a new engineer's development environment using a custom image, an IDE and the Cloud SDK. Name one limit or tradeoff of baking the tools into an image.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would write a recipe that starts from a standard base image and installs the Cloud SDK at a pinned version, plus our language runtime, linter and editor setup, then runs a smoke test that checks each tool's version before saving the result as a named image release. New engineers create their workstation from that release, so everyone starts from the same toolset. The IDE settings and plugins are kept in version control and applied on first login. Each person signs in to the SDK with their own account rather than a shared key. The tradeoff is that the image goes stale: security patches and new tool versions only reach people when we rebuild and roll out a new release, so we need a schedule for rebuilding and a way to move existing workstations to it.
rubricPoints: A custom image is built from a recipe with pinned tool versions, so the toolset is repeatable.
The IDE and SDK are configured the same way for everyone, with settings kept under version control.
Credentials stay out of the image; engineers sign in with their own short-lived access.
A limit: images go stale and need a rebuild and rollout process to pick up patches.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product setup steps and concepts about images, editors and SDK installation, which a reading lesson covers better than any current or planned hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: An AI assistant is a tool that reads your question and whatever context you give it, then drafts an answer, some code, or a suggested command. For engineers working in Google Cloud, there are three kinds: one that helps write code inside your editor, one that helps you understand what is happening in your cloud project, and one that works from the terminal and can propose and run steps. Think of it as a fast, well-read junior colleague. It is useful for drafts and first diagnoses, but it can be confidently wrong, so you check its work against real logs, tests, and documentation before you change anything.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your AI assistant suggests a fix for a production error in one confident sentence. What is the first thing you would do before applying it, and why?
lessons.teach:
Three terms first. A prompt is the text you send to an AI model, usually with extra context such as code or log lines. Grounding means tying the model's answer to real sources you can check, such as your project's logs or the code in your repository. A hallucination is a confident answer that is not true, and it is the main risk with these tools.

The three kinds of tool sit at different points in your workflow. An AI coding assistant lives in your editor and suggests code, tests, and explanations for the file you are working on. An AI operations assistant works in the cloud console and answers questions about your resources, logs, and recent changes, often summarising what it finds. An AI command-line agent runs in your terminal, reads files, proposes commands, and can execute them with your permission. The more a tool can act, the more its access must be limited to what the task needs.

Why this helps: models are good at recalling common causes of a given error message and at turning raw text into a readable summary. They are weak at knowing the live state of your specific system.

Worked example. A deploy starts returning 403 errors. You ask the operations assistant why. Step one: it points to a log entry saying the service's identity lacks one permission on one storage bucket. Step two: you check that the entry exists in the real logs with a matching timestamp. Step three: you confirm which service account the workload runs as. Step four: you grant only the single role the log names, on only that bucket, then re-test. The assistant's answer became a hypothesis that you verified.

Common mistake: pasting secrets, keys, or customer data into a prompt, or accepting a suggested fix without checking it. A broad administrative role would clear the error but silently give the workload power over the whole project.

Consequence: a fast, wrong change to a running system can widen access or break a live service, so AI output is a draft to verify, never an authority.

questions.prompt: A team uses an editor assistant to fix a failing unit test for an invoice-total function in a billing service. Step one: you paste the test failure output into the assistant, and it suggests changing a rounding call. Step two: before changing anything, you run the same failing test on your own machine and confirm it fails with the same message. Step three: you apply the suggested change on a feature branch. Step four is missing from this list. Step five: you open a pull request for review. Which step fills the gap?
choices: Merge the branch straight to main, since the one failing test now passes.
Run the full test suite on the branch to check the change has not broken other tests.
Ask the assistant to write a new test that matches its own suggested change.
Delete the original failing test so the suite reports no failures.
questions.why: Running the whole suite on the branch checks that the suggested change has not introduced failures elsewhere, which the single test cannot reveal.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does grounding mean when you use an AI tool for operations work?
choices: Limiting the model so it only answers with yes or no.
Training the model permanently on your company's private data.
Asking the model to repeat its answer twice so you can compare the two versions.
Tying the model's answer to real sources you can check, such as log entries or the code in your repository.
questions.why: Grounding means connecting an answer to sources you can verify, such as real logs or repository code, rather than accepting the model's words alone.

questions.prompt: A developer wants help explaining why a Cloud Run service's response time rose yesterday, using the recent change history and logs visible in the cloud console. Which kind of AI tool fits this task best?
choices: An AI coding assistant that lives in the editor and suggests code for the open file.
A prompt pasted by hand into a general chat app with no access to the project.
An AI command-line agent that reads local files and runs commands in the terminal.
