The tradeoff is a new dependency: if the vault is unreachable or the job lacks permission, the deploy fails at startup, so the team must monitor access and plan for that failure. Rotation also needs a process for updating consumers, because old versions can break anything still using them.
rubricPoints: Explains that a repository or image copy spreads the secret to many places and keeps it in history
Describes the vault as a single encrypted, access-controlled source with read records
Notes that run-time fetch with a narrowly scoped identity allows rotation without code changes
Names a tradeoff such as the vault becoming a runtime dependency or rotation needing coordination

suggested.rationale: This mission has you fix how a deploy authenticates without exposing the secret, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Almost every application that talks to a database or another service needs a password or key, called a secret. The key question is when that secret gets handed to the software. One option is to hand it over while the software is being packaged, so the secret ends up sealed inside the finished package. The other is to hand it over only when the software actually starts running, so the package itself carries no secret. This lesson covers how to choose between those two moments and why the second is usually safer.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a database password is baked into a container image during the build, and that image is copied to a shared registry that many people can read, what is the risk, and what would you change to avoid it?
lessons.teach:
Build-time secret injection means a secret value is passed into the build step, for example as a build argument or a file in the build workspace, and it ends up inside the output artifact. An artifact is the packaged thing a pipeline produces, such as a container image or a compiled binary. Runtime secret injection means the artifact is built without the secret. When the workload starts, it receives the value from a secret store, which is a managed service that keeps secrets encrypted and records who reads them. The workload usually proves its identity to that store with a workload identity, a credential the platform issues so the service needs no stored password of its own.

Why it matters: an artifact is copied, cached, stored and shared. Anything inside it travels with every copy. A runtime value exists only in the running environment, and it can be changed without rebuilding anything.

Worked example. A service needs a database password. With build-time injection, the pipeline reads the password from its vault, passes it into the build, a build step writes it into a configuration file, and the image is pushed to the registry. Anyone who can read that image can extract the password. To rotate it, you rebuild and redeploy. With runtime injection, the image holds only a configuration line saying to fetch the password from the store under a given name. At startup the service uses its identity to fetch the current value into memory. To rotate, you add a new version in the store and the next start picks it up.

Common mistake: believing that deleting a secret in a later build step removes it. Image layers keep the earlier content, so the secret can still be recovered from the image history.

Consequence: a leaked build-time secret compromises every copy of that image, including ones in older environments, and fixing it means a full rebuild and redeploy. With runtime injection, rotation is a store update followed by a restart, and the image itself stays safe to share. Runtime injection is the default choice for credentials that must stay secret.

questions.prompt: A video company runs its thumbnail service on a managed container platform. The pipeline now uses runtime injection: the image holds only a reference to the secret 'thumbnail-api-key' in a secret store, and at startup the service uses its workload identity to fetch the current version into memory. An engineer who knew the key has left, so the team must rotate it. Step 1: add a new version of the key to the secret store. Step 2: ____. Step 3: the service fetches the new value at its next start. Which step 2 completes the rotation?
choices: Rebuild the image with the new key passed as a build argument, then push it to the registry
Restart the running instances so they start and fetch the new version
Delete every older image layer that contains the previous key value
Rename the secret so the service ignores the old name
questions.why: With runtime injection the value is read at startup from the store, so restarting the instances makes them fetch the new version without any rebuild.

questions.prompt: A nightly reporting job runs in a container. An engineer wants the read-only API token written into the Dockerfile as a build argument so the image starts with the token already present. What should a reviewer flag about this design?
choices: The token will expire too quickly because build arguments have short lifetimes
The nightly job will fail because containers cannot read build arguments at all
The image will run slower because the token is loaded from disk at startup
The token will be stored inside the artifact, so every copy of the image carries it
questions.why: Build-time injection places the secret inside the output artifact, and anything inside an artifact travels with every copy of it.

questions.prompt: A team passes a deploy key into a build step, then adds a later build step that deletes the key file before the image is pushed. A reviewer says the key is still exposed. What is the reviewer's reason?
choices: The delete step is too slow, so it never finishes before the push begins
Earlier image layers keep the earlier content, so the key can still be recovered from the image history
Deleting a file in one step only removes the link to it, so the bytes stay in the cache for later builds
The registry copies the key back from the build cache during the push
questions.why: Image layers retain content from earlier steps, so a later delete does not remove the secret from what was already recorded in the image.

questions.prompt: Staging and production both run the same image, which was built with a database password passed in at build time. The password is found to be leaked. Which action fixes the exposure for every environment?
choices: Delete the image tag from the registry while leaving the copies in staging running
Change the password only in production, since staging is not public
Rebuild without the old password and redeploy everywhere
Restart all running containers so they reread the build arguments
questions.why: Because the old password is baked into the artifact, every copy must be replaced by rebuilding and redeploying without it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would inject a database password at build time versus at runtime, and name one limit or tradeoff of the runtime approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would inject a database password at runtime in almost every case, because the image then contains no secret and can be copied or stored without exposing it. The build step only needs to reference a secret name, and the running service fetches the value from the secret store using its workload identity when it starts. Rotation becomes a new version in the store plus a restart, with no rebuild. Build-time injection is only reasonable for values that are safe to be public, such as a non-secret setting. The tradeoff of runtime injection is a dependency: if the secret store is unreachable or the service identity lacks permission, the service cannot start, so startup failures and access grants must be monitored and tested before a release.
rubricPoints: Build-time injection leaves the secret inside the artifact, so every copy and cached layer exposes it.
Runtime injection keeps the artifact free of secrets and fetches the value when the workload starts.
Rotation is cheap with runtime injection and requires a rebuild and redeploy with build-time injection.
Runtime injection adds a startup dependency on the secret store and the workload's identity permissions.

suggested.rationale: The mission asks the learner to fix secret wiring in a failing deploy without leaking the secret, which directly practices choosing where the secret enters the pipeline.

lessons.plain: Before software goes out to users, a team can check the packaged parts it is built from, such as container images and libraries, for known security holes. Artifact analysis means looking inside those packaged files to list what they contain and which versions they use. Vulnerability scanning compares that list against public catalogues of known flaws and reports which ones are present and how serious they are. The goal is to catch a risky component while it is still a file in storage, rather than after it is running for customers. Scanning only helps when someone decides what to do with the findings, such as blocking a release or fixing a library.
lessons.guessPrompt: A container image was built last week from a base image and twelve libraries. Today a public database publishes a new security flaw in one of those libraries. Without any tools, what would you need to know about the image to find out whether you are affected, and why would that information be enough?
lessons.teach:
An artifact is any packaged output a pipeline produces, such as a container image (a sealed bundle holding an application and everything it depends on) or a language package. Artifact analysis means reading an artifact and recording its contents: the operating system packages, library names and exact versions. This record is often called a software bill of materials, or SBOM. A vulnerability is a publicly catalogued security flaw, usually given an identifier such as a CVE number and a severity rating. Vulnerability scanning matches the recorded components against those catalogues.

Why it works: a flaw only matters if a vulnerable version is present, so the scanner's job is essentially a lookup. Once you know exact versions, the question 'are we exposed?' becomes a comparison rather than a guess.

Worked example: a team pushes an image called web version 1.4. Step 1, the registry stores it and the analyser lists 214 packages, including openssl at version 3.0.2. Step 2, the catalogue links openssl 3.0.2 to a high-severity flaw that is fixed in 3.0.7. Step 3, the result is attached to that exact image digest, which is a fingerprint of its contents. Step 4, the pipeline reads the result and blocks promotion to production until the base image is rebuilt with the fixed library.

Common mistake: scanning only the source code, or scanning once at build time and never again. A clean scan today does not stay clean, because new flaws are published against old, unchanged images, so deployed images need continuous rescanning.

Consequence: if a deploy gate ignores findings, a vulnerable image can reach production and be exposed to attackers without anyone noticing.

questions.prompt: A payments team builds an image called ledger-api at version 2.3. Its base image includes libcurl at version 8.5.0. Step 1: the registry stores the image, and the analyser records 187 packages, including libcurl 8.5.0. Step 2: the catalogue links libcurl 8.5.0 to a high-severity flaw that is fixed in 8.6.0. Step 3 is missing from this list. Step 4: the pipeline reads the result and blocks promotion to production until the base image is rebuilt with the fixed library. What must step 3 be?
choices: The image is deleted from the registry so that no later pipeline step can pull it.
The scan result is attached to the mutable tag latest, so anyone pulling that name sees the finding.
The scan result is attached to the git commit that changed the source code, not to the image itself.
The scan result is attached to the exact image digest, the fingerprint of the image's contents.
questions.why: The result must be tied to the immutable digest so the pipeline can be certain it is judging the exact contents being promoted, which is why the other options fail: a tag can be moved, a commit does not describe the built image, and deletion removes the evidence.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a software bill of materials (SBOM) for a container image?
choices: A signed approval record that a human reviewer wrote before the image was promoted.
A list of deployment targets the pipeline is permitted to send the image to.
A running count of how many times the image has been pulled from the registry.
A recorded list of the packages inside an artifact and their exact versions.
questions.why: An SBOM is the recorded inventory of an artifact's contents with exact versions, which is what the scanner compares against vulnerability catalogues.

questions.prompt: A team scanned their service image in March and got a clean result. In June, a new flaw is published against a library version that the unchanged image still contains, and that image is still running in production. Which gap most directly explains why nobody noticed?
choices: The scanner only reads source code, so the library inside the image was never checked.
The deployment used a different region from the one where the scan originally ran.
The team stored the March result in a report but never rescanned the deployed image.
The image was never given a version number, so the catalogue could not match it.
questions.why: Flaws are published against old unchanged images over time, so deployed images need continuous rescanning; a one-time clean scan does not stay valid.

questions.prompt: A service image's SBOM records zlib at version 1.2.11. The catalogue entry for a flaw in zlib says it is fixed in 1.2.13. Using only the comparison method described for scanning, what is the correct conclusion?
choices: The image cannot be assessed until the source code repository is also scanned for flaws.
The image is exposed, because the vulnerable 1.2.11 is present and is older than the fixed 1.2.13.
The image is not exposed, because 1.2.11 and 1.2.13 share the same major version number.
The image is exposed only if zlib is the sole package in the image, since other packages dilute the finding.
questions.why: Scanning reduces to a lookup: if the recorded version is older than the fixed version listed in the catalogue, the vulnerable version is present and the image is exposed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what artifact analysis and vulnerability scanning tell you, and what they cannot tell you. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of blocking a release based on scan results.
lessons.modelAnswer: Artifact analysis reads a built image or package and lists what is inside it, including each library and its exact version. Vulnerability scanning takes that list and matches it against databases of published flaws, so we learn which known issues the artifact carries and how severe they are. It cannot tell us whether a flaw is reachable in our application, and it cannot find unknown flaws or logic bugs in our own code. Results also go stale as new flaws are published, so a passing scan is only a point-in-time fact. The tradeoff of gating releases on findings is that strict gates can hold up urgent fixes, and noisy alerts teach people to ignore them. A sensible approach is to block on high-severity findings that have an available fix, allow documented exceptions with an expiry date, and rescan deployed images regularly.
rubricPoints: Artifact analysis records what an artifact contains, such as packages and exact versions
Vulnerability scanning matches that inventory against catalogues of known flaws
A scan only reflects known flaws at the time it runs, so rescanning is needed
Gating releases on findings has tradeoffs, such as delaying urgent fixes or causing alert fatigue

suggested.rationale: Deciding whether a scan result should block a release is an exam-style judgement that a short scenario trains better than reading facts alone.

lessons.plain: Software supply chain security is about making sure the program you run in production is the one your team actually built and tested, and that it came out of an approved process. Think of a sealed food package with a tamper seal and a record of where each ingredient came from. Binary Authorization is a gatekeeper on the cloud platform: before a container image is allowed to start, it checks that the image carries the right signed approvals. SLSA, pronounced salsa, is a graded checklist describing how well a build process is protected and how trustworthy its records are, with levels that rise as the protections get stronger. Neither is a single switch. They are ideas and tools that work together to keep the path from source code to running program honest.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a build server produces a container image and someone later replaces the image stored under the same name with a different one. What would you add so the production platform refuses the swapped image, and why is the name alone not enough to trust?
lessons.teach:
A container image is a packaged program ready to run. A digest is a fingerprint computed from the exact bytes of an image, so two images with different contents always have different digests, even if they share a name or a tag. A tag, such as latest, is only a label that can be moved to point at a different image. An attestation is a signed statement that makes a claim about an artifact, such as tests passed or this image was built from commit X by a trusted builder. An attestor is the party whose signing key backs that statement, and the key itself is usually kept in a key management service. Binary Authorization is a deploy-time policy check. Before admitting an image, the platform looks for attestations from the attestors the policy requires, and it refuses images that lack them. SLSA describes build maturity in levels. Higher levels require provenance, a record of source, inputs and builder, that the build steps cannot forge, and a build platform isolated enough that one job cannot tamper with another.

Worked example. A build produces an image with digest D1 and provenance naming the source commit. A test stage signs an attestation saying tests passed for D1. The deploy request names the image by digest D1. The admission check finds a signed attestation for D1 from the required attestor and allows it. Now someone pushes a different image under the same tag. Its digest D2 has no attestation, so the check denies it.

Common mistake: deploying by tag. If the pipeline names the image only as latest, the check cannot tell which bytes will run, and the protection is weakened. Always pin by digest.

Consequence: a denied deployment looks like a failed rollout. If a legitimate image lacks its attestation because a pipeline step was skipped, the release stalls until the pipeline is fixed or a documented exception is added.

An image's trust comes from signed evidence tied to its digest, not from its name.

questions.prompt: Lumen Harbor is a fictional payments team. Its policy requires two attestations before any image is admitted: one from the build attestor saying the image came from a named commit, and one from the security attestor saying a vulnerability scan passed for that same image. Step 1: the build produces an image with digest F7 and signs a provenance attestation for F7 naming commit 9c2e. Step 2 is left blank for you to fill in; it must produce the second required attestation. Step 3: the deploy request names the image as F7 by digest. Step 4: the admission check finds both required attestations for F7 and admits the image.
choices: The security stage retags F7 as stable so the deploy step can find it by name.
The security stage scans F7 and signs a scan-passed attestation for F7 with the security attestor's key.
The admission check is changed to accept any image whose tag matches the commit name.
The security stage rebuilds the image from commit 9c2e to get a fresh digest for the scan.
questions.why: The second requirement is a signed attestation from the security attestor tied to the exact digest F7, so the scan result must be signed for F7 itself.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does an image digest let a deployment system rely on?
choices: A fingerprint computed from the image's exact bytes, so a changed image always gets a different value.
A timestamp showing when the image was last pushed, used to decide which copy is newest.
A human-readable label that the registry can move to a newer build whenever a team wants.
A list of the people who approved the image for release, kept in the registry's metadata.
questions.why: A digest is computed from the exact contents of the image, so it identifies those bytes, while a tag is only a movable label.

questions.prompt: A team keeps an attested image under the tag prod-api. Later someone pushes a freshly built, unattested image under the same tag and the deployment names only prod-api. What does a policy requiring attestations do with the new image, and why?
choices: It admits the new image because the tag still matches the previously approved one.
It admits the new image after a warning, because tags are checked before digests.
It admits the new image only if the registry marks the old tag as deprecated.
It denies the new image if its digest has no required attestation, because the tag alone does not pin the bytes that run.
questions.why: Admission depends on attestations for the digest that actually runs, and a deployment naming only a tag cannot prove which bytes it will get.

questions.prompt: A company's build platform lets one job write directly into the directory that holds another job's signing material. Which SLSA-style property does this most directly break, and what would fix it?
choices: It breaks build isolation, since one job can tamper with another; the fix is a build platform where each job cannot alter other jobs or the signing material.
It breaks the deploy-time check, fixed by removing Binary Authorization from the deployment path.
It breaks the use of digests, fixed by switching every image to a longer tag name.
It breaks the requirement that provenance be recorded for the source commit, fixed by storing commit hashes in a spreadsheet.
questions.why: Higher SLSA levels require a build platform isolated enough that one job cannot tamper with another, so the fix is isolating the jobs and their signing material.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we can stop worrying about tampered releases because Binary Authorization is turned on for production. Explain to them, in your own words, what it actually checks, what it does not check, and one tradeoff of enforcing it strictly.
lessons.modelAnswer: Binary Authorization checks that an image being deployed carries signed attestations from the attestors the policy requires, matched to the image's digest. So it stops images that were never through the approved pipeline, or that were swapped under a tag. It does not prove the code is bug-free, and it trusts the attestors: if a signing key is stolen or a test stage signs without really testing, the check still passes. It also does not cover what happens after admission, or images deployed outside the gated path. The tradeoff of strict enforcement is that a legitimate release can be blocked when a required attestation is missing, so teams need a fast way to see which attestation is absent and a controlled exception process rather than turning the check off.
rubricPoints: Binary Authorization admits images only when required signed attestations exist for the image digest.
It defends against swapped or unapproved images, not against bugs inside an approved image.
Trust depends on the attestors and their signing keys being protected.
Strict enforcement can block valid releases, so exceptions and visibility must be planned.

suggested.rationale: Choosing which supply chain check governs a given deployment is best learned by reasoning through exam-style scenarios, and no current mission covers signing or admission policy.

lessons.plain: Many teams run a pipeline that builds software and pushes it toward live systems. The pipeline itself acts as an identity with real permissions, much like a robot employee holding keys. Scoping IAM by environment means giving each stage only the keys it needs for its own environment. A test environment's pipeline should not be able to change production, and a build job should not need to read production secrets. IAM stands for identity and access management, the system that decides which identity may perform which action on which resource. Getting the scope right limits the damage when a pipeline is compromised or misconfigured.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your build job runs in the test environment, but its service account also has permission to deploy to production. A bug in a test script runs a deploy command. What do you think happens, and what single change would prevent it?
lessons.teach:
An identity is the account a piece of software runs as. In Google Cloud a service account is an identity for a workload such as a pipeline job. A permission is one allowed action, such as creating a release. A role is a named bundle of permissions. A binding attaches a role to an identity on a particular resource. The scope of a binding is the level where it applies: organization, folder, project, or a single resource.

Why scope matters: grants flow downward. A role granted at the organization or folder level also applies to every project beneath it. If each environment (development, staging, production) is its own project with its own pipeline service account, and roles are bound only on that project, a mistake in one environment cannot reach the others.

Worked example. The staging pipeline runs as a service account called deploy-staging. Step 1: the job runs as that identity. Step 2: it asks to create a release in the staging delivery pipeline. A binding on the staging project allows this, so it succeeds. Step 3: the same job asks to deploy to the production project. No binding for this identity exists there, so the request is denied. Step 4: the denial is recorded in the audit logs, where a team can see it.

Common mistake: granting the pipeline identity a broad basic role such as Editor or Owner at the organization or folder level so that nothing ever breaks. Consequence: a compromised test build can modify production resources, read production secrets, or change IAM policies themselves.

In a running system, environment-scoped IAM is what turns a bad test script into a failed test rather than an outage.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Retail keeps its payments work in a folder called Payments, which holds two projects: payments-dev and payments-prod. Its deploy job runs as the service account svc-ci-dev. The team granted svc-ci-dev a deploy role on the Payments folder, and nothing on either project directly. Step 1: the job runs as svc-ci-dev. Step 2: the job asks to write a release to payments-prod. Step 3 is left blank. Which sentence correctly fills it in?
choices: Allowed only if svc-ci-dev also holds a role on the organization itself.
Allowed, but only for read actions, since folders cannot grant write permissions.
Allowed, because the folder binding flows down to payments-prod.
Denied, because no binding for svc-ci-dev exists directly on payments-prod.
questions.why: Grants flow downward from a folder to every project beneath it, so the folder-level binding reaches payments-prod even though no binding sits on that project.

questions.prompt: A deploy job at Quillfield Labs must be allowed to create releases in one project only. Which term names the attachment of a role to that identity on that particular project?
choices: A permission
A binding
A service account
A scope
questions.why: A binding is the attachment of a role to an identity on a particular resource; a permission is one allowed action, a service account is the identity itself, and a scope is the level where a binding applies.

questions.prompt: Tallow Analytics has three projects, ana-dev, ana-test and ana-live, each with its own pipeline service account. The dev pipeline account has a role bound only on ana-dev. A test build's script tries to read a secret in ana-live using that same dev account. What happens?
choices: The read succeeds once the script labels itself as a test build.
Denied: no binding for that identity exists on ana-live.
The read succeeds, because all three projects share one service account.
The read is denied because the secret is in a different environment's project.
questions.why: Bindings are scoped per project, and the identity has no binding on ana-live, so the request is denied and the denial appears in the audit logs.

questions.prompt: A team at Harbel Systems grants its pipeline identity the Editor basic role at the organization level so that no deploy ever fails. Which outcome best describes the main risk of this choice?
choices: Nothing changes, because roles at the organization level do not reach individual projects.
Only audit log entries change, because the grant itself is recorded there.
A compromised test build could reach production resources and secrets.
Only new projects are affected, since existing projects keep their own bindings.
questions.why: A broad role at the organization level flows down to every project beneath it, so a compromised test job could modify production resources, read production secrets, or change IAM policies.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why each environment's pipeline gets its own service account with roles bound only on that environment's project, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: We give each environment's pipeline its own service account and bind roles only on that environment's project so that a fault or compromise stays contained. If the staging pipeline is hijacked or a script misfires, it cannot deploy to or read secrets from production, because no binding grants that. Roles on the organization or folder would flow down to every project, so we avoid them. The tradeoff is operational overhead: each environment needs its own identity, its own bindings, and regular review, and a team that copies one broad grant across environments to save effort loses the isolation. Teams also need to make sure a promotion from staging to production uses a deliberate approval or a production-scoped identity rather than a widened staging one.
rubricPoints: Each environment has its own pipeline identity, so compromise or error stays in that environment.
Roles are bound at the narrowest useful scope, usually the environment's project, not the organization.
Broad basic roles at higher levels flow down and expand the blast radius.
A real tradeoff exists: more identities and bindings to create and review.
Promotion to production needs a deliberate, separately authorized step.

suggested.rationale: An authorization policy evaluator would let learners test which identity may act on which environment and see why a request is allowed or denied.

lessons.plain: An SLI is a measurement of how well a service is doing, such as the share of requests that succeeded or how many finished quickly enough. An SLO is a target for that measurement, such as keeping successful requests at 99.9 percent over a month. An SLA is a promise made to a customer, usually in a contract, with a consequence such as credits or refunds if it is missed. Think of a bus company: the SLI is the count of buses that arrived on time, the SLO is the company's internal goal of 95 percent on time, and the SLA is the refund policy it publishes for passengers.
lessons.guessPrompt: A website is up and returning pages for 99 percent of the minutes in a month, but every page takes around twenty seconds to load. Would you say it is meeting its reliability goal? What single measurement would you want to track to find out whether users are being served well?
lessons.teach:
An SLI, or service level indicator, is a measured ratio that describes one aspect of the user experience. The usual form is good events divided by valid events. An availability SLI is the number of valid requests that returned a non-error response divided by all valid requests. A latency SLI is the number of valid requests that finished under a chosen threshold divided by all valid requests. Counting a fraction rather than averaging matters, because an average can look fine while a tenth of users wait ten seconds.

An SLO, or service level objective, is the target you set for an SLI over a time window, such as at least 99.9 percent of requests succeeding over 28 days. An SLA, or service level agreement, is the external promise, normally written into a contract, with a penalty such as credits if it is missed. SLOs are usually stricter than SLAs, so the team gets warning before a contract is breached.

Worked example. A service receives 1,000,000 valid requests in a window. 999,300 of them return a non-error response, so the availability SLI is 99.93 percent. Against a 99.9 percent SLO, this is compliant. For latency, 980,000 requests finish within 300 ms, so the latency SLI is 98 percent. Against a 99 percent latency SLO, the service is out of compliance, even though availability looks healthy.

Common mistake: setting the SLO at 100 percent. No real system achieves that, and it leaves no room for planned maintenance or change, so the team ends up freezing releases.

When an SLI falls below its SLO, the team treats that as a signal to slow risky changes and focus on reliability work. The agreed target, not gut feeling, is what governs that decision.

questions.prompt: A file-conversion service records 400,000 valid requests in a 28-day window, and 397,200 of them return a non-error response. Step 1 is to identify the availability SLI, which is good events divided by valid events. Step 2 is to compute 397,200 divided by 400,000, which gives 99.3 percent. Step 3 is missing: the team compares that SLI with its 99.5 percent availability SLO. Which statement completes step 3 correctly?
choices: The SLO should be lowered to 99.3 percent so that the service passes the check.
The service is compliant, because the SLA is always the stricter target and overrides the SLO.
The service is compliant, since 99.3 percent is close enough to 99.5 percent to count.
The service is out of compliance, because 99.3 percent is below the 99.5 percent SLO, so the team should slow risky changes and focus on reliability work.
questions.why: An SLI below its SLO means the objective is missed, and the agreed target governs the response, which is to slow risky changes.

questions.prompt: A customer-facing ordering system has a 99.95 percent availability SLO and a separate contract that promises 99.9 percent with service credits. Which statement best describes the relationship between the two targets?
choices: The SLO and the SLA are the same number, so one of them is redundant.
The SLA is the internal target that the team tracks daily, and the SLO is the contractual promise with the credit penalty.
The SLO is the internal, usually stricter target over a time window, and the SLA is the external contractual promise with a penalty, so the team gets warning before the contract is breached.
The SLO is the external promise with a penalty, and the SLA is a stricter internal goal the team uses for planning.
questions.why: SLOs are internal targets usually stricter than the external SLA, which carries the contractual penalty, giving the team early warning.

questions.prompt: A search endpoint has an average response time of 120 ms over a window. However, 6 percent of its valid requests take about 8 seconds. The team wants a latency SLI that reflects user experience. Which approach best fits the idea of a latency SLI?
choices: Keep reporting the average response time, since 120 ms looks healthy and matches the mean.
Count the number of users who visited the search page and divide by the number of pages served.
Report the 8-second worst case as the SLI, so every slow request is visible on its own.
Count valid requests that finished under a chosen threshold, divide by all valid requests, and set an SLO on that fraction.
questions.why: A latency SLI is a fraction of valid requests under a threshold, which avoids the averaging problem where a slow tail is hidden by a healthy mean.

questions.prompt: A product manager proposes a 100 percent availability SLO for a new billing API, arguing that customers should never see an error. What is the main problem with this target?
choices: It is too strict to be written into a contract, so it must be turned into an SLA with no penalty.
It makes the error budget grow larger, so the team becomes careless about reliability.
No real system reaches 100 percent, and the target leaves no room for planned maintenance or change, so releases tend to get frozen.
It is impossible to measure availability at all, so the SLI cannot be calculated.
questions.why: A 100 percent SLO cannot be met by any real system and leaves no allowance for maintenance or change, which pushes teams into freezing releases.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between an SLI, an SLO and an SLA, using a latency example. Then name one limit of using a single average response time as your measurement.
lessons.modelAnswer: An SLI is the measurement itself, for example the percentage of requests that finish within 300 ms. An SLO is the internal target for that measurement, say 99 percent over 28 days. An SLA is the external promise to customers, usually in a contract, with a penalty such as service credits if it is breached. The SLO should be stricter than the SLA so we get warning before we break a contract. The limit of using an average response time is that averages hide the tail: if most requests take 100 ms but one in twenty takes 8 seconds, the average can look healthy while a real group of users has a terrible experience. A fraction-under-threshold SLI exposes that. Another limit is that an SLI only measures what we choose to count; if we measure only at the server and not at the load balancer, failures that never reach the server go unseen.
rubricPoints: Defines an SLI as a measured indicator, with the latency example given
Defines an SLO as an internal target over a time window
Defines an SLA as an external contractual promise with a consequence
Names a limit of averages, such as hidden tail latency, or of measurement placement

suggested.rationale: Being able to explain the three terms and their limits to a teammate is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine covers SLO definitions directly.

lessons.plain: An error budget is the amount of unreliability a service is allowed to have before it breaks its promise to users. If a service should work correctly for 99.9 percent of requests, the remaining 0.1 percent is the budget: permission to fail a little, which a team can spend on new releases and risky changes. While budget remains, the team can move quickly. When it runs out, the team slows down and fixes reliability first. The budget turns the argument between being careful and shipping features into a number both sides can read.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a service must succeed 99.9 percent of the time, and it receives 1,000,000 requests in a month, roughly how many failed requests can it afford before it misses its target?
lessons.teach:
Three terms first. A service level indicator (SLI) is a measurement of one aspect of service health, usually a ratio of good events to total events, such as the share of web requests that succeed within 300 milliseconds. A service level objective (SLO) is the target that SLI must meet over a time window, such as 99.9 percent over 30 days. The error budget is what the SLO leaves over: 100 percent minus the target, expressed as an allowance of bad events in that window.

Why it works: the budget converts reliability into something you can spend. Perfect reliability is expensive, and users often cannot tell a 99.99 percent service from a 99.9 percent one, while extra caution slows every release. Stating the allowance in advance lets a team decide, with data, when a risky change is affordable.

Worked example. The SLO is 99.9 percent of requests succeeding over 30 days, and the service receives 10 million requests in that window. Step one: the budget is 0.1 percent of 10 million, which is 10,000 failed requests. Step two: count failures so far, say 4,000. Step three: 4,000 divided by 10,000 is 40 percent spent, so 60 percent remains and a planned migration can go ahead while the burn is watched.

Common mistake: setting the SLO at 100 percent. That leaves a budget of zero, so every failure becomes a violation and no change can ever be justified. Consequence: when a service exhausts its budget, the usual policy is to pause feature launches and direct effort to reliability until the window recovers.

Cloud Service Mesh, Google's managed service mesh, reports SLIs from traffic it observes. Which requests count as good or bad, and the window it uses, are that product's own definitions; read them in its documentation rather than assuming they match the generic examples here. The error budget is the number that decides whether velocity or reliability wins a given week.

questions.prompt: A payments API has an SLO of 99.5 percent of requests succeeding over a 28-day window, and it receives 2 million requests in that window. Step one: the error budget is 0.5 percent of 2 million, which is 10,000 allowed failed requests. Step two: 7,500 failed requests have been counted so far. Step three is missing: work out what share of the budget is spent and what share remains.
choices: 25 percent of the budget is spent and 75 percent remains, because the 7,500 failures are subtracted from the budget.
75 percent of the budget is spent and 75 percent remains, since the total budget is counted twice.
75 percent of the budget is spent and 25 percent remains.
7,500 of the budget is spent, so 2,500 requests of allowance remain.
questions.why: Dividing 7,500 failures by the 10,000-failure budget gives 75 percent spent, and the rest of the budget (25 percent) remains.

questions.prompt: An SLO is 99.95 percent of events succeeding over a window. Which expression gives the error budget for that window?
choices: 99.95 percent of the total events in the window
0.05 percent of the total events in the window, counted as allowed bad events
The total number of events in the window, minus the number of successful events
0.95 percent of the total events, since the SLO is the complement of the budget
questions.why: The error budget is 100 percent minus the SLO target, applied to the total event count, which gives 0.05 percent of total events as the allowed bad events.

questions.prompt: A team running an internal job queue sets its SLO to 100 percent of jobs succeeding over 30 days. What is the main consequence of this choice?
choices: The team's measurement window becomes shorter, so the SLI is recalculated more often.
The team gets an unlimited budget, so it can ship any change without review.
The budget becomes zero, so any single failure is a violation and no risky change can be justified on the budget.
The SLI can no longer be measured, because a perfect target cannot be expressed as a ratio.
questions.why: A 100 percent target leaves 100 minus 100, which is zero allowed failures, so every failure uses up the entire allowance immediately.

questions.prompt: A service receives 4 million requests in a 30-day window and has an SLO of 99.8 percent of requests succeeding. So far 2,400 requests have failed. What share of the error budget has been spent?
choices: 30 percent, because the budget is 8,000 failures and 2,400 is 30 percent of that
70 percent, because 2,400 failures are subtracted from the 8,000 budget
60 percent, because the budget is 0.4 percent of requests
3 percent, because 2,400 is compared against 80,000 requests
questions.why: The budget is 0.2 percent of 4 million, which is 8,000 failures, and 2,400 divided by 8,000 is 30 percent spent.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants to ship a risky change to the checkout service this week, but the service has already used most of its monthly error budget. Explain to them what an error budget is, how it applies to this decision, and one limit of using it this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: An error budget is the allowed shortfall from a reliability target: if the SLO is 99.9 percent of requests succeeding over a month, the budget is the 0.1 percent of requests that may fail. For checkout, most of that allowance is already spent, so the budget says the service has little room left for failures. That makes the risky change hard to justify right now. The usual policy is to hold feature launches and put effort into stability until the budget recovers as the window rolls forward. One limit is that the budget only measures what the SLI counts. If the SLI misses a failure users actually feel, such as a slow but successful checkout, the budget can look healthy while customers suffer, so the team should check that the indicator reflects real experience.
rubricPoints: An error budget is the allowed amount of failure, equal to 100 percent minus the SLO target over a time window.
The SLI measures good events against total events, and the SLO is the target that measurement must meet.
The budget is used to decide whether a risky change is affordable, trading velocity against reliability.
When the budget is nearly or fully spent, the usual policy is to slow launches and prioritise reliability work.
The budget is only as honest as the SLI, so a poorly chosen indicator can hide user-visible failures.

suggested.rationale: Deciding whether a release is affordable under a given budget is an exam-style trade-off that is best reasoned through in a concrete situation.

lessons.plain: Reliability is not free, and it is not infinite. Every extra nine of uptime, such as going from 99 percent to 99.9 percent, shrinks the time a service may be down, but it usually costs more money and engineering effort. Opportunity cost means what you give up when you choose one option. Spending heavily on one more nine is money and time not spent on features or on other risks. The skill is asking whether the reliability gained is worth what it costs, given what an outage really hurts.
lessons.guessPrompt: A service is up 99 percent of the month. Going to 99.9 percent sounds like a small change. Roughly how much less downtime per month does that buy you, and why might the price of that improvement be far bigger than the number suggests?
lessons.teach:
A nine is shorthand for an availability target written as a percentage of time the service works. 99 percent is two nines, 99.9 percent is three, and 99.99 percent is four. Each added nine cuts the allowed downtime by a factor of ten. The allowance is the gap between 100 percent and your target, the room you have left for failure. Teams often call that allowance the error budget. Its full mechanism is taught separately, so here we only treat it as the amount of downtime you may spend.

Why this works as a decision tool: the gain from a nine is fixed and easy to measure in minutes, but the cost of achieving it rises fast. Moving from three nines to four usually means redundancy in more places, faster automatic failover, more on-call coverage, and slower, more careful releases. Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up. Money spent on a fourth nine is money not spent on features or on reducing other risks.

Worked example. A 30-day month has 43,200 minutes. Three nines allows 0.1 percent of that, which is 43.2 minutes of downtime. Four nines allows 4.32 minutes. Say an hour of outage costs the business 5,000 credits in lost orders. Three nines carries about 3,600 credits of expected loss per month, and four nines carries about 360. The fourth nine avoids about 3,240 credits a month. If the extra architecture costs 4,000 credits a month, it loses money. If it costs 2,000, it wins.

Common mistake: treating a higher target as automatically better, or forgetting that users experience the combined reliability of every dependency. Three serial dependencies each at 99.9 percent give about 99.7 percent overall, so the chain is weaker than any single link.

Consequence: a team that promises four nines while depending on a three-nines database has promised something its architecture cannot deliver.

questions.prompt: A payments API team runs a 31-day month, which has 44,640 minutes. At a 99.9 percent target, the allowed downtime is 44.64 minutes. Moving to 99.95 percent leaves 22.32 minutes. The team values an hour of outage at 8,000 credits. Step 1 is to find the avoided downtime: 44.64 minus 22.32 gives 22.32 minutes. Step 2 is missing: it turns those avoided minutes into a credit value. Step 3 is to compare that value with the cost of the upgrade. Which completion correctly fills in step 2?
choices: Divide 22.32 by 100 and then multiply by 8,000 to get 1,785.6 credits.
Divide 22.32 by 60 to get 0.372 hours, then multiply by 8,000 to get 2,976 credits.
Multiply 22.32 by 8,000 to get 178,560 credits.
Add 22.32 and 8,000 to get 8,022.32 credits.
questions.why: The cost is stated per hour, so the avoided minutes must first be converted to hours (22.32 divided by 60 is 0.372) before multiplying by 8,000 credits.

questions.prompt: A service has a 99.5 percent availability target over a 28-day month, which has 40,320 minutes. How many minutes of downtime does the target allow?
choices: 2,016 minutes
0.5 minutes
201.6 minutes
20.16 minutes
questions.why: The allowance is 0.5 percent of 40,320 minutes, which is 201.6 minutes; the other options come from misplacing the decimal point or skipping the percentage step.

questions.prompt: A team has three services in a chain: one at 99.95 percent and one at 99.9 percent, where a user request needs both to work. Which overall availability is the best estimate for a user request?
choices: About 99.95 percent
About 99.90 percent
About 99.99 percent
About 99.85 percent
questions.why: When every link in a serial chain must work, the availabilities multiply (0.9995 times 0.999 is about 0.9985), so the result is weaker than either single service.

questions.prompt: A team currently runs at 99.8 percent annual availability and is considering 99.9 percent. Downtime costs 1,200 credits per hour, and the upgrade costs 14,000 credits a year. Using a 365-day year of 525,600 minutes, what should the team decide?
choices: Do not upgrade, because a 99.9 percent target cannot be measured.
Upgrade, since a higher availability target is always the better choice for users.
Upgrade, because 525.6 avoided minutes is more than eight hours.
Do not upgrade, because the avoided loss of about 10,512 credits is less than the 14,000-credit cost.
questions.why: The extra nine avoids 525.6 minutes (8.76 hours, about 10,512 credits), which is less than the 14,000-credit cost, so the opportunity cost makes the upgrade a losing trade.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why moving from 99.9 to 99.99 percent availability is not automatically worth doing. Name the cost you would weigh against the gain, and name one limit of the calculation.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each nine divides the allowed downtime by ten. 99.9 percent allows about 43 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month, and 99.99 percent allows about 4 minutes, so the gain is roughly 39 minutes a month. Whether that is worth it depends on what those minutes cost us and what the extra reliability costs to build. Extra regions, automatic failover, and more on-call coverage all cost money and slow down releases. That is the opportunity cost. We should compare the expected loss avoided with the monthly cost of the change. One limit is that the answer depends on an outage cost we may have only estimated. Another is that our reliability is capped by our dependencies: if a third-party service offers only three nines, a four-nines target is not realistic until that changes.
rubricPoints: Explains that each added nine cuts allowed downtime by a factor of ten
Names the cost of the extra reliability, such as redundancy, on-call, or slower releases, as the opportunity cost
Compares expected loss avoided against the cost of the change rather than assuming more nines are better
States a limit, such as estimated outage cost or the reliability ceiling set by dependencies

suggested.rationale: A planned cost model engine would let the learner price the cost of each extra nine against downtime loss in fictional credits and see where the trade-off flips.

lessons.plain: A service has a life, much like a bridge. It is planned before anyone uses it, opened to traffic, changed and kept safe while it runs, and eventually closed and taken down. Managing that life well means deciding before launch what working well enough means, releasing changes in small steps so a mistake is cheap to undo, keeping the service patched and supported while people depend on it, and retiring it without breaking the people who still rely on it. The design review, the opening day, the scheduled inspections, and the planned demolition with a clear detour are all part of owning the bridge, not afterthoughts.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants to release a change to a service that thousands of people use every day. Before looking anything up, what would you do to limit the damage if the change turns out to be broken, and why would that choice help?
lessons.teach:
The service lifecycle is the set of stages a service goes through: planning, deployment, maintenance, and retirement. Planning means deciding before launch who owns the service, what level of reliability it must meet (a service level objective is a stated target, such as the share of requests that must succeed), how much load to expect, what it depends on, and what should happen when it fails. Deployment means putting a new version into production. A staged rollout, sometimes called a canary, sends a small share of traffic to the new version first, compares its health with the old version, and only then widens the share. Maintenance is the ongoing work: security patches, runtime and library upgrades, and capacity changes. Each of these is itself a deployment, so the same care applies. Retirement means announcing that a service or version will stop, moving its consumers to a replacement, stopping traffic, and removing resources and data according to the retention rules.

This works because small steps limit the blast radius, which is the number of users a bad change can hurt. A plan written before launch turns vague advice into concrete checks.

Worked example: a pricing service version 2 is ready. Step 1: planning has already set the target that at least 99.9 percent of requests succeed, and version 1 remains deployable. Step 2: send 5 percent of traffic to version 2. Step 3: over ten minutes, version 2 fails 0.4 percent of requests while version 1 fails 0.1 percent. That is above the agreed target, so all traffic goes back to version 1, and only 5 percent of users were ever exposed. Step 4: fix the defect, then repeat the staged rollout at 5, 25, and 100 percent.

Common mistake: treating retirement as simply deleting something. Other services may still call the old endpoint, and they fail the moment it disappears. In a running system, an unannounced removal turns a planned change into an outage for the callers you never checked. A lifecycle is only complete when the last consumer has moved off.

questions.prompt: A route-planning service at a delivery company is moving from version 4 to version 5. Planning set a service level objective (SLO), a stated reliability target, that at least 99.5 percent of requests must succeed, and version 4 stays deployable. Step 1: send 10 percent of traffic to version 5. Step 2: over 20 minutes, version 5 succeeds on 99.7 percent of its requests while version 4 succeeds on 99.8 percent. Step 3 is missing. Which action comes next?
choices: Keep version 5 at 10 percent for 30 days before making any decision.
Send all traffic to version 5 at once, because it stays within target.
Roll back to version 4, because version 5 succeeds slightly less often than version 4.
Widen version 5 to 25 percent of traffic and keep comparing its health before any further step.
questions.why: Version 5's failure rate of 0.3 percent is under the 0.5 percent the SLO allows, so the staged rollout continues by widening the share, while still comparing health at each stage.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is the blast radius of a change to a service?
choices: The time it takes for the change to reach every server in the fleet.
The count of lines of code that differ between the two versions.
The amount of memory the new version uses compared with the old version.
The number of users a bad change could hurt before it is noticed or rolled back.
questions.why: The teaching text defines blast radius as the number of users a bad change can hurt, and small staged steps exist to limit it.

questions.prompt: A ticket-printing service plans to retire its version 1 endpoint. Two internal dashboards still call that endpoint, and version 2 is live. What should the team do to finish the retirement correctly?
choices: Announce the removal, move both dashboards to version 2, confirm no callers remain on version 1, then stop traffic and remove resources per the retention rules.
Stop traffic to version 1 immediately and restore it only if someone complains.
Leave version 1 running indefinitely so that no consumer is ever affected.
Delete the version 1 endpoint on Friday and let the dashboard owners report any errors.
questions.why: A lifecycle is complete only when the last consumer has moved off, so the announced move and the check for remaining callers come before stopping traffic and removing resources.

questions.prompt: A team removes an old image-resize endpoint on a Friday afternoon without announcing it. They had not listed which other services depended on it. What is the most likely result?
choices: Nothing changes, because unused endpoints cannot cause failures.
Callers the team never checked begin failing as soon as the endpoint disappears, turning a planned change into an outage.
The removal is automatically reversed by the platform after one hour.
Only the team's own staging environment is affected, since production traffic is never routed to retired endpoints.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that other services may still call a removed endpoint and fail the moment it disappears, which is the outage an unannounced retirement causes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would take a new version of a service through planning, staged deployment, and eventual retirement of the old version. Name one limit or tradeoff that a staged rollout introduces.
lessons.modelAnswer: Before launch I would write down the reliability target, the expected load, the owner, and what counts as a failed release, so the team agrees on the rules in advance. For deployment I would send a small share of traffic to the new version, compare its failure rate with the old version, and widen the share only if it stays within the target. Maintenance changes like patches go through the same staged process. For retirement I would announce the deprecation date, confirm that no callers still use the old version, switch traffic off, and then remove the resources. The main tradeoff of a staged rollout is that it takes longer to finish, and a problem that only shows up at high traffic may not appear until the rollout is wide. A small slice also gives weak signals for rare failures, so the team must keep watching after each step.
rubricPoints: Planning sets the reliability target, owner, and expected load before the first release.
A staged rollout exposes only a small share of users first and compares health against the old version.
Retirement requires announcing the change and confirming no consumers remain before removal.
A staged rollout trades speed for safety and can miss rare failures that appear only at higher traffic.

suggested.rationale: The deployment-strategies engine would let the learner step a release through traffic shares and decide when to widen or revert, which is the deployment and maintenance half of this objective.

lessons.plain: Capacity planning is deciding, before you need it, how much computing room your system can actually get. Cloud providers limit how much you can use in several ways: a quota is a cap on how much of something your account may consume, a limit is a fixed ceiling that often cannot be raised, and a reservation is a promise that a specific amount of capacity will be there when you need it. Some work, such as large batch jobs, can also wait for scarce hardware to free up. Knowing which of these is your real constraint decides whether a surge of traffic or a big job succeeds or fails.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's nightly batch job needs 40 machines at once, and the job fails with a message about exceeding a quota even though the cloud console shows plenty of unused machines in the region. What do you think the quota is, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
A quota is a cap that a cloud provider sets on how much of a resource your project may use, such as CPU cores in one region or API calls per minute. Quotas are usually raised by request. A limit is a fixed maximum on a single kind of object, such as how many instances one group may hold, and it often cannot be changed. A reservation is a promise that a set amount of capacity will exist in a specific zone, so a scale-up does not fail because the shared pool is empty. You pay for reserved capacity whether or not you use it. Dynamic Workload Scheduler, or DWS, is a scheduler for batch and machine learning jobs that need scarce accelerators such as GPUs. In flex-start mode you request capacity and the job starts when it becomes free, within a time window. In calendar mode you book a future window of fixed length.

Why this works: capacity is finite, so you match predictable demand to reserved or scheduled supply, and you raise quotas before you need them. Worked example: a training job needs 8 GPUs for 6 hours. Step 1: check the GPU quota for the region; if it is 4, the job can never start, so request an increase. Step 2: submit the job to DWS in flex-start mode so it queues until 8 GPUs are free. Step 3: if the job must run at 02:00 every night, book a calendar window instead. Step 4: watch the job status, not just the quota.

Common mistake: treating quota as guaranteed supply. A project can have quota for 100 CPUs while the zone has no free machines, so requests fail with a capacity error, not a quota error. In a running system this shows up during a traffic surge, when autoscaling cannot add instances even though the cap has room.

Quota is permission to use capacity, not a promise that capacity exists.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company expects its checkout service to scale from 40 to 180 virtual machines in one zone for a 2-hour sale on Friday. Step 1: it checks the regional CPU quota and finds 500 cores, which covers 180 machines of 2 cores each (360 cores), so the cap has room. Step 2: it decides no quota increase is needed. Step 3: it reviews the zone's history and sees that machines of that type ran out in this zone during past sales. Step 4 (missing): to make sure the scale-up succeeds on Friday, the company should take which action?
choices: Raise the CPU quota to 2000 cores, since quota is what decides whether a scale-up can succeed
Raise the autoscaler maximum to 1000 instances so the instance cap never blocks the sale
Submit the checkout service to Dynamic Workload Scheduler in flex-start mode so it starts when capacity frees up
Create a reservation for 180 machines of that type in that zone before Friday, accepting that the reserved capacity is paid for even if it sits idle
questions.why: Quota already has room, and the past failures came from the zone running out of free machines, which only a reservation in that zone guarantees, at the cost of paying for it whether used or not.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates a quota from a limit?
choices: A quota is a fixed maximum on one kind of object, and a limit is an adjustable cap on total project usage
A quota is an adjustable cap on how much of a resource a project may use, usually raised by request, while a limit is a fixed maximum on a single kind of object that often cannot be changed
Both are fixed maximums that cannot be changed, and both guarantee that capacity exists when needed
A quota and a limit are two names for the same cap, and neither can be raised by request
questions.why: The teaching text defines a quota as an adjustable cap raised by request and a limit as a fixed maximum on one kind of object that often cannot be changed.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a nightly job that needs 4 GPUs for 2 hours. Its project quota shows 8 GPUs in the region, yet the job fails with a capacity error and never starts. What is the most accurate explanation and fix?
choices: The zone has no free GPUs at that moment, because quota is permission to use capacity and not a promise that capacity exists; queueing the job in flex-start mode or reserving capacity addresses it
The quota is too low, so the firm should raise it to 16 GPUs and the job will start
The job should be booked in calendar mode for a window shorter than 2 hours, because shorter windows always get capacity
The reservation is consuming the quota, so the firm should cancel its reservation to free up GPUs
questions.why: Because quota permits use but does not guarantee free machines, a capacity error with quota available points to a supply shortage in the zone, which queueing or reserving addresses.

questions.prompt: A research group needs 16 accelerators for exactly 6 hours every day, starting at 01:00 sharp. Which Dynamic Workload Scheduler option fits this requirement, and why?
choices: A reservation, because it guarantees the capacity without any time window and so meets the schedule automatically
Raising the quota, because the quota is what sets the start time of scheduled jobs
Calendar mode, because it books a future window of fixed length, which suits a job that must start at a set time
Flex-start mode, because it starts the job at the exact requested clock time whenever capacity frees up
questions.why: Calendar mode books a fixed-length future window, which matches a job that must run at a set time, whereas flex-start only starts the job within a flexible time window once capacity is free.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a quota, a reservation, and a Dynamic Workload Scheduler job, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on each for a surge of traffic or a large batch run.
lessons.modelAnswer: A quota is a cap on how much of something our project may use, like GPUs in a region. It is permission, not a guarantee that machines exist. A reservation is a promise that a set amount of capacity will be free in a given zone, so scale-ups do not fail for lack of room. The tradeoff is cost: we pay for reserved capacity even when idle. Dynamic Workload Scheduler lets a batch or ML job wait for scarce accelerators, either in flex-start mode, where it starts when capacity frees up, or in calendar mode, where we book a future window. Its limit is timing: a flex-start job may wait, so it fits batch work, not a live traffic surge. For a surge we need a reservation or headroom already in place, and we should check quota well before the event.
rubricPoints: Defines quota as a project-level cap that can be raised on request, separate from actual available capacity
Explains that a reservation guarantees capacity in a zone at the cost of paying for it when idle
Describes DWS as a scheduler for batch or ML jobs that wait for scarce accelerators, with flex-start and calendar modes
Names a concrete tradeoff, such as cost of idle reservations or waiting time for scheduled jobs

suggested.rationale: Choosing between a quota increase, a reservation, and a scheduled job for a given scenario is an exam-style judgement that benefits from reasoning through situations.

lessons.plain: Autoscaling means a service adds copies of itself when it is busy and removes them when it is quiet, so you do not pay for idle machines or run out during a rush. On Google Cloud this is configured in three places: a group of identical virtual machines, a serverless container service, or a Kubernetes cluster. Each one needs a rule that says what to measure, the minimum and maximum number of copies allowed, and how quickly to react. Designing it well means choosing a signal that truly reflects load and accounting for the delay before new copies can start helping.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web service runs on 3 virtual machine copies, each at 95 percent CPU, and traffic is still climbing. What would you expect the scaling system to do over the next few minutes, and what could stop it from adding capacity as quickly as you would like?
lessons.teach:
Autoscaling is the rule-driven adjustment of how many running copies of a workload exist. A managed instance group (MIG) is a set of identical virtual machines created from one template and kept at a target size by the platform. Cloud Run is Google's serverless container platform, where a service runs as container instances that the platform creates and stops for you. Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) runs containers as pods on a cluster of nodes; a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the number of pods, and a cluster autoscaler changes the number of nodes.

Why it works: each platform repeatedly compares a measured signal with a target and calculates how many copies would bring that signal back to the target. Every design needs four decisions: the signal (CPU utilization for a MIG, concurrent requests per instance for Cloud Run, CPU or a custom metric for pods), a minimum count, a maximum count, and a cooldown or stabilization period that stops the system reacting to a momentary spike.

Worked example: a MIG has 4 instances, a target of 60 percent CPU, a minimum of 2 and a maximum of 10. Average CPU is 90 percent. Desired size is 4 times 90 divided by 60, which is 6. The group adds 2 instances. Once they start and CPU falls, the group settles without exceeding the maximum.

Common mistake: setting the maximum too low, or ignoring startup time. New instances take minutes to boot and warm caches, so a group may keep adding copies while the first ones are not yet serving traffic, or it may hit its maximum during a surge and start dropping requests.

Consequence: under a sudden surge, a service whose scaling is too slow or capped too tightly shows rising latency and errors before capacity catches up. Good autoscaling design picks a signal that tracks real load, sets a maximum that fits the budget and downstream limits, and allows for startup delay.

questions.prompt: A Cloud Run service is set to a target of 50 concurrent requests per instance, with a maximum of 12 instances. Right now 240 concurrent requests are in flight across 2 instances. Step 1: the platform divides total concurrent requests by the target, giving 240 divided by 50, which is 4.8. Step 2 (missing from this write-up): decide how to turn 4.8 into a whole number of instances, since the platform cannot run part of an instance. Step 3: apply the maximum of 12 as a ceiling. What instance count does the service move to?
choices: Round 4.8 up to 5, since a fraction of an instance still needs a whole instance to serve it
Use 120 as the new count because that is the load per instance
Keep 240 divided by 50 as 4.8 instances
Round 4.8 down to 4, since partial instances are not allowed
questions.why: Desired count is a whole number of instances that can carry the load, so the fractional 4.8 is rounded up to 5, which stays under the cap of 12.

questions.prompt: A GKE pod autoscaler keeps adding and removing pods every few seconds during a short traffic spike. Which setting is designed to stop the system reacting to a momentary spike?
choices: The stabilization period
The node pool machine type
The minimum pod count
A CPU target set to zero
questions.why: A stabilization or cooldown period is the window that stops an autoscaler reacting to brief, momentary changes in its signal.

questions.prompt: A managed instance group has a maximum of 6 instances, but a traffic surge would require about 9 to meet its target. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The group switches its signal from CPU to memory to get more headroom
The group raises its own maximum to 9 once CPU passes the target
Capacity stays capped at 6, so latency and errors can rise until load falls or the cap is raised
The group creates 9 instances and then deletes 3 at random
questions.why: The maximum is a hard ceiling, so the group cannot add copies beyond 6 and the shortfall shows up as slower responses or dropped requests.

questions.prompt: In Google Kubernetes Engine, which component changes the number of nodes in the cluster, as opposed to the number of pods?
choices: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
The Cloud Run concurrency setting
The managed instance group template
The cluster autoscaler
questions.why: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes pod counts, while the cluster autoscaler adjusts the number of nodes the cluster runs on.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up autoscaling for a service on Cloud Run compared with a managed instance group, and name one limit or tradeoff of the setting you would choose for each.
lessons.modelAnswer: For a managed instance group, I would scale on CPU utilization with a target around 60 percent, a sensible minimum for availability, and a maximum that the budget and any downstream database can actually handle. The limit is that CPU lags behind real load and new VMs need minutes to boot, so the group reacts late to a sharp spike. For Cloud Run, I would rely on request concurrency per instance and set a maximum instance count to cap cost and protect the database. The tradeoff is that a low maximum can cause queueing and timeouts during a surge, while a minimum above zero keeps instances warm and avoids cold-start latency but costs money even when idle. I would tell the team that these numbers are starting points to check against load tests, not guarantees.
rubricPoints: Names a concrete signal for each platform, such as CPU for a MIG and concurrency for Cloud Run
Explains min and max counts and what each protects against
States a tradeoff or limit, such as startup lag, cost of warm instances, or a cap causing queueing
Notes that settings should be validated under realistic load

suggested.rationale: The planned autoscaling-policies engine would let the learner set signals, bounds and cooldowns and watch the resulting behaviour under a simulated surge, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: When part of a running service starts misbehaving during an incident, one fast way to stop customers feeling it is to take that part out of rotation. Picture a shop with several checkout lanes where one scanner keeps failing. You close that lane, send the queue to the open lanes, and repair the scanner calmly afterwards. Engineers do the same with individual servers, zones or whole regions: they stop sending new requests to the bad part and move traffic to healthy parts. The goal is to reduce harm now, not to find the root cause first.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your API runs on three identical servers behind one front door, and one server returns errors for half its requests. Before you know why it fails, what is the fastest way to stop most users seeing errors, and what would you check first to make sure that action is safe?
lessons.teach:
Draining means removing a backend, such as one server, one zone or one replica, from the set that receives new requests, while letting requests already in progress finish. A load balancer is the component that spreads incoming requests across backends. A health check is a periodic probe the load balancer uses to decide whether a backend is fit to receive traffic. Connection draining is the grace period that lets in-flight requests, meaning requests already being processed, complete before the backend is fully removed. Redirecting means changing where traffic goes, for example sending users to a healthy region or a standby copy of the service. Both are mitigations: they limit user impact now, and they are reversible, which is why they are often chosen before diagnosis is finished.

Why it works: failures usually sit in one identifiable part of the fleet. If the load balancer stops routing to that part, the healthy parts absorb the work and the error rate falls, even though the broken part is still broken.

Worked example: an API runs on three backends behind a load balancer, and one backend returns errors for 40 percent of requests. Step one: confirm from metrics that the errors are concentrated on that backend. Step two: drain it, so the load balancer stops sending it new requests while its current requests finish. Step three: watch the error rate fall toward zero as the two healthy backends take the load. Step four: investigate the broken backend offline, and return it to service only after its health check passes.

Common mistake: draining so much capacity that the remaining backends overload, which turns one partial failure into a full outage. Always check that the survivors can carry the load before removing a part.

Consequence in a running system: a backend that holds state, such as an unflushed write buffer, can lose work if it is removed abruptly, so confirm the part is safe to remove before you drain it.

questions.prompt: A checkout service runs in two regions. Region us-west takes 70 percent of traffic and region us-east takes 30 percent. Metrics show that 35 percent of requests in us-west return errors after a bad configuration push, while us-east is clean. The team follows these steps. Step 1: confirm from metrics that the errors are concentrated in us-west. Step 2: redirect traffic away from us-west so that users are sent to us-east. Step 3: missing. Step 4: watch the error rate fall as us-east serves the traffic. Which choice is the missing step 3?
choices: Check that us-east has enough spare capacity for all the traffic.
Wait for the us-west error rate to reach zero before changing routes.
Roll back the configuration push in us-west before redirecting anything.
Lower the us-west health check timeout so that it fails sooner.
questions.why: Before redirecting, the team must confirm that the healthy region can carry the full load, because us-east currently handles only 30 percent and an overload would turn a partial failure into a wider outage.

questions.prompt: A video transcoding service has six workers behind a load balancer, which is the component that spreads incoming requests across backends. Worker 5 starts failing its health check, which is a periodic probe that decides whether a backend is fit to receive traffic. What does the load balancer do with worker 5?
choices: It deletes the in-flight requests that worker 5 is still processing.
It sends worker 5's in-flight requests to a backend in another region.
It stops sending worker 5 new requests while the other five workers take the traffic.
It kills worker 5's running processes to free its memory.
questions.why: A failed health check tells the load balancer that the backend is not fit to receive new traffic, so it stops routing new requests to it while the rest of the fleet absorbs the work.
