questions.prompt: A reporting API runs on four backends, and each one is at 60 percent of its capacity, meaning each handles 60 units of work against a limit of 100 units. An operator wants to drain one backend to fix it. Should the operator drain it?
choices: Yes, because draining removes the load from the backend, so the other three still run at 60 percent.
No, because draining one backend always causes a full outage.
No, three backends can never carry the load that four can carry.
Yes, the three remaining backends would each run at about 80 percent of capacity, which is within limits.
questions.why: The total load is 240 units, which spread across three backends is 80 units each, below the 100-unit limit, so the survivors can safely carry it and the drain is acceptable.

questions.prompt: A team drains a backend that holds an unflushed write buffer, meaning writes that have been accepted but not yet saved to durable storage. The buffer is lost when the backend is removed. Which check was missed before draining?
choices: Whether the load balancer uses round-robin or least-connections routing.
Whether the backend's health check URL returns a success status code.
Whether the backend was deployed in the same zone as its clients.
Whether the backend holds state, such as unflushed writes, that could be lost when it is removed.
questions.why: Draining lets in-flight requests finish but does not protect state held only in the backend, so the team must confirm the backend is safe to remove before draining it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would drain a backend during an incident instead of fixing it in place, and name one limit or risk of draining.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would drain a backend when it is clearly the source of user-facing errors and I cannot yet tell why it fails. Draining removes it from the load balancer's rotation, so new requests go to healthy backends, while requests already running are allowed to finish. That cuts user impact quickly and is reversible, so the broken machine can be investigated safely afterwards. The main limit is capacity: the remaining backends must absorb the extra load, or draining just moves the outage onto them, so I check their utilisation first. Another risk is state: a backend holding unsaved work may lose data if removed abruptly, so I confirm it is safe to drain. Draining mitigates the symptom; it does not fix the cause, so the investigation still follows.
rubricPoints: Draining stops new requests reaching a bad backend while letting in-flight requests finish.
The aim is to reduce user impact quickly, before the root cause is known.
Draining is reversible, so the broken part can be investigated safely afterwards.
A key limit is that surviving backends must have enough capacity, or the outage just moves.

suggested.rationale: Its work of moving dispatcher reads off a lagging replica is the closest existing practice to redirecting traffic away from a bad part during an incident.

lessons.plain: During a production incident, one of the fastest fixes is to add more machines or more processing power so the service can handle the work it is receiving. Think of a checkout line that has backed up: opening another till can shorten the queue quickly. This is called adding capacity. It buys time and can stop customers from seeing errors, but it does not explain why the line grew in the first place. Adding capacity helps when the real problem is too little room, and it can make things worse when the real bottleneck is somewhere else.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web service starts timing out because twice as many users arrive as usual, and every server is already at full processor load. Before anyone reads a single log, what is the quickest step that might stop customers seeing errors in the next ten minutes, and what is one reason that step might fail to fix the problem?
lessons.teach:
An incident is an unplanned event that degrades a service users depend on. Capacity means how much work a system can handle at once, such as requests per second. A bottleneck is the one part of a system that runs out of room first and limits everything else. An SLI (service level indicator) is a measurement of how well a service is doing, such as the share of requests that succeed. An SLO (service level objective) is the target for that measurement, such as 99.9 percent of requests succeeding over 30 days. The error budget is the failure room the SLO allows, here the 0.1 percent of requests that may fail.

Adding capacity works because it raises the amount of work the system can absorb, so the overloaded part stops rejecting or delaying requests. Worked example: five servers each handle 200 requests per second, giving 1,000 per second in total. Traffic rises to 1,500 per second. Step 1: the extra 500 requests per second have nowhere to go, so about one third of requests fail. Step 2: add three servers, raising capacity to 1,600 per second. Step 3: the 1,500 requests now fit, and failures fall to nearly zero. Step 4: check the error budget. Over 30 days at an average of 500 requests per second, the budget is about 1.3 million failed requests. Twenty minutes of one third failing is about 600,000 failures, roughly 46 percent of the month's budget spent in one event.

The common mistake is adding capacity without finding the bottleneck. If every new web server opens connections to a database that has a fixed connection limit, the database fails sooner and the incident spreads. New instances may also start with empty caches, which adds load at first. In a running system, extra capacity is a mitigation that stops the budget burning. It is not a fix until the cause is understood.

questions.prompt: A ticket-search service runs 4 servers, each handling 300 requests per second, so capacity is 1,200 per second. Traffic rises to 1,800 per second. Step 1: the extra 600 requests per second have nowhere to go, so one third of requests fail. Step 2: add 2 servers, raising capacity to 1,800 per second. Step 3 is missing from this list. Step 4: the 1,800 requests now fit, and failures fall to nearly zero. Which choice best fills Step 3?
choices: Raise the SLO target to 99.99 percent so the incident no longer counts against the error budget.
Restart the original four servers to clear their request queues before adding anything else.
Find the shared dependency that every request also uses, here a geocoding quota of 1,000 calls per second, and confirm it can absorb the new 1,800 calls per second before trusting the added servers.
Recalculate the error budget using 7 days of data instead of 30 so the incident looks smaller.
questions.why: A new bottleneck can appear in a shared resource that all the added capacity depends on, so checking that resource is the step that keeps the added servers from being wasted.

questions.prompt: An SLO (service level objective, the target for a measurement) is 99.5 percent of requests succeeding over 28 days. The error budget (the failure room the SLO allows) is therefore 0.5 percent of requests. Which statement best explains how adding capacity during an incident helps protect that budget?
choices: It changes the SLI, the measurement itself, so that only successful requests are counted.
It resets the 28-day budget counter so the incident is forgiven.
It lowers the SLO target so fewer requests count as failures.
It raises the amount of work the system can absorb, so the overloaded part stops rejecting requests and failures stop accumulating.
questions.why: Adding capacity works because it lets the overloaded part handle more work, which stops the failures that would otherwise spend the error budget.

questions.prompt: A team adds 10 new application instances during an outage, but the error rate stays high. All the instances open connections to one shared database that has a fixed connection limit. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: The new instances moved the bottleneck to the shared database, so the extra capacity cannot be used.
The error budget resets whenever instances are added, so the error rate is being measured incorrectly.
Adding instances always reduces error budget burn, so the team should wait longer before checking anything.
The SLO is set too high and should be lowered to match current traffic.
questions.why: When added capacity pushes load into a part with a fixed limit, that part becomes the new bottleneck and the extra capacity goes unused.

questions.prompt: A service has an SLO of 99.5 percent success over 28 days and averages 800 requests per second. The error budget is 0.5 percent of all requests in that window. During a 15-minute incident, 40 percent of requests fail until capacity is added. Roughly what share of the month's error budget does this one incident use?
choices: 0.3 percent
30 percent
3 percent
12 percent
questions.why: The incident produces about 288,000 failures (800 times 900 seconds times 0.40), and the budget is about 9.7 million failures, so the incident uses roughly 3 percent.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when adding capacity is a sound way to mitigate an incident and when it is not. Use the terms SLI, SLO and error budget in your answer, and name the main limit or tradeoff of adding capacity.
lessons.modelAnswer: Adding capacity is a sound mitigation when the service is failing because it simply has more work than it can handle, and when a fast reduction in failures matters more than finding the cause right now. We can check the SLI, such as the share of successful requests, and see whether the SLO is at risk and how fast the error budget is burning. The main tradeoff is that extra capacity hides the symptom and costs money. It can also push the overload to a downstream part, such as a database with a connection limit, and make things worse. So after adding capacity we should confirm the bottleneck has moved or cleared, watch the error budget stop falling, and then find the real cause before we treat the incident as resolved.
rubricPoints: Adding capacity is a mitigation that buys time and reduces errors, not a root-cause fix.
Use the SLI and SLO to judge whether the incident is hurting users enough to act, and track how fast the error budget burns.
Name the bottleneck first, because more capacity at the wrong part can overload a downstream dependency.
Name the tradeoffs: added cost, hidden symptoms, and possible cold-start or connection-limit effects.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner work through a capacity-exhausted incident during a traffic surge, which is the situation this objective describes.

lessons.plain: When a new version of a service goes out and things start breaking, you have two basic moves. You can put back the previous version that was working, which is called rolling back, or you can ship a new fix on top of the broken release, which is called fixing forward. Choosing between them during an incident is about speed and risk: how quickly users stop being harmed, and whether the fallback itself is safe to run. This lesson shows how to choose, using the reliability targets your team already agreed on.
lessons.guessPrompt: A release went out 10 minutes ago and the error rate tripled. The fix you are confident in will take about 40 minutes to build, test and ship. Would you undo the release now or ship the fix first, and what fact would change your answer?
lessons.teach:
A release is a new version of software pushed to live users. A rollback is redeploying the last known good version, meaning the most recent version you have evidence was healthy. Fixing forward means shipping a new change that corrects the problem instead of going back. An SLI (service level indicator) is a measurement of health, such as the share of requests that succeed. An SLO (service level objective) is the target for that measurement, such as 99.9 percent over 30 days. The error budget is the failure you are allowed under that target, here 0.1 percent of requests.

Rollback usually wins when the bad change is recent and the previous version is still compatible with the data and other services. The old version has already served real traffic, so its behaviour is known, and redeploying it is a fast, low-risk action. Fixing forward needs a build, tests and a new rollout, all of which take time while users keep failing.

Worked example. The SLO is 99.9 percent success, so the error budget is 0.1 percent of requests. The release pushes errors to 6 percent. Step one: each minute at 6 percent failure consumes far more than the whole budget allows. Step two: a rollback takes about 5 minutes and returns errors to baseline. Step three: a 40-minute fix-forward would keep burning budget for roughly 40 minutes before any relief. Step four: roll back first, then fix the change calmly and redeploy it later.

Common mistake: rolling back without checking whether the release also ran a database migration or wrote data that the old version cannot read. The rollback then creates a second outage. Check compatibility before you act.

In a running system, a rollback that is quick but incompatible can turn one failure into two, and the error budget keeps draining while people debug. A rollback is the default first move when the old version is safe to run and the new one is clearly the cause.

questions.prompt: A ticketing service called Harbor Tickets has a 99.5 percent success SLO over 28 days, so its error budget is 0.5 percent of requests. Its latest release raises failed requests to 3 percent. A rollback to the previous version takes about 8 minutes, and a fix-forward would take about 30 minutes. Work the decision. Step one: the 3 percent failure rate burns budget far faster than the 0.5 percent allowance. Step two: the rollback is much faster than the fix. Step three: [missing]. Step four: roll back now and fix the change calmly later. Which choice correctly completes step three?
choices: Check whether the fix-forward patch can wait until the error budget is fully spent.
Confirm the release did not run a database migration or write data that the previous version cannot read.
Ask the team to rewrite the release notes before deciding anything.
Measure the release's average response time against a 200 millisecond target.
questions.why: Before rolling back, you must confirm the old version can still read whatever the new release wrote, because an incompatible rollback can cause a second outage.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines a rollback during an incident?
choices: Shipping a new change that corrects the bug while the faulty release keeps serving users.
Pausing all traffic until the on-call engineer finishes debugging.
Redeploying the most recent version you have evidence was healthy.
Lowering the SLO target so fewer requests count as failures.
questions.why: A rollback redeploys the last known good version, the most recent version with evidence it was healthy, which is different from fixing forward with a new change.

questions.prompt: A team rolls back a release that changed the stored data layout in a way the previous version cannot read. What is the most likely result?
choices: The SLO target is automatically raised to match the new version.
Nothing changes, because rollbacks never affect stored data.
The error budget refills immediately because the version number changed.
The old version may fail on the changed data, so the rollback itself can create a second outage.
questions.why: Rolling back to a version that cannot read the newly written data is the classic failure case, and it turns one failure into two while the error budget keeps draining.

questions.prompt: A service has a 99.95 percent SLO over one month and receives 2,000,000 requests that month. How many failed requests is its error budget, and what does that imply for a release?
choices: 1,000 failed requests; a release that pushes failures far above that rate spends the budget quickly.
No failures are allowed at all, because any SLO above 99.9 percent means zero tolerance.
10,000 failed requests, since 0.5 percent is the allowance.
2,000 failed requests, since 0.1 percent of traffic is the allowance.
questions.why: The error budget is 0.05 percent of 2,000,000, which is 1,000 failed requests, so a release that drives failures well above that rate burns the budget quickly.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never run an incident how to decide between rolling back and fixing forward. Use the SLO and error budget in your explanation, and name one limit or tradeoff of rolling back.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking whether the previous version is safe to run again. If the bad release is recent and the old version still works with the current data and other services, rolling back is usually the fastest way to stop the errors. We can check the SLI, the error rate, and see how fast the error budget is being used. If a fix would take much longer, every extra minute at that failure rate spends budget we may not have. The limit is that a rollback can fail if the release changed a database schema or wrote data the old version cannot read, so I check that first. Another tradeoff is that rolling back hides the cause, so after the service is healthy we still need to find and fix the original bug before we ship it again.
rubricPoints: Defines rollback as redeploying the last known good version and fix-forward as shipping a correction.
Uses the SLI, SLO or error budget to justify speed, showing how fast budget is being consumed.
Names a limit of rollback, such as schema or data incompatibility with the older version.
Notes that rollback restores service but does not fix the root cause, which still needs follow-up.

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner decide and carry out a rollback under pressure, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Before you can answer a question about a running system, the system has to write down what happens. This objective is about how those records get collected and sent to a central place where you can search them. Some records come from software installed on a server, some come from the application code itself, some are automatic records of who changed what in a cloud account, some summarise network traffic between machines, and some come from the layer that routes traffic between services. Each source answers a different kind of question, so knowing which one to turn to is most of the skill.
lessons.guessPrompt: A virtual machine was deleted at 03:05 and an application on another machine started timing out soon after. Which kind of record would most directly tell you who deleted the machine, and which would most directly show network traffic between the two machines?
lessons.teach:
Logs are timestamped records that a system writes about what it did. Collecting means moving those records off the machine or service into a central store. Five sources matter here.

The Ops Agent is software you install on virtual machines. It reads log files and host metrics on that machine and forwards them to the cloud logging service. It only sees what is on that one machine, so an application on a machine without the agent is invisible to it.

OpenTelemetry is an open, vendor-neutral standard and set of libraries for instrumenting application code. Your code emits traces, metrics and logs in a common format, and a collector process can forward them to many backends. It describes what the application did from the inside.

Cloud Audit Logs record administrative actions against cloud resources: who called which API, when, and from where. Admin Activity logs are on by default and cannot be turned off. Data Access logs, which record reads and writes of data, are off by default for most services and must be enabled on purpose.

VPC Flow Logs sample network flows between virtual machines in a subnet, recording source, destination, port and byte counts. They are enabled per subnet and are sampled, so they show patterns rather than every packet.

Cloud Service Mesh is a managed service mesh based on the Istio project. It places a proxy beside each service, and those proxies emit request-level telemetry about traffic between services without changing application code.

Worked example: a virtual machine was deleted at 03:05 and you need to know who did it. Start with Cloud Audit Logs, because a deletion is an administrative action recorded there. Flow logs show traffic patterns, not the identity behind a delete.

Common mistake: assuming Data Access logs are already on. Consequence: an incident review finds no record of who read a sensitive dataset, because nothing was ever collected.

Pick the source by asking what kind of fact you need: an administrative action, an internal code path, a network traffic pattern, or a request between services.

questions.prompt: A team at a retail company wants to know whether any user read the order-export records held in a managed database last Tuesday. Work through it: (1) The fact needed is a read of data, not an administrative change, so the source is the Data Access records in Cloud Audit Logs. (2) Data Access logs are off by default for most services, so first check whether they were enabled on that database before Tuesday. (3) ___ (4) If they were not enabled, no record exists, so the honest answer is 'unknown', not 'nobody read it.'
choices: If they were enabled, search the audit log for read events on that database for Tuesday, filtering by caller and time.
Turn on OpenTelemetry tracing in the application code so each query records its user from now on.
Switch on VPC Flow Logs for the database subnet to see which users read the rows.
Enable Admin Activity logs now so Tuesday's reads appear retroactively.
questions.why: Step 3 is the actual lookup: once Data Access logs are confirmed on, you query that log for read events on the database in the right time window and filter by caller.

questions.prompt: Which audit log category is on by default and cannot be turned off?
choices: VPC Flow Logs for every subnet in the project
Data Access audit logs for managed databases
Admin Activity audit logs, which record administrative actions against resources
Ops Agent host metrics collected from virtual machines
questions.why: Admin Activity logs are on by default and cannot be disabled, while Data Access logs must be enabled on purpose and VPC Flow Logs are a network source, not an audit category.

questions.prompt: A team installed the Ops Agent on their web virtual machines, but their checkout service runs on a separate managed container platform where no agent is installed. Why do the checkout service's log lines not appear in the central store?
choices: Cloud Audit Logs must be enabled on the container platform before any application output can be collected from it.
The Ops Agent only reads files and host metrics on the machine where it is installed, so it cannot see a service running elsewhere.
The Ops Agent sampled the checkout requests and discarded the ones that were slow to finish before forwarding anything to the store.
VPC Flow Logs only cover the web virtual machines, so the checkout traffic is dropped at the network layer before it can be recorded.
questions.why: The Ops Agent only sees what is on the single machine it runs on, so a service on a machine without the agent is invisible to it.

questions.prompt: A batch job on one virtual machine sends data to a database virtual machine in the same subnet. The team wants to know which ports were used and roughly how many bytes moved during one afternoon. Which source fits, and what limit should they keep in mind?
choices: Cloud Audit Logs, which record every byte sent between virtual machines, so the totals are exact.
VPC Flow Logs enabled on that subnet, which show source, destination, port and byte counts, but are sampled so totals are patterns, not exact figures.
Cloud Service Mesh request telemetry, which records the port and size of every packet exchanged between the two machines.
OpenTelemetry traces from the batch job's code, which give the exact byte count for each outgoing connection.
questions.why: VPC Flow Logs record network flows with ports and byte counts, but because they are sampled they show traffic patterns rather than exact totals.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which of these collection sources to turn on for a new production service, and name one limit or tradeoff of the source you would be least keen to rely on for a question about who did something.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the question the team needs answered. For who changed a resource, I would rely on Cloud Audit Logs, because they record administrative actions with an identity, and Admin Activity logs are always on. For what the application did internally, I would use the Ops Agent on virtual machines for log files and OpenTelemetry in the code for traces and metrics. For traffic patterns between machines, I would turn on VPC Flow Logs on the relevant subnet. The limit I would name is that Flow Logs are sampled and per subnet, so they can miss short flows and tell you nothing about which person or process started a connection. They answer where traffic went, not who asked for it.
rubricPoints: Matches each question type to the right source, such as audit logs for who did what
Notes that Ops Agent only collects from the machines where it is installed
Names a real limit, such as Flow Logs being sampled or per subnet
Says Data Access logs must be enabled deliberately

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right collection source for a realistic incident question is best practised by reasoning through a scenario, which none of the listed missions currently covers exactly.

lessons.plain: Logs are the written record a running system produces: one line per event, such as a request that failed or a user that logged in. Keeping every line is useful, but storing and searching them costs money, and most lines are routine noise. Optimizing logs means deciding which lines to keep, which to drop, which to keep only a fraction of, how long to keep the rest, and where the lines come from in the first place. The goal is to keep the evidence you need during an incident without paying for chatter nobody reads. Think of a security camera that records every hallway at full resolution forever, versus one that records only the doors that matter and keeps the footage for a sensible length of time.
lessons.guessPrompt: A service writes one log line for every health check, about 10 million lines a day, while only a few hundred lines a day are errors. Before any teaching, what would you change first to reduce the logging bill, and what would you be worried about losing?
lessons.teach:
A log sink is a route that sends log entries from the logging service to a destination. A log bucket is storage inside the logging service where kept entries live. Each bucket has a retention period, the number of days entries are kept before deletion. An exclusion filter is a rule attached to a sink or bucket that says which entries should be discarded before they are stored. Sampling keeps only a fraction of matching entries, so you still see the pattern at a fraction of the volume. Ingestion, the act of accepting an entry, is usually the main cost driver, together with how long entries are retained.

Why it works: most volume comes from a small number of noisy sources, such as health-check requests or debug messages. Dropping or sampling those cuts cost sharply while leaving severe entries untouched, because filters can match on severity, resource, or log name.

Worked example: a service writes 10 million health-check lines a day plus 50,000 error lines. Step one: write an exclusion that matches health-check requests and samples them so that 99 percent are dropped. Step two: leave the error lines unmatched, so they are all stored. Step three: the stored volume is roughly 100,000 health lines plus 50,000 errors, about 150,000 a day, down from about 10 million. Errors remain complete, so incidents still have evidence.

Common mistake: writing a broad exclusion, such as everything from one service, which silently removes the severe errors you will need during an incident. Always test a filter against recent entries before relying on it.

Consequence: an entry dropped by an exclusion is not stored in the bucket, so it cannot be searched later. If you may need the full detail, export the raw stream to cheaper storage before excluding anything.

questions.prompt: A fleet-tracking company's telemetry service writes 4,000,000 heartbeat lines a day, 20,000 warning lines, and 2,000 critical lines. The team's plan has three steps. Step one: write an exclusion that matches heartbeat lines and samples them so 95 percent are dropped. Step three: compute the stored volume, which is 200,000 heartbeat lines plus 20,000 warnings plus 2,000 critical lines, about 222,000 a day. The plan is missing step two, the one that protects the critical lines before the exclusion goes live. Which step two completes the plan?
choices: Lower the bucket retention period to 7 days so older heartbeat lines age out sooner
Add a second sampling rule that keeps only 1 percent of the warning lines
Delete the heartbeat lines already stored so the bucket starts the new rule with an empty history
Test the exclusion against recent entries and confirm that no critical-severity line matches it
questions.why: Filters match on severity, so testing the exclusion against recent entries confirms that critical lines fall outside it before any of them are discarded, which is what the plan needs to protect them.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does the retention period of a log bucket control?
choices: The destination a sink routes matching entries to
The maximum number of entries the bucket will accept per second
The number of days entries stay in the bucket before they are deleted
The severity level below which entries are automatically discarded
questions.why: Retention is defined in the teaching text as the number of days entries are kept before deletion, so it governs how long stored entries last, not how fast they arrive or where they go.

questions.prompt: A content delivery network edge emits 8 million access lines an hour. An operations engineer needs to see the hourly request-rate trend but wants lower storage costs. Which approach best meets both needs?
choices: Sample a fraction of the matching access lines so the pattern remains visible at a fraction of the volume
Raise the bucket retention period to 365 days so the trend can be seen over a longer window
Exclude all access lines so storage stops growing, and rely on a separate dashboard for trends
Store every access line in the bucket but change its retention period to one hour
questions.why: Sampling keeps a fraction of matching entries, which preserves the pattern while cutting volume, whereas full exclusion removes the pattern and longer retention raises cost rather than lowering it.

questions.prompt: A team writes a broad exclusion that matches every entry from a service called payments-api, and it is applied to the bucket immediately without testing. A few hours later, a production incident occurs with a spike in errors from that service. What is the consequence?
choices: The error entries are kept for the full retention period, so the exclusion only affects new buckets
The error entries are sampled automatically, so the team still sees a representative set of them
The error entries are discarded before storage, so they cannot be searched later during the incident
The error entries are stored in the bucket but hidden from search until the exclusion is removed
questions.why: An exclusion discards matching entries before they are stored, so the severe errors it caught are gone and cannot be searched during the incident.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would reduce the cost of a noisy service's logs without losing the errors you need during an incident. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by finding out which log entries make up most of the volume, usually routine request or health-check lines, and how much they cost to store and keep. Then I would add an exclusion that drops that noisy category, or keeps only a sample of it, while leaving error and warning entries untouched. Before deploying, I would test the filter against recent entries to confirm it matches only what I intend. The tradeoff is that dropped entries are gone from the log bucket, so if someone later needs the full detail for a rare bug, it is not there. To hedge, I would route the raw stream to cheaper archive storage for a fixed period, and I would note in the runbook that the sampled category is partial. Counts from sampled data are estimates, so any metric built from them has to be read that way.
rubricPoints: Identifies the high-volume sources before choosing what to exclude.
Keeps severe entries such as errors intact while dropping or sampling routine noise.
Tests a filter against recent entries before relying on it.
States the tradeoff: excluded or sampled entries cannot be searched later unless exported first.
Notes that ingestion volume and retention period both drive cost.

suggested.rationale: A fictional-credit cost model lets the learner see how volume and retention change the bill before touching a real project.

lessons.plain: Metrics are numbers recorded over time, such as requests per second, memory in use, or the share of failed calls. Collecting metrics means getting those numbers out of the things that produce them and into a store where you can graph them and set alerts. Some numbers come from the application itself, some from the platform that runs it, some from the network between parts, and some from a service mesh that sits between services. A metric answers how much or how often, which makes it the right first signal when you need to know whether something is getting worse and how fast.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a service's latency dashboard has been empty for ten minutes but users report the service still responds, what could be wrong with the collection path rather than the service itself?
lessons.teach: A metric is a number recorded at regular times, such as a count of requests or the percentage of memory in use. Each distinct combination of metric name and labels (key-value tags such as route or status code) forms one time series. Collecting metrics means getting those numbers from where they are produced into a store that can graph and alert on them. There are two common directions. In pull collection, a collector such as Prometheus reaches out to an HTTP endpoint on a schedule and reads its current values, a step called scraping. In push collection, the source sends values to a collector. Managed Service for Prometheus is Google's hosted version of the open-source Prometheus system, so you keep the same scraping model without running the storage yourself. Cloud Service Mesh is a layer of proxies placed beside each service that carries its traffic and reports request metrics without changing application code. Platform and network metrics come from the infrastructure itself, while hybrid or multicloud machines outside your project need an agent or a reachable endpoint so the collector can read them. Worked example: a payments service exposes a counter, a number that only goes up, named requests_total with a status label. The collector scrapes at 09:00:00 and reads 1000 for status 200. At 09:00:30 it reads 1450. The rate is (1450 minus 1000) divided by 30 seconds, which is 15 requests per second. The raw counter is rarely what you graph; the rate is. Common mistake: putting a unique value such as a user ID into a label. Every new value creates a new time series, so storage cost grows without limit and queries slow down. Consequence: if a scrape target stops answering, its series go stale and dashboards show gaps. A missing series is a signal too, so alert on absence deliberately. Collecting metrics means making sure every relevant number arrives where you can see it.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking service exposes a counter named seats_held_total. A collector scrapes it at 18:00:00 and reads 2400, then scrapes again at 18:00:40 and reads 2880. Step 1: the increase is 2880 minus 2400, which is 480. Step 2 is missing and you must supply it. Step 3: the reported rate is 12 seats per second. What is the missing Step 2?
choices: Divide 480 by 60 to get a per-minute figure
Multiply 480 by 40 to get the total held seats
Add 2400 and 2880 and divide the sum by 2
Divide 480 by 40 seconds, the time between the two scrapes
questions.why: A rate is the increase divided by the elapsed time between the two scrapes, and 480 divided by 40 seconds gives the stated 12 per second.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is one time series?
choices: One metric name together with one specific set of label values
The scrape interval set on a collector
Every metric name that a single server has ever exposed
A graph panel that shows a metric over one day
questions.why: A time series is defined by a distinct combination of metric name and labels, so each new label combination is a separate series.

questions.prompt: A logistics company adds customer_email as a label on its delivery latency metric, and it has 90,000 customers. What is the main consequence?
choices: Each distinct email value creates a new time series, so storage cost grows and queries slow down
The latency values are averaged across all customers automatically
Nothing changes, because labels only affect how a dashboard looks
Scraping stops until the label is removed
questions.why: Every new label value creates a new time series, so an unbounded value like an email address makes storage and query cost grow without limit.

questions.prompt: A bank runs a legacy batch server in its own data centre, outside its Google Cloud project. Its metrics collector runs in the cloud. What does the collector need so it can read this server's metrics?
choices: Nothing, because metrics from machines outside the project arrive automatically
A Cloud Service Mesh proxy installed beside the batch job
An agent on the server or an endpoint the collector can reach over the network
A copy of the server's log files stored in a bucket
questions.why: Hybrid machines outside the project need an agent or a reachable endpoint so the collector can read their values.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we need Managed Service for Prometheus when our platform already reports CPU. Explain in your own words what application-level metrics add beyond platform metrics, and name one limit or tradeoff of pull-based scraping.
lessons.modelAnswer: Platform metrics such as CPU and memory tell us the machine is busy, but not whether users are being served well. Application metrics, like request counts by status code or request duration, show what the service is actually doing, so we can see errors or slow routes even when CPU looks fine. Managed Service for Prometheus lets us collect those application endpoints using the same scraping model as open-source Prometheus, without running the storage ourselves. The tradeoff with pull-based scraping is that the collector must be able to reach each endpoint on a schedule. If a target is behind a firewall, on another network, or briefly down, its data has gaps, and short-lived jobs may finish before a scrape happens. Pushing from the source avoids that reachability issue but moves the work of retries and buffering into the application.
rubricPoints: Explains that platform metrics show machine health while application metrics show service behavior
Describes scraping as the collector reading an endpoint on a schedule
Names a real limit such as reachability, gaps, or short-lived jobs missed by scrapes
Mentions that hybrid or multicloud sources need an agent or reachable endpoint

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly about which metric sources and collectors exist and how they connect, which is best learned from reading the product catalogue and console steps, and no listed mission or planned engine teaches collection directly.

lessons.plain: A synthetic monitor is a scheduled robot that pretends to be a user. Instead of waiting for a real customer to discover that a website or booking form is broken, it sends a request to an address on a timer, from one or more locations, and checks the answer: did it respond, how fast, and does the page contain what it should? If the check fails repeatedly, it raises an alert. The name contrasts with real-user monitoring, which only measures people who already arrived. Synthetic checks give you a steady heartbeat even at 3 a.m. when traffic is quiet, so you learn about a broken login before your customers do.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your homepage returns status 200 every minute from one server, yet customers say checkout is broken. Name one reason a probe like that could stay green, and one change that would make it turn red.
lessons.teach:
A synthetic monitor is a scheduled probe that runs a fixed check against your system on a timer, so you find failures without waiting for real users. A probe is one attempt: send a request, read the reply, record the result. A simple uptime check probes one address, for example a web page, over HTTP, HTTPS or TCP, and asserts that the answer is acceptable. The assertion is the rule you write down: the status code must be 200, the response must contain a given phrase, and the reply must arrive within a latency limit such as 2 seconds. A multi-step synthetic check scripts a workflow, such as load the login page, submit credentials, then fetch the account page, and asserts each step.

Why it works: real traffic is lumpy. At 3 a.m. there may be no customers, so a broken login would sit unnoticed. A probe runs whether or not anyone is using the system. Running it from several vantage points (locations on different networks) helps separate a fault in your service from a fault in one network route.

Worked example. You probe https://shop.example/login every 60 seconds from three regions and require status 200, the phrase Sign in, and a response under 2 seconds. At 09:00 the Frankfurt probe gets 200 in 180 ms, Virginia gets 200 in 210 ms, and Singapore times out at 10 seconds. Step one: one failing location is a warning, not proof of an outage. Step two: the rule says alert only when at least two of three locations fail in the same window. Only Singapore failed, so the alert stays quiet and the failure is logged for review.

Common mistake: checking only that the homepage returns 200. A broken app can serve an error page with status 200, so assert on content that only a healthy page contains.

Consequence: a check that pages on-call for every single-location blip trains people to ignore alerts. Each check also costs money per execution, so frequency and location count are design choices. A synthetic monitor is only as good as the assertion you wrote for it.

questions.prompt: A payments team probes https://pay.example.test/health every 30 seconds from four locations. Each probe must return status 200, the body must contain the word ready, and the reply must arrive within 1.5 seconds. The rule is to alert only when at least three of the four locations fail in the same window. At 14:00 the results are: Tokyo returns 200, contains ready, in 240 ms. Dublin returns 200, contains ready, in 310 ms. Toronto returns 503 in 80 ms. Mumbai returns 200, contains ready, in 2.1 s. Step one: Toronto fails the status rule because 503 is not 200. Step two: Mumbai fails the latency rule because 2.1 s is over 1.5 s. Step three: two of four locations failed, so the failure count is 2. Missing step: decide whether the alert fires.
choices: Alert only if Tokyo also fails, because the healthy locations must all agree.
Do not alert. Two of four is below the three-of-four threshold, so log both failures for review.
Alert now, because any two failing locations out of four is an outage.
Wait 30 minutes of repeated failures before deciding, since the rule does not cover a single window.
questions.why: The rule requires at least three failing locations in the same window, and only two failed, so the correct action is to log the failures without alerting.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a probe in a synthetic monitor?
choices: A single attempt that sends a request, reads the reply, and records the result.
A rule that stops a deployment when error logs grow too long.
A dashboard graph that shows average traffic over the last day.
A permanent copy of your database used for testing queries.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a probe as one attempt: send a request, read the reply, and record the result.

questions.prompt: A job-board search page is checked only for status 200. During a database outage the site shows a 'No results found' page with status 200, and the check stays green. Which change best fixes the check?
choices: Raise the latency limit from 2 seconds to 10 seconds so slow replies are accepted.
Run the same status check from more locations so the error is seen from more networks.
Change the check to run once a day so it uses fewer executions.
Add an assertion for a phrase that only a healthy results page contains, such as the results heading.
questions.why: A status code alone cannot detect an error page served with status 200, so the assertion must check content that only a healthy page would contain.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking flow is monitored with a multi-step synthetic check: load the seat map, reserve a seat, then fetch the confirmation page. The seat map loads fine but the reserve step returns an error. What is the correct outcome?
choices: The check fails at the reserve step, because each step has its own assertion and the workflow is only healthy if every step passes.
The check is skipped for that run, because a partial success cannot be recorded.
The check passes, because the first step succeeded and the later steps are optional.
The check passes after a retry, because a multi-step check always retries failed steps automatically.
questions.why: A multi-step check asserts each step, so a failure at any step, here the reserve step, makes the workflow check fail even when earlier steps succeeded.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a synthetic monitor differs from waiting for real-user reports, and name one limit or tradeoff of running it.
lessons.modelAnswer: A synthetic monitor runs a scripted check on a timer, so it tests the system whether or not customers are using it. Real-user reports only arrive after someone is already affected, and they are uneven across the day. The tradeoff is that a probe only tests the path it was written for. If the checkout form is not in the script, a broken checkout can stay green while the homepage passes. Probes also cost money per run, and a check run from one location can raise false alarms from a local network fault. So I would check from several regions, assert on page content rather than status code alone, and alert only when more than one location fails. A probe's result is a sample of behaviour, not a guarantee that everything works.
rubricPoints: Synthetic monitors run scheduled checks independent of real traffic, so failures can surface before customers report them.
A probe only covers the paths and assertions it defines, so coverage gaps are the main limit.
Checks from several locations and content assertions reduce both false alarms and false greens.
Probes cost money per execution, so check frequency and location count are tradeoffs.

suggested.rationale: Choosing which path, location and assertion to probe is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style production situation.

lessons.plain: A metric is a number recorded over time, like how many requests a service handled each minute. Platforms give you built-in numbers for common things such as CPU use. A custom metric is a number you define yourself for something only your application knows, such as orders placed or payments failed. A log-based metric is a number you create by counting or measuring log lines that match a rule you write, so information already in your logs can become a chart and an alert without changing the app. Both let you watch trends and set thresholds, which raw logs make slow to answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your payment service writes one log line every time a payment fails, but nobody has a chart of failures per minute. Without changing the code, how could you get a per-minute failure count you can alert on, and what would you need to decide first?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a time series: a named number sampled at regular intervals, with optional labels that split it into groups, such as by region or by status. A custom metric is one you define yourself rather than one the platform provides. In Google Cloud Monitoring you can write custom metric data through the API or from an instrumented application, and you can also derive a metric from logs that already exist.

A log-based metric is built from log entries. You give it a filter, a rule that selects only the log lines you care about, and it turns each match into a number. A counter metric counts the matching entries. A distribution metric reads a numeric value from each matching entry, such as a latency field, and records how those values spread out. You can also copy a field from the log entry into a label, so the counter is split by, for example, the error type.

Why it works: the event is already written to the logs, so you need no code change and no new agent to start counting. A stored metric is much cheaper and faster to chart than scanning raw log lines each time, which is why it suits alerting.

Worked example: each failed payment writes a log line with severity ERROR and a field naming the failure reason. Step one, write a filter that matches only payment-failure lines. Step two, create a counter log-based metric from that filter. Step three, add a label taken from the reason field. Now each minute holds a count of failures per reason, which you can chart and alert on.

Common mistake: a filter that is too broad, such as matching every ERROR line, so the chart mixes unrelated failures and the alert fires for the wrong reason.

Consequence: a label with many distinct values, such as user ID, creates a huge number of separate time series, which raises cost and slows the charts. Choose labels with a small, fixed set of values.

questions.prompt: A shipping company's booking service writes an INFO log line for each rate lookup. Each line has a field named lookup_ms holding how many milliseconds the lookup took, and a field named region. The team wants a chart of lookup times per region. Step one is a filter that matches only the rate-lookup lines. Step two is creating a distribution log-based metric from that filter. Step three is missing: it tells the metric which number to record from each matching entry. Which choice completes the setup?
choices: Set the distribution to read lookup_ms as its numeric value
Narrow the filter to ERROR severity only
Use a counter instead, since counters are the only type that reads numbers
Add lookup_ms as a label, so each timing value gets its own series
questions.why: A distribution metric reads a numeric value from each matching entry, so pointing it at lookup_ms records the timings, whereas using that value as a label would create a separate series for every distinct number.

questions.prompt: A colleague says that every custom metric requires a new agent installed on each server before it can start counting. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Agents are required for every custom metric, since no metric can be derived without one
No agent is needed for a log-based metric, because it is derived from log lines that already exist
Agents are required only for distribution metrics, never for counters
Agents are required only when the metric has labels attached to it
questions.why: A log-based metric turns entries that are already written to the logs into numbers, so it needs no code change and no new agent to start counting.

questions.prompt: A video transcoding service writes a WARNING log line whenever a job falls back to a slower codec. Each line has a field called codec naming the codec used. The team wants a count of these fallbacks for each codec. Which setup fits best?
choices: A counter metric filtered on the WARNING fallback lines, with codec copied into a label
A distribution metric filtered on all log lines, with job_id as the label
A counter metric filtered on every log line, with no label
A distribution metric filtered on the WARNING fallback lines, reading the codec field as its value
questions.why: A counter counts matching entries, the filter should select only the fallback warnings, and copying codec into a label splits the count by codec, which has a small fixed set of values.

questions.prompt: A log-based counter metric is labeled with request_id, which is different on almost every request. It has produced thousands of separate time series, and the charts have become slow. What is the best fix?
choices: Replace request_id with a field that has a small fixed set of values, such as a status class
Convert the counter into a distribution, which automatically merges labels together
Remove the filter so that more log lines feed the same counter
Keep request_id and raise the chart refresh rate so the series load faster
questions.why: Each distinct label value creates its own time series, so a label with a huge number of values raises cost and slows charts, and the fix is to use a label with a small, fixed set of values.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should just alert on a raw log search instead of creating a log-based metric. Explain to them when a log-based metric is the better choice, and name one limit or tradeoff of using it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Matching raw log lines works for spotting individual events, but it does not give you a steady number you can chart over weeks, compare with last week, or set a rate threshold on. A log-based metric turns matching log lines into a counter or distribution stored as a time series, so you can chart it, set a threshold, and alert on it efficiently. It needs no change to the application because the logs already exist. The tradeoff is that it only counts from the moment it is created, so it cannot tell you about last month's failures. A poorly chosen label with many distinct values can also create a large number of series and raise cost. And if the filter stops matching because a log field was renamed, the count quietly drops to zero.
rubricPoints: A log-based metric turns matching log entries into a number stored as a time series that can be charted and thresholded.
It needs no application code change because the event is already in the logs.
It only counts from its creation date, so it cannot show historical events.
A high-cardinality label, or a filter that breaks when log fields change, causes cost or silent data gaps.

suggested.rationale: The planned metric alarm builder would let the learner set thresholds on metrics, the step that follows creating one, though it would not cover creating log-based metrics themselves.

lessons.plain: Cloud logging stores the messages that running software writes down. Each message is a log entry with a time, a severity, and details about where it came from. When something breaks at 3 a.m., you need to find the few entries that matter among millions. The Logs Explorer is the console page for searching those entries, and the logging query language is the small filter language you type into it to say which entries you want, such as only errors from one service in the last hour. Writing precise filters is the difference between finding the cause in minutes and scrolling forever.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web service returned errors for ten minutes last night, and you have a million log lines from the past day. Before any training, which three pieces of information would you filter on first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A log entry is one record written by a program or platform. It carries a timestamp, a severity level (such as INFO, WARNING, or ERROR), a payload (either message text or a set of structured fields), and resource labels that say which service or machine produced it. The Logs Explorer is the console page where you search these entries. The logging query language is the filter syntax you type into its query box. A query is a list of conditions, each comparing a field to a value, joined by AND by default, with OR and NOT available for more complex logic. Text inside the payload can also be matched as a substring.

Why it works: the platform indexes entries by their fields, so each condition narrows the set before you read anything. A severity condition removes most noise at once. A resource condition removes other services. A timestamp condition limits the time window. Each added condition is another cut, so a precise query returns a handful of relevant entries.

Worked example: you want payment-service errors from the last 30 minutes. Step 1: add a condition matching the payment service's resource. Step 2: add a severity condition for ERROR or higher. Step 3: add a timestamp lower bound 30 minutes before now. Read the matching entries, note a field such as an error code, then add that code as a condition to confirm the pattern across the window.

Common mistake: searching for the bare word error across everything. That matches harmless lines in every service and buries the real failure. Forgetting the time window is the other frequent error, because old incidents drown out current ones.

Consequence: during a live incident, a loose query costs minutes of guessing while users wait. A precise query surfaces the first failing entry quickly, which is what shortens the outage.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a fictional freight company, Northwind Routes, wants to find the timeout failures in the route-planner service from the last 2 hours. Step 1: add a condition matching the route-planner resource. Step 2: add a severity condition for WARNING or higher. Step 3 is missing. Read the matching entries and note the message pattern. What belongs in the missing step?
choices: Add a timestamp condition with no lower bound, so the search covers all history
Add a condition that the payload contains the substring "timeout"
Remove the resource condition and search the word timeout across every service
Add a severity condition set to INFO so no entries are excluded
questions.why: A substring condition on the payload is the remaining cut that narrows the results to entries whose message includes timeout, and the other choices either widen the search or remove a condition that is already doing useful work.

questions.prompt: In the Logs Explorer, what do a log entry's resource labels tell you?
choices: The time at which the entry was written, to the second
The exact text of the message, stored as a substring index
How serious the entry is, from DEBUG up to CRITICAL
Which service or machine produced the entry
questions.why: Resource labels say which service or machine produced the entry, which is what a resource condition in a query uses to remove other services' entries.

questions.prompt: A team at a fictional bank, Keystone Savings, wants ERROR-or-higher entries from the ledger-api service in the last 15 minutes, excluding the nightly batch job's entries. Which query logic does this?
choices: Severity ERROR or higher across every service in the project, filtered by the word timeout in the payload
ledger-api resource with INFO severity across the whole day, to see all activity
Any service whose payload mentions ledger, at ERROR or higher, with no time limit so nothing is missed
ledger-api resource, ERROR or higher, last 15 minutes, NOT the batch job's resource
questions.why: Each condition is a cut: the resource, severity, and timestamp narrow the set, and NOT removes the batch job's entries, which matches the stated goal exactly.

questions.prompt: An engineer types the bare word failed into the Logs Explorer query box with no other conditions and gets thousands of results, mostly from a health-check service. Why is this query hard to use during an incident?
choices: Logs Explorer cannot search for the word failed, which requires a metric instead.
The payload must first be converted into a trace before any substring can match.
Severity should be set to DEBUG, because failures are only recorded at that level.
The query has no resource or time condition, so matching lines from unrelated services and old entries bury the real failure.
questions.why: Without a resource condition or a time window, nothing removes harmless lines from other services or old incidents, so the real failure is buried among them.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, 'I'll just search the logs for the word timeout.' In your own words, explain why filtering on structured fields first usually works better, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would use instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: Searching for the word timeout across all logs will match any line containing that text, including harmless debug messages from unrelated services, so the real failure gets buried. Filtering first on structured fields such as the resource, the severity, and a time window cuts the set down before any reading happens, and the platform can use those indexed fields to do that quickly. Then I can add the text match inside the narrowed set. The tradeoff is that structured filters depend on the fields being present and labelled consistently. If a service writes unstructured text or uses different field names, my precise filter can miss entries entirely, so I would check a few raw entries first and widen the filter if the expected records do not appear.
rubricPoints: Explains that field-based conditions (resource, severity, time) narrow the set before reading.
Explains why a bare text search is noisy and can hide the real failure.
Names a concrete limit, such as inconsistent or missing fields causing a filter to miss entries.
Gives a practical check, such as inspecting a few raw entries before trusting the filter.

suggested.rationale: This mission has you find the cause of an API failure by searching logs on a server, which practises the same filter-then-read habit, though on local files rather than the Cloud Logging console.

lessons.plain: Logs are the diary entries a system writes about what it did. They usually sit in one place for a limited time, which is fine for last night's bug but not for an audit next year or for a team that wants to ask questions across months of data. Exporting logs means copying a chosen subset of them, as they arrive, to another home: a table you can query with SQL, a message stream that other programs can read in near real time, or cheap files kept for years. Think of a mail sorter that makes a second copy of certain letters and drops them into different boxes.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company's log store keeps entries for 30 days, but an auditor asks for all API request logs from last year. What would you set up, and would it help with last year's logs?
lessons.teach:
A log sink is a rule in the Cloud Logging log router that says: take the log entries that match this filter and send a copy to this destination. The filter is a query over log fields, such as resource type or severity. The destination is usually one of three kinds. BigQuery is a data warehouse: entries land in tables you query with SQL, which suits trend analysis and audits. Pub/Sub is a managed message queue: entries are published to a topic so other programs, such as a security tool or a custom pipeline, can subscribe and react within seconds. Cloud Storage is object storage: entries are written as files in a bucket, which is cheap for long-term archive, often combined with a lifecycle rule that moves old files to colder, cheaper storage classes.

Why it works: the router sees each entry as it is written and forwards matching copies, so the original stays where it was and the copy lives on independently. That is why export matters for retention. The copy outlives the short retention window of the default log store.

Worked example: a team needs a year of request logs from one Cloud Run service for an audit. Step one, create a sink whose filter selects that resource type. Step two, choose a Cloud Storage bucket as the destination. Step three, grant the sink's writer identity, a service account the sink uses to write, permission to create objects in that bucket; without this grant the sink exists but delivers nothing. Step four, wait: only entries written from that moment on are copied. Requests from before the sink existed are not recovered.

Common mistake: assuming a new sink brings back history, or forgetting the writer identity grant. Consequence in a running system: a sink whose filter is too narrow silently drops the entries you need, and nobody notices until an incident review or audit asks for them.

questions.prompt: A payments team wants ERROR-or-worse entries from its Kubernetes containers sent to a Pub/Sub topic named payments-errors, so an alerting subscriber can react within seconds. The steps are: (1) create a sink whose filter selects Kubernetes container entries at ERROR severity or higher; (2) choose the payments-errors topic as the destination; (3) [blank: fill in this step]; (4) the subscriber begins receiving new entries. Which step belongs in the blank?
choices: Grant the sink's writer identity permission to publish to the payments-errors topic
Change the filter to include INFO entries so the sink captures more of the cluster's activity
Set a lifecycle rule on the topic to move old messages to colder storage classes
Re-run the filter over the last week so that past errors are copied into the topic
questions.why: A sink needs its writer identity to be allowed to write to the destination, and without that grant the sink exists but delivers nothing, so the publish permission must be granted on the topic.

questions.prompt: A company wants each new Cloud Logging entry handed to its own fraud-detection service within seconds, so the service can react as events happen. Which destination type fits best?
choices: BigQuery, because entries become SQL-queryable tables
Pub/Sub, because entries are published to a topic that subscribers read
A Persistent Disk attached to the fraud-detection virtual machine
Cloud Storage, because entries are written as files in a bucket
questions.why: Pub/Sub is a managed message queue that delivers published entries to subscribing programs quickly, which matches a real-time reaction requirement, while the other options are for querying or archiving rather than prompt delivery.

questions.prompt: A retailer must keep its web-tier logs for seven years at the lowest possible cost. The logs are almost never read, and when they are, a few hours' wait is acceptable. Which setup best fits?
choices: A Cloud Storage bucket receiving the logs, with a lifecycle rule that moves old files to colder, cheaper storage classes
A Pub/Sub topic that holds messages until someone reads them
A second sink to the default log bucket, with its retention period set as long as possible
A BigQuery table partitioned by day with no expiry, kept indefinitely
questions.why: Cloud Storage is object storage suited to cheap long-term archive, and a lifecycle rule moves aging files into colder, cheaper classes, which is the cost pattern the scenario describes.

questions.prompt: A team created a sink on Monday with a filter that matches only CRITICAL severity entries. On Thursday an auditor asks for WARNING-level HTTP 500 entries from Wednesday. What is the most likely explanation for why they are missing from the destination?
choices: The sink backfilled all of Wednesday when it was created, so the entries should be in the destination
The BigQuery destination cannot store WARNING-level entries, so it deleted them on arrival
Pub/Sub kept the warnings only until a subscriber acknowledged them, and none did
The filter excluded WARNING entries, so they were never copied; the originals exist only in the default store for its retention window, if still there
questions.why: A sink only copies entries written after it was created and that match its filter, so a too-narrow filter silently leaves out the needed entries, and the original copies depend on the default store's short retention.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a log sink does, when you would pick BigQuery, Pub/Sub, or Cloud Storage as its destination, and one limit you must plan around.
lessons.modelAnswer: A log sink takes log entries that match a filter and forwards a copy to a destination, while the original stays in the default log store. I would send entries to BigQuery when we need SQL queries over weeks of history, to Pub/Sub when another system needs to react quickly, and to Cloud Storage when we only need cheap long-term archive. The main limit is timing: a sink copies only entries written after it is created, so it cannot rescue logs from before setup. We also have to grant the sink's writer identity permission on the destination, or nothing arrives. Finally, the filter decides what survives, so a narrow filter can silently drop data we later need. I would verify each new sink by checking that entries actually land in the destination.
rubricPoints: A sink forwards copies of matching entries, leaving the original log in place
Each destination suits a different need: BigQuery for SQL analysis, Pub/Sub for real-time consumers, Cloud Storage for cheap archive
Sinks are not retroactive; they copy only entries written after creation
The writer identity needs permission on the destination or delivery fails silently
The filter determines what is kept, so a too-narrow filter loses data

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine walks through log routing, so reading the sink concepts and then checking a destination in the console is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Logs are the running diary of a system, and sometimes that diary accidentally records things like a person's name, email address, phone number, or medical details. Redacting means removing or disguising that sensitive data before it is stored or shown to people who should not see it. A log processor is a step that sits between the program writing the log and the place the log is kept. It reads each entry, spots the sensitive parts, and masks, replaces, or drops them on the way through. The original value never reaches storage, so it cannot leak later from there.
lessons.guessPrompt: A ride-share app writes a log line for every failed payment that includes the rider's full card number and email address. Where would you most want the sensitive parts removed: inside the app's code, in a processor between the app and storage, or only after the logs are already stored and searched? Pick one and say why.
lessons.teach:
Personally identifiable information (PII) is any data that can identify a specific person, such as a name, email, phone number, or card number. Protected health information (PHI) is medical or health-related data tied to a person, which carries stricter handling rules. A log processor is a transformation step that runs on each log entry before the entry is written to storage. Redaction is any change that hides the sensitive content, including masking (replacing characters with symbols), replacing a value with a fixed label, hashing it so it cannot be read back, or dropping the field entirely. Detection usually relies on patterns, such as a run of sixteen digits that looks like a card number, or text that matches an email shape.

It works because the cleaning happens at write time, so the raw value never lands in the place where logs are kept. Once a raw copy is stored, it spreads to backups, exports, and analyst queries, and a later rule change cannot reach those copies.

Worked example. The app writes: payment failed for rider jane.doe@example.com card 4111 1111 1111 1111 trip 881. Step 1: the processor receives the entry. Step 2: it matches the email shape and replaces the address with the label EMAIL. Step 3: it matches the sixteen-digit card pattern and keeps only the last four digits, producing asterisks followed by 1111. Step 4: trip 881 matches no sensitive pattern, so it is left alone. The stored entry reads: payment failed for rider EMAIL card asterisks 1111 trip 881.

Common mistake: hiding values only in the log viewer. The raw text is still stored and still appears in exports, so the redaction protects the screen but not the data. A second mistake is writing a pattern that misses real formats, such as card numbers with dashes or spaces, which gives false confidence.

In a running system, a log export that feeds an analytics dataset copies every raw value into that dataset, so a processor placed after the export is too late to protect it. Redaction belongs at the point where the entry is first written, and it must be tested against realistic samples.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic's booking service writes this entry: booked visit for caller 415-555-0142, reason root canal, room 7. The log processor runs in this order. Step 1: it receives the entry before anything is stored. Step 2: it matches the phone-number shape and replaces the number with the label PHONE. Step 3: it replaces the treatment term with the fixed label HEALTH_INFO. Step 4 is not shown. Which completion correctly finishes the example?
choices: Step 4: the processor sends the raw entry to the analytics export, where a separate job masks it afterwards.
Step 4: the processor writes the redacted entry to storage, and room 7 stays as it is because it matches no sensitive pattern.
Step 4: the processor also writes the original entry to a backup, so a later rule change can re-run redaction on it.
Step 4: the processor replaces room 7 with asterisks so the entry keeps the same length as before.
questions.why: The processor writes only the cleaned entry, which is the point of write-time redaction, and it leaves text that matches no sensitive pattern unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines a log processor in this course's sense?
choices: A tool that deletes old log files once their retention period has passed.
A query language used to search stored logs for a particular error message.
A transformation step that runs on each log entry before the entry is written to storage.
A dashboard that hides sensitive values from people who view logs on screen.
questions.why: A log processor is defined as a transformation applied to each entry at write time, before storage, which is the third option.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's pattern for detecting card numbers only matches sixteen digits in a row with no separators. A tracking entry contains the card as 5500-0000-0000-0004 with dashes. What is the likely result?
choices: The pattern matches anyway because dashes are ignored by default in every processor.
The card number is replaced with a label, but the rest of the entry is deleted.
The processor refuses to write the entry, so the error stops the pipeline until it is fixed.
The card number is stored raw, and the team may wrongly believe the logs are protected.
questions.why: A pattern that misses the dashed format leaves the raw value in storage while giving the team false confidence that it was redacted.

questions.prompt: A shipping company's driver app writes national ID numbers into logs. The team masks the numbers only in the log viewer, and the analytics export still contains the full values. What is the main problem?
choices: The team must hash the numbers, because masking is never allowed in any situation.
The viewer masking is slower than the export, so the export loads incorrectly.
The export is a separate copy, so the raw values remain stored and spread to analysts.
The national ID numbers are too short to be treated as personal data under the course.
questions.why: Hiding values only in the viewer leaves the raw text stored in the export, so the redaction protects the screen but not the data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we redact sensitive fields in a log processor before storage instead of only hiding them in the log viewer, and name one limit or tradeoff of redacting this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: Hiding values in the viewer only changes what is displayed. The raw text still sits in the stored log bucket, in any exports to BigQuery or Pub/Sub, and in backups, so anyone who can reach those copies sees the original. Processing entries before storage replaces the sensitive value at the moment the entry is written, so every downstream copy holds only the masked version. The tradeoff is that the change is one-way. If someone later needs the masked part to debug a problem, it cannot be recovered, so the rules must be right before deployment. Pattern-based detection also misses formats it was not written for, so we test the processor with realistic samples and check stored output for leaks.
rubricPoints: Viewer-only hiding leaves raw data in storage and exports
Processing before storage means downstream copies hold only masked values
Redaction is one-way, so masked data cannot be recovered later
Pattern-based detection can miss formats and needs testing against real samples

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining why redaction happens at write time and what it costs, which is best checked by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: Gemini Cloud Assist is an AI helper built into Google Cloud that can read a large set of log entries and summarize what looks wrong. Logs are the written event records your software produces, usually one line per event, and during an outage there can be thousands of them. Instead of scanning every line yourself, you ask the assistant a question about the logs, such as why requests started failing at a certain time, and it proposes likely causes and points you to the entries behind them. Think of it as a fast reader who still needs you to check its reasoning against the evidence.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose 5,000 error lines appeared in the last ten minutes after a deploy. What is the fastest reliable way you would narrow down the likely cause, and what would you still verify yourself before acting on a guess?
lessons.teach:
A log entry is one timestamped record of something a program did or failed to do. Its severity is a label such as INFO, WARNING or ERROR. A log is a collection of these entries from one or more services. AI-assisted log analysis means you give a language model a question plus a slice of log data, and it returns a summary, a list of error patterns and a candidate root cause. A root cause is the underlying fault that, once removed, stops the symptom. A hypothesis is a candidate explanation that still needs testing. The model is useful because it groups thousands of similar lines quickly, but its output is a hypothesis, not a finding.

Why it works: most incidents leave repeated messages. Grouping those messages by text and time is tedious by hand and easy for a model to do, so the model turns a wall of lines into a few patterns you can check.

Worked example. A checkout service is deployed at 09:00. From 09:02, error logs show connection refused to db-replica port 5432. Step 1: set the time window to 08:55 through 09:15 and the service to checkout. Step 2: ask the assistant which error patterns dominate in that window.
