Step 3: it reports that nearly all errors share the same connection refused message and come only from the newly started pods. Step 4: you open a few of the raw entries and confirm the timestamps and host name, then compare the new configuration against the old one. Step 5: the new config points at a replica name that does not exist in that environment. Only after this check do you act on the hypothesis.

Common mistake: asking a vague question across all logs for all time, then trusting the first confident sentence. Consequence: in a running system, an unverified guess can send responders to roll back the wrong change and extend the outage. Also remember that log text sent to an AI service may contain personal or secret data, so check what you are allowed to share.

AI log analysis speeds up finding candidate causes; evidence from the raw entries decides which cause is real.

questions.prompt: A payments API at a different company, running on a managed container platform, was updated at 14:10. From 14:12, its error logs show many lines reading 'upstream timed out after 30s' for the host ledger-svc. Step 1: you set the time window to 14:05 through 14:30 and the service to payments-api. Step 2: you ask the assistant which error patterns dominate. Step 3: it reports that most errors share the timeout message and all come from pods started after 14:10. Step 4: [missing step: what you do before acting on the candidate cause]. Step 5: you find the new configuration sets the ledger timeout to 3 seconds, where the old one was 30 seconds, so the new pods give up on requests that the old pods waited for.
choices: Ask the assistant again for a shorter summary of the same window to confirm its answer
Delete the pods started after 14:10 so that fresh logs appear and the old pattern disappears
Check several raw timeout entries for their timestamps and host names before acting on the hypothesis
Roll back the deployment now, since the assistant has already named the cause and the window is clear
questions.why: The assistant's pattern is a hypothesis, so you confirm it against raw entries (timestamps and host names) before acting, which is the step the worked pattern requires..

questions.prompt: A team lead says the AI log assistant reported a likely root cause of a full disk on a storage node. In the terms used for AI-assisted log analysis, what is that report?
choices: A hypothesis, a candidate explanation that still needs testing against the raw entries
A log entry with severity ERROR, because it describes a failure
A confirmed finding, because the assistant read the logs itself
A metric series, because it reports a number over time
questions.why: The teaching text says the model's output is a hypothesis, not a finding, so the disk claim must be checked against raw log evidence.

questions.prompt: An engineer asks the assistant a broad question across all logs for the past six months: why is the site slow? The assistant gives one confident sentence and the engineer rolls back a release right away. Which risk does this approach carry?
choices: The answer will be accurate but will take too long to return
The assistant will refuse to answer any question about a slow site
Old logs will be deleted automatically once the query runs
The unverified guess may send responders to roll back the wrong change and extend the outage
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a vague question across all logs and time, trusted without checking, can lead responders to roll back the wrong change and prolong the outage.

questions.prompt: A team wants to paste a slice of application logs into an external AI service to speed up their analysis. Which check must come first?
choices: Whether the time window is shorter than ten minutes
Whether the log text may contain personal or secret data and whether sharing it is allowed
Only that the severity labels in the slice read INFO
Nothing, because the model only reads timestamps and not message text
questions.why: The teaching text notes that log text sent to an AI service may contain personal or secret data, so you must confirm you are allowed to share it first.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Gemini Cloud Assist can and cannot do for log analysis, and name one limit or tradeoff you would keep in mind before trusting its answer during an incident.
lessons.modelAnswer: Gemini Cloud Assist can take a question and a window of logs and quickly group repeated errors, then suggest likely causes and point to relevant entries. That saves a lot of scanning when hundreds or thousands of lines appear after a change. It cannot know what your system actually does beyond the logs it sees, and its answer can sound confident while being wrong or incomplete. So the main tradeoff is speed against trust. Before acting, I would open the cited raw entries, check timestamps and the exact host or version named, and confirm the cause with a second signal such as a metric or a recent change diff. I would also watch what log content I send to the tool, since logs can contain personal or secret data.
rubricPoints: Describes the assistant as a fast summarizer and hypothesis generator over log data, not an authority on root cause
States that suggested causes must be verified against raw log entries or other evidence before acting
Names a real limit, such as confident but wrong answers, missing context outside the logs, or data-sharing concerns
Explains that a narrow time window and a specific service make the question answerable

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers this assistant feature, so reading the concept and its verification habits is the best fit.

lessons.plain: A metric is a number that gets recorded again and again over time, such as how many requests a service handled each minute or how much memory a machine is using. Metrics Explorer is the part of Google Cloud's monitoring console where you pick one of those numbers, narrow it to the machines or services you care about, and draw it as a chart. Analyzing metrics means asking a question with that chart: is the problem getting worse, did it start after a change, or which group is responsible? Used well, the chart answers those questions in a minute. Used carelessly, its settings can hide the very spike you are looking for. This lesson shows how each control changes what you see.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web service's average response time looks fine on a dashboard, yet some customers report timeouts. Name one reason an average can look healthy while a slice of requests is very slow, and say which chart setting would help you see that slice.
lessons.teach:
A metric type is the named measurement, for example request latency or CPU utilization. Each metric is recorded for specific resources, such as one virtual machine or one load balancer. A time series is one line on a chart: the values for one metric from one particular resource over time. Labels, sometimes called resource labels or metric labels, are the tags that tell series apart, such as zone, service name, or instance ID. A filter keeps only the series that match a condition. Group by splits the remaining series into buckets by a label and combines each bucket. The aligner works inside one alignment period (a fixed window such as one minute): it reduces the raw points to one value per window, using a mean, a max, or a percentile. For a counter, which only goes up, a rate aligner turns the total into a per-second speed. The aggregator then combines the aligned series across a group.

Worked example. Suppose checkout latency is recorded by four instances, two in zone a and two in zone b. Step 1: choose the latency metric. Step 2: filter to service equals checkout. Step 3: set the alignment period to one minute and the aligner to 95th percentile. Step 4: group by zone and use max as the aggregator. If zone b's line climbs while zone a stays flat, you have a lead worth investigating.

Common mistake: charting latency with a mean aligner. A mean blends fast and slow requests, so a few very slow users disappear into it. Percentiles show the tail.

Consequence: if the on-call engineer reads only the mean, the dashboard looks calm while some users time out, and any alert built on that mean never fires.

questions.prompt: A ride-booking company, Tidewater Rides, records a counter called booking requests on six servers across two regions. The team wants requests per second for each region. Step 1: choose the booking requests metric. Step 2: filter to service equals booking-api. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: set the alignment period to one minute. Step 5: group by region and use sum as the aggregator. What belongs in the missing step 3, which is the aligner choice for this counter?
choices: Set the aligner to rate, which turns the ever-rising counter into a per-second speed
Set the aligner to mean, which averages the raw request counts inside each one-minute window
Group by server first, so each machine gets its own line before the regions are combined
Set the aligner to 95th percentile, so the tail of the request counts is visible
questions.why: A counter only goes up, so a rate aligner converts its running total into a per-second speed for each window, which is what the team asked for.

questions.prompt: A database team charts disk write throughput for three database nodes. Which of the following best describes one time series on that chart?
choices: The zone label that tells the three nodes apart from one another
The write values from one node over time, drawn as a single line
The disk write metric type itself, which names the measurement being recorded
All three nodes merged into one combined number at each moment
questions.why: A time series is one line: the values of one metric from one particular resource over time, so one node's writes over time is exactly one series.

questions.prompt: A search service's response time is charted with a mean aligner over one-minute windows. The dashboard looks calm, yet support tickets report some users waiting around 20 seconds. What is the most useful change to the chart?
choices: Change the aggregator from max to sum so that slow requests are added together
Add a filter on zone so the dashboard shows fewer series
Lengthen the alignment period to one hour so the mean has more data to smooth over
Switch the aligner to a high percentile such as the 99th within each one-minute window
questions.why: A mean blends fast and slow requests and hides the slow tail, so a percentile aligner per window exposes the users who wait longest.

questions.prompt: An engineer wants to compare error counts across three availability zones, but only for the orders service, on an API that also serves other services. Which sequence of actions is correct in Metrics Explorer?
choices: Group by zone first, then filter, because grouping removes the series that do not match
Filter to zone equals the target zone, then group by service, which gives the same result
Skip the filter, because group by already removes series from other services
Filter to service equals orders, then group by zone so each zone becomes one bucket
questions.why: A filter keeps only the matching series first, and group by then splits the remaining series into buckets by a label such as zone.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use Metrics Explorer to decide whether one zone is causing a latency problem. Name one limit or tradeoff of the chart settings you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by picking the request latency metric for the checkout service, then filter to that service so unrelated traffic is excluded. Next I would group by zone so each zone gets its own line, and I would use a 95th percentile aligner rather than a mean, because the mean hides the slow tail that users actually feel. If one zone's line rises while the other stays flat, that is a strong lead, but it is not proof of cause. A tradeoff is the alignment period: a one minute window shows fast changes but is noisier, while a longer window is smoother and can hide a short spike. Percentiles also cannot be averaged across series, so the aggregator I choose changes the meaning of the number. I would confirm the lead with logs or traces from that zone before blaming it.
rubricPoints: Chooses the right metric and filters to the affected service
Uses grouping by a label such as zone to isolate the source
Explains why percentiles reveal slow requests that means hide
Names a tradeoff of the alignment period or aggregator and notes a chart is a lead, not proof

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an incident where the chart settings change the conclusion adds the most, and no existing mission teaches metric analysis directly.

lessons.plain: A dashboard is a single screen of charts that shows how a system is doing at a glance. Building one means choosing which measurements to show, narrowing them with filters so each chart answers one question, sharing the saved view so teammates see the same picture, and attaching a playbook, which is a written list of steps to take when a chart looks wrong. PromQL is a query language for asking a time-series store precise questions about numbers that change over time, such as how fast errors are rising. Think of a dashboard as a car's instrument panel and PromQL as the way you ask the sensors behind each gauge a specific question.
lessons.guessPrompt: A dashboard shows total requests per minute across all services, and the chart looks steady and healthy. Why might that one chart hide a failing service, and what would you add to the dashboard to reveal it?
lessons.teach: A metric is a number recorded repeatedly over time. Each distinct set of labels, which are key-value tags such as service=positions and region=eu-west, produces one time series. A dashboard is a set of panels, and each panel is one chart driven by one query. A filter narrows which series a panel uses, for example only the positions service. An aggregation such as sum by (status) combines many series into fewer ones while keeping the named label. Sharing gives teammates the same saved view, and a playbook is a linked, written set of steps for responding to what a panel shows. PromQL is the Prometheus Query Language. A counter only goes up, such as total requests served, so the useful question is its rate of change. Worked example: the counter http_requests_total for one service reads 1000 at 10:00 and 1600 at 10:05. Step one: subtract the earlier value from the later one, 1600 minus 1000, giving 600. Step two: take the window length, 5 minutes, or 300 seconds. Step three: divide, giving 2 requests per second. In PromQL that is rate(http_requests_total{service="positions"}[5m]), and rate also handles counter resets when a process restarts. Common mistake: graphing the raw counter, which climbs forever and hides drops, or applying rate() to a gauge such as current memory use, where the result has no meaning. Consequence: a panel showing a raw counter can look healthy while a service has quietly stopped, and an alert built on that panel fires late or never. Each panel is only as trustworthy as the query and filter behind it.

questions.prompt: A checkout team tracks checkout_orders_total, a counter for one service. It reads 4200 at 14:00 and 5100 at 14:15, and the goal is orders per second. Step one: subtract the earlier reading from the later one, 5100 minus 4200, giving 900 orders. Step two is missing. Step three: divide the increase by the window length in seconds to get the rate. The window here is 15 minutes. What is step two?
choices: Divide 900 by 15 to get 60, then treat 60 as the rate.
Switch to the gauge type so that the reset handling is skipped.
Add the two readings together to get 9300 orders.
Convert the window to seconds: 15 minutes is 900 seconds.
questions.why: Step three divides by the window length in seconds, so step two must convert the 15-minute window into 900 seconds, which is the unit the division needs.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, why does a counter need a rate calculation before it is useful on a dashboard?
choices: Because a counter only goes up, so its raw total mostly shows age and hides how fast events are happening now.
Because a counter resets to zero every hour, so its raw value is always meaningless.
Because a counter stores text labels, which must be converted into numbers first.
Because a counter can only be filtered by region, not by service.
questions.why: A counter only increases, so its raw value grows forever; the rate of change is what shows current activity.

questions.prompt: A platform team wants to chart the number of free disk gigabytes on a file server, which is recorded as a gauge that rises and falls. Which approach is correct?
choices: Apply rate() over a 10-minute window to the gauge.
Plot the gauge value directly, because rate() only makes sense for values that only go up.
Sum the gauge by region and then apply rate() to the result.
Replace the gauge with a counter named disk_free_gb_total so that rate() can be used.
questions.why: Rate of change is meaningful for counters; applying it to a gauge like free disk space has no useful meaning, so the value is plotted directly.

questions.prompt: A cache service's request counter stopped increasing at 02:00 because the service silently failed. A panel shows the raw counter, which is still a large number. What is the most likely consequence for the team?
choices: The panel looks healthy because the total never drops, so an alert based on it fires late or never.
The rate() function automatically marks the service as down, so no alert is needed.
The panel resets to zero at 02:00, which makes the outage obvious to everyone.
The panel shows a sharp spike, so the on-call engineer is paged immediately.
questions.why: A raw counter that has stopped climbing still displays a large total that looks normal, so a dashboard or alert built on it can miss the failure.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would change a dashboard that shows total error counts so that it shows whether one service is getting worse. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would stop graphing the raw error counter, because it only ever goes up and tells you nothing about the present. Instead I would filter the panel to the one service I care about and apply rate() over a window like five minutes, so the chart shows errors per second right now. Then I would group by service or status so the comparison stays readable. The limit is that the window smooths things out: a five-minute window hides a spike that lasts only seconds, and a very short window gets noisy. So I would note the window size on the panel, and if the spike matters I would check a shorter window too before trusting the trend.
rubricPoints: Explains that a raw counter only rises and needs a rate over a time window
Describes filtering the panel to the one service of interest
Names a concrete tradeoff of the window size, such as smoothing versus noise
Mentions making the window or grouping visible so teammates read the chart correctly

suggested.rationale: Dashboard creation, sharing and PromQL syntax are facts and console steps best learned by reading and then checking them in a real console.

lessons.plain: An alerting policy is a rule that watches a measurement and notifies someone when it goes wrong. A good one does not fire on every small blip. It is tied to a service level indicator (SLI), which is a measure of how well the service is doing for its users, such as the share of requests that succeeded quickly. A service level objective (SLO) is the target for that measure over a period, such as 99.9 percent of requests good over thirty days. The gap between perfect and the target is the error budget, the amount of failure you are allowed. Alerts should fire when that budget is being used up too fast. Cost control uses the same idea for money: alert early, before the bill surprises you.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a service has a target of 99.9 percent successful requests over a month, roughly how many minutes of total failure could it absorb before missing that target, and would you rather be paged the moment one request fails or only when failures are piling up?
lessons.teach:
An SLI is a ratio of good events to valid events, for example successful requests divided by all valid requests, written as a percentage. An SLO is a target for that ratio over a time window, such as 99.9 percent over 30 days. The error budget is 100 percent minus the SLO, the failure you are allowed inside the window. A burn rate compares how fast you are spending that budget against an even pace. A burn rate of 1 uses the budget exactly over the window. A burn rate of 20 uses it twenty times faster.

Why it works: paging on raw errors wakes people for trivia and misses slow leaks. Paging on burn rate ties each alert to real user impact and to how long the budget will last.

Worked example. The SLO is 99.9 percent over 30 days, so the budget is 0.1 percent. In the last hour, 2 percent of requests failed. Step 1: divide 2 percent by 0.1 percent, giving a burn rate of 20. Step 2: at 20 times the even pace, a 30-day budget lasts 30 divided by 20, or 1.5 days. Step 3: a rule that pages when burn rate stays above roughly 14 for an hour is justified, because the budget is disappearing quickly.

Common mistake: alerting on CPU or on a single error spike, with no link to the SLO. Another is measuring the SLI only inside the application, which misses failures the load balancer returns before requests reach it.

Cost control works the same way. A billing budget with threshold alerts notifies you as spend approaches a limit, but it does not stop spending by itself unless something else is wired to act on that notification.

In a running system, a paging policy that fires on every blip trains on-call engineers to ignore pages, so the one alert that reflects a real budget burn gets missed.

questions.prompt: A team's SLO is 99.5 percent over 28 days, so its error budget (the failure allowed inside the window, 100 percent minus the SLO) is 0.5 percent. In the last 6 hours, 3 percent of requests failed. Step 1: divide 3 percent by 0.5 percent to get a burn rate (how many times faster than the even pace the budget is being spent) of 6. Step 2 is missing. What should the team calculate next to learn how long the whole budget lasts at this pace?
choices: 0.5 days, because the budget itself is the number that lasts
4.7 days, found by dividing the 28-day window by the burn rate of 6
28 days, because a higher burn rate does not change the length of the window
168 days, found by multiplying the 28-day window by the burn rate of 6
questions.why: At a burn rate of 6 the budget is used six times faster than the even pace, so the 28-day window is divided by 6, giving about 4.7 days.

questions.prompt: A payments service counts 48,000 valid requests in a day, and 47,616 of them succeeded. Using the idea that an SLI (the ratio of good events to valid events, written as a percentage) is good divided by valid, what is the SLI?
choices: 99.2 percent
384 percent
0.8 percent
47,616 percent
questions.why: The SLI is good events divided by valid events, which is 47,616 divided by 48,000, or 99.2 percent.

questions.prompt: A team sets its SLO (the target for the SLI over a time window) at 99.95 percent over 30 days. Their SLI is computed only from requests their application logs. When a backend fails, the load balancer in front of the app returns errors that never reach the app's logs. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The reported SLI looks healthier than what users experience, so the budget burns without the team noticing
The SLI is accurate, because the load balancer errors are counted by the app automatically
The error budget is spent faster than the team expects, because the load balancer adds latency
The team gets paged more often, because the SLI counts too many valid events
questions.why: Failures returned by the load balancer are missing from the in-app measurement, so the SLI overstates reliability and real budget burn goes unseen.

questions.prompt: A team sets a monthly billing budget of 5,000 dollars with threshold alerts at 50, 90, and 100 percent. On the 20th of the month, spend reaches 90 percent and the alert emails the team. What is true about spending at that point?
choices: Spending stops automatically at 90 percent because the budget has a built-in cap
The spend is capped at 5,000 dollars once the 100 percent alert fires, so no further charges can occur
Spending continues unless something else is wired to act on the notification, because the alert only notifies
The alert reduces spend, because notifications throttle the resources that are running
questions.why: A billing budget alert notifies the team as spend approaches the limit but does not stop spending by itself unless separate automation acts on it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only set CPU threshold alerts how an SLO-based alerting policy differs, and name one limit or tradeoff of alerting on error budget burn rate.
lessons.modelAnswer: A CPU alert tells you a machine is busy, which may or may not hurt users. An SLO-based alert starts from what users experience: an SLI counts good requests, the SLO sets the target, and the error budget is the failure we tolerate. The policy pages when the budget is being spent too fast, measured as a burn rate. That makes pages line up with user impact and tells the on-call engineer how urgent the situation is, because a high burn rate means the budget could be gone in hours. The main limit is that burn rate depends on the window and the SLI being measured correctly. A short window reacts fast but can be noisy, and a long window is quiet but slow to warn. If the SLI misses failures that happen outside the measured path, the alert stays silent while users suffer. Teams usually pair a fast burn alert with a slower one to balance these.
rubricPoints: Defines SLI, SLO and error budget in plain terms
Explains that burn rate compares spend of budget to an even pace
Says alerts tie to user impact rather than raw resource metrics
Names a tradeoff such as window length or SLI blind spots
Notes that a billing budget alert notifies but does not stop spending by itself

suggested.rationale: Building metric alarms with thresholds and burn-rate windows is the hands-on skill this objective needs, and the planned alarm-builder engine would provide it.

lessons.plain: When your monitoring notices something wrong, it has to reach a person or system that can act. A third-party alerting tool is a service outside your cloud provider that takes those signals, decides who should be told, repeats the call if nobody responds, and tracks the response. Two common ways to connect them are a webhook, which is a web address your monitoring system calls with a message when an alert fires, and a dedicated integration built for one tool, such as PagerDuty for on-call paging or Rootly for coordinating incidents. Think of the monitoring system as a smoke detector and the alerting tool as the switchboard that decides who gets woken up at 3 a.m. and keeps trying until someone answers.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your monitoring fires an alert at 03:00 reporting a high error rate, but no engineer is paged. Name two places along the path from detection to a human where the alert could have been lost, and say which one you would check first and why.
lessons.teach:
A notification channel is the destination an alerting policy uses when its condition is met. In Google Cloud Monitoring, an alerting policy watches a metric, a log-based signal, or an uptime check, and opens an incident when its condition holds. The channel decides where the notification goes. Three kinds matter here. A webhook channel sends an HTTP POST with a JSON body to an endpoint you control or that a tool gives you. A PagerDuty channel uses an integration key issued for a PagerDuty service, which routes the event to that service's on-call schedule. Rootly is an incident management platform; connecting it lets alerts open or update incidents so the people coordinating the response see them.

Why this works: the monitoring system only detects. Paging, escalation, acknowledgement and on-call schedules live in the alerting tool, so the path from signal to human is completed there.

Worked example: an alerting policy fires when the 5xx error ratio stays above two percent for five minutes. Step 1: the condition holds and the policy opens an incident. Step 2: the policy sends a notification to its PagerDuty channel. Step 3: PagerDuty receives the event through the integration key and pages the primary on-call engineer. Step 4: if nobody acknowledges within the escalation window, PagerDuty pages the secondary. Step 5: when the metric recovers, the policy sends a resolve notification, which closes the PagerDuty incident.

Common mistake: confirming that a channel exists without ever testing a full page from alert to phone, or pointing a webhook at an endpoint that returns errors. The failure is silent, because the policy still shows an open incident in the console while nobody is notified.

Consequence: customers can be affected for a long time while dashboards look alarming to no one. A verified end-to-end path from alert to a responsible human is part of the alert itself.

questions.prompt: A payments team at a different company has an alerting policy that watches an uptime check on their checkout API. The policy sends notifications to a webhook channel that points at their own internal endpoint. Here is how the path is supposed to run, with one step missing. Step 1: the uptime check fails three times in a row, the condition holds, and the policy opens an incident. Step 2: the policy sends an HTTP POST with a JSON body to the webhook endpoint. Step 3: the endpoint's server answers that POST with an HTTP 500 error. Step 4: [missing]. Which statement completes step 4 correctly?
choices: The policy closes the incident, because a notification was attempted.
Nobody is notified through that channel, and the incident stays open in the console with no page sent to a person.
The policy opens a second incident for the same condition each time a POST fails.
PagerDuty pages the secondary on-call engineer once the escalation window passes.
questions.why: A webhook that returns errors delivers nothing to a human, so the failure is silent and the console still shows the incident as open.

questions.prompt: In Google Cloud Monitoring, what does a notification channel decide?
choices: How long the alerting policy waits before it evaluates its condition.
The thresholds that the uptime check uses to mark a service as failed.
Where the notification goes when the policy's condition is met.
Which metric the alerting policy is allowed to read.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a notification channel as the destination an alerting policy uses when its condition is met, and the channel decides where the notification goes.

questions.prompt: A team wants alerts from a Google Cloud alerting policy to reach the on-call schedule of an existing PagerDuty service. Which item does the team need to set up the PagerDuty channel?
choices: The full URL of the team's internal status dashboard.
An integration key issued for that PagerDuty service.
A Rootly incident template with the team's severity labels.
The name of the metric the alerting policy watches.
questions.why: A PagerDuty channel uses an integration key issued for a PagerDuty service, and that key routes the event to the service's on-call schedule.

questions.prompt: A team confirmed that a webhook channel exists in the console but never sent a full test page from alert to phone. Their endpoint has been returning errors for days. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Rootly closes the incident as soon as the webhook sends its JSON body to the endpoint.
The alerting policy automatically switches to the PagerDuty channel and pages the on-call engineer.
The console shows the incident as open while no one is notified, so customers can be affected for a long time with nobody responding.
The policy resolves the incident after the first failed delivery to prevent duplicate pages.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a channel which was never tested end to end, or an endpoint returning errors, fails silently while the policy still shows an open incident, leaving customers affected with no responder notified.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an alert in Cloud Monitoring reaches an on-call engineer through PagerDuty or a webhook, and name one limit or tradeoff of routing alerts through a third-party tool.
lessons.modelAnswer: The alerting policy in Cloud Monitoring watches a metric and opens an incident when its condition holds. It then sends a notification to each channel attached to the policy. For PagerDuty, the channel carries an integration key tied to a service, so PagerDuty creates an event, pages the on-call engineer, and escalates to the secondary if nobody acknowledges. For a webhook, Monitoring sends an HTTP POST with a JSON body to an endpoint, and whatever receives it has to forward or act on it. The tradeoff is dependency: the alert now relies on the third-party service and the network path to it, and if the webhook endpoint fails or the key is wrong, notifications can be lost without a clear error in the monitoring console. So we test the full path and watch delivery failures, not just the policy's open incident state.
rubricPoints: Describes the alerting policy as the detector and the channel as the delivery destination.
Explains that PagerDuty uses an integration key tied to a service to route events to on-call.
Notes that webhooks send an HTTP POST that the receiving endpoint must handle correctly.
Names a real limit, such as dependency on a third party or silent delivery failure, and a mitigation like end-to-end testing.

suggested.rationale: Tracing an alert through policy, channel and escalation in an exam-style situation teaches the routing logic better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: A metric is a number recorded repeatedly over time, such as how many requests a service handled each minute, how long responses took, or how full a disk is. Reading metrics means looking at their shape: whether they are rising, flat, spiking, or drifting away from normal, and since when. Gemini Cloud Assist is a Google Cloud feature that uses an AI model to answer questions about your resources in everyday language and to summarise what the numbers suggest. It can help you start an investigation faster, but it does not replace looking at the chart yourself or knowing exactly what the number measures.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web service's error count jumped at 09:00, but its request count stayed flat at about the same level all morning. Before any teaching, what would you check first on the chart, and what does the flat request count tell you about the cause?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a measurement sampled at regular intervals and stored as a time series, which is one stream of numbers for one resource with one set of labels, such as one service in one region. Aggregation is how many streams are combined into a single line, for example a sum across all servers or a percentile across all requests. A ratio, such as errors divided by total requests, often tells you more than a raw count, because a raw count can rise simply because traffic rose. A baseline is the normal range a metric usually sits in, and an anomaly is a clear departure from that baseline. Gemini Cloud Assist is an AI assistant inside the Google Cloud console. You ask it a question in plain language, and it summarises what it sees in the metrics and suggests where to look next. Its output is a lead to check, not a verified fact.

Worked example: errors per minute go from 2 to 60 at 09:00, while total requests stay near 1000 per minute. Step 1: divide to get the error ratio, which moves from 0.2 percent to 6 percent. Step 2: the flat request count means traffic is probably not the cause. Step 3: ask the assistant why the error ratio rose at 09:00, then confirm that its time window matches the deployment time. Step 4: only then form a hypothesis such as a bad release.

Common mistake: accepting a summary without checking the time window, the aggregation, or the units. A correct-sounding sentence can describe the wrong series.

Consequence: if you act on a wrong explanation, you may roll back the wrong component or scale up a healthy service while the real fault continues, which lengthens the outage. Treat the assistant's reading as a hypothesis, and make the metric, time window and aggregation explicit before you act on it.

questions.prompt: A payments API in europe-west1 logs failed card charges. Failed charges rise from about 5 per minute to 120 per minute at 14:20, while total charge attempts stay near 4,100 per minute. Step 1: divide failed charges by total attempts to get the failure ratio, which moves from about 0.1 percent to about 2.9 percent. Step 2: the flat attempt count means higher traffic is probably not the cause. Step 3: ask Gemini Cloud Assist why the failure ratio rose at 14:20. Step 4: ___
choices: Switch to traces, because a ratio can only be checked with a trace rather than a metric.
Roll back the payments service at once, because the assistant named a release as the likely cause.
Treat the assistant's answer as a lead, and confirm its time window, aggregation and units match the failure-ratio series you checked before acting.
Scale up the payments service so it can absorb the extra failed charges while you investigate.
questions.why: The assistant's output is a hypothesis to verify, so the missing step is to confirm that its time window, aggregation and units match the series you actually computed before acting on it.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a time series in a metric?
choices: A list of every log line written by all services in a project.
A saved dashboard that groups several charts together for a review meeting.
A single sampled stream of numbers for one resource with one set of labels.
The average of all metrics across a whole organisation, shown on one chart.
questions.why: A time series is one stream of sampled numbers tied to one resource and one label set, which is why it is distinct from logs, org-wide averages or dashboards.

questions.prompt: A service's errors rise from 3 to 6 per minute while its requests rise from 100 to 200 per minute. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The ratio doubled to 6 percent, so reliability got worse.
Raw counts are the better signal, since they show how many users were hit.
The count rose 100 percent, so a release has broken something and needs rollback.
The error ratio stayed at 3 percent, so the rise follows traffic, not reliability.
questions.why: Errors divided by requests is 3 percent before and after, so the raw doubling is explained by the doubling of traffic rather than a change in failure rate.

questions.prompt: An assistant summary says CPU rose in us-central1 at 10:00. When you open the chart, the series is actually europe-west1, the spike is at 11:00, and the values are summed across all instances. What is the main risk of acting on the summary as written?
choices: Restarting the us-central1 fleet, which may not be the failing component.
Only a slower page load, since the chart refreshes too often to read.
Nothing, since the assistant always reads the correct series.
You may fix the wrong component while the real fault continues, lengthening the outage.
questions.why: Acting on a summary that describes the wrong region, time window and aggregation can send effort to a healthy component while the real fault keeps running.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says the AI assistant told them the database caused a latency spike, so they plan to restart it right away. Explain to them how you would use Gemini Cloud Assist together with the metrics to check that claim, and name one limit or tradeoff you would keep in mind.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not restart anything yet. I would open the latency chart for the affected service and note the exact time the spike began, then ask the assistant the same question and compare its answer with what the chart shows. I would check that its time window matches the spike, that it is looking at the right service, and whether it is reporting a percentile or an average. Then I would look at related metrics, such as database query time, connection count, and error ratio, to see whether they moved at the same moment. The main limit is that the assistant summarises the data it can see and can be confidently wrong, so its explanation is a hypothesis. A restart also has a cost: it can drop connections and cause its own spike, so I would confirm the cause first.
rubricPoints: Use the assistant to start the investigation, not to end it
Check the time window, the service, and the aggregation against the actual chart
Compare related metrics before drawing a conclusion
Name the limit that AI summaries can be confidently wrong or incomplete
Note that an action such as a restart has its own risk

suggested.rationale: Choosing which metric answers a production question and checking an AI summary against it is best practised by reasoning through an incident-style situation, which the incident missions only partly cover.

lessons.plain: A trace is the story of one request as it travels through several services. Imagine following a parcel: every hand-off it passes through gets a timestamped note, and the notes link together so you can see where the time went. OpenTelemetry is a free, vendor-neutral set of tools that programs use to write those notes in a common format, so the same instrumentation can send data to different backends. When a user says the app is slow, a metric tells you that it is slow and a log tells you what one service said, but a trace shows which step in the chain used the time.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user says the checkout page takes 4 seconds. Your dashboard shows average latency is up, and the logs from the frontend service look normal. Before reading anything else, what kind of data would most quickly tell you which service and step is responsible, and why?
lessons.teach:
A span is one timed operation, such as handling an HTTP request, querying a cache, or running a database statement. It has a name, a start time, an end time, and attributes, which are key-value details like the route or whether a cache lookup hit. A trace is a set of spans that share one trace ID and form a tree through parent span IDs. Context propagation is the step where a service passes the trace ID and its current span ID to the next service, usually in HTTP headers or message metadata. OpenTelemetry is the open standard and set of SDKs and collectors that create spans and export them. The backend that stores and displays them is a separate piece.

Why it works: each service knows only its own work, but the shared trace ID lets a backend stitch the pieces into one waterfall, where each bar is a span drawn against time, and nesting shows which call waited on which.

Worked example: a positions request takes 900 ms. The gateway span lasts 900 ms. Inside it, a child span for the cache lookup lasts 20 ms and reports a miss. Next, a child span for the database query lasts 850 ms, nested under the gateway span. Reading the waterfall, almost all the time sits in the database span, so the cache is not the bottleneck even though it was the first thing you suspected.

Common mistake: starting spans in each service but not propagating the context, or creating a new trace ID at each hop. The result is several short, disconnected traces, and the slow hop disappears from view.

Consequence in a running system: traces are usually sampled to control cost, so a rare slow request may not be recorded. Sampling should keep errors and slow requests if you need the trace exactly when something goes wrong.

questions.prompt: A booking company's trace has three spans that all carry trace ID 4c9e. A trace ID is the shared label that ties every span of one request together. A span is one timed operation with a name, a start time, and an end time. Step 1: the frontend span lasts 640 ms and has no parent, so it is the root of the tree. Step 2: [missing from this worked example]. Step 3: the payment span lasts 480 ms and is the longest child, so payment is the first suspect. Which statement correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Start a new trace ID for the payment span so its timing is measured separately from the frontend.
Read the inventory span's cache attributes to decide whether the payment call was a cache miss.
Confirm that the payment span lists the frontend span's span ID as its parent, so the waterfall nests payment under the frontend call.
Add the three durations together and divide by the sampling rate to estimate the real request time.
questions.why: A waterfall only shows which call waited on which when each child span points to its parent through the parent span ID, so that link has to be checked before reading the durations.

questions.prompt: A checkout request passes from a web service to a fraud-check service. The web service sends the trace ID and its current span ID along with the request. The fraud-check service starts its own spans but never reads those values from the incoming request. What is the most likely result in the tracing backend?
choices: The fraud-check spans appear nested inside the web service spans with identical durations.
One trace containing every span, with the fraud-check spans placed at the top of the waterfall.
The fraud-check spans are dropped automatically because the backend rejects spans that arrive without a parent.
Two or more short, disconnected traces, so the fraud-check delay is hidden from the web service trace.
questions.why: Without context propagation, the downstream service has no shared trace ID to join, so its spans form separate traces and the slow hop disappears from the web service's view.

questions.prompt: A logistics API uses sampling, which means recording only a fraction of requests to control cost. It keeps 1 in 300 requests. A rare timeout happens about once in 2,000 requests, and an engineer wants a trace for every timeout. Which change best serves that goal?
choices: Raise the sample rate to 1 in 100 for all requests so that more traces exist overall.
Turn off tracing entirely and rely on the request counts shown in the metrics dashboard.
Keep the 1-in-300 rate but also keep every error and slow request so timeouts are always recorded.
Lower the sample rate to 1 in 3,000 to reduce the storage cost of the traces.
questions.why: Sampling by rule for errors and slow requests guarantees the rare failing traces are kept, whereas a higher or lower flat rate still leaves most timeouts unrecorded or adds cost without that guarantee.

questions.prompt: An edge span lasts 1,500 ms. Nested under it are an auth span lasting 35 ms and a search query span lasting 1,380 ms. Where is the most useful first place to look for the delay?
choices: Neither span, because 35 ms plus 1,380 ms is more than the total, so the trace must be corrupt.
The search query span, because it is nested inside the edge and covers almost all of the time the edge waited.
The edge span alone, because nested spans never add detail beyond their parent's duration.
The auth span, because it starts first and so gates everything that follows it.
questions.why: Reading the waterfall, the nested span that takes nearly all of its parent's time is the one that made the parent wait, and 35 ms plus 1,380 ms is actually less than 1,500 ms, so there is no contradiction.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only used logs and metrics: what a trace shows that they cannot, how OpenTelemetry fits in, and one limit or tradeoff of tracing in production.
lessons.modelAnswer: A metric tells us that latency rose, and a log tells us what one service recorded, but neither shows the path a single request took across services. A trace does that: it is a tree of timed spans sharing one trace ID, so we can see which downstream call consumed the time. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral way to create those spans and pass the trace ID between services, and the storage and display backend is separate, so we can switch backends without rewriting code. The main tradeoff is cost and coverage. Recording every request is expensive, so teams sample, and sampling can drop the rare slow request we most want to see. Also, if any service fails to propagate the context, the trace breaks into fragments. So we should keep errors and slow requests in the sampling rules and check that the trace IDs appear in our structured logs.
rubricPoints: A trace is a tree of timed spans linked by a shared trace ID, showing where time went across services.
OpenTelemetry creates and exports spans in a vendor-neutral way, separate from the storage backend.
Context propagation between services is required, or the trace breaks into fragments.
Sampling reduces cost but can drop the rare slow or failed requests.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a slow-checkout situation to choose between logs, metrics, and traces adds the most here, and no listed mission covers tracing directly.

lessons.plain: When a user request passes through several services before it returns a result, it can be hard to tell which step made it slow. A trace is a record of one such request as it travels through the system. It is split into pieces called spans, where each span is one timed step, such as a call to a database or a wait for another service. A trace waterfall is a picture that lays these spans out along a time line, so you can see which steps ran one after another, which ran at the same time, and which took the longest. It is the right tool when the question is where the time went, not just whether something failed.
lessons.guessPrompt: A checkout request takes 3 seconds. It calls an inventory service, a payment service, and a database, and the payment call runs inside the inventory call. Without any tool, which of those three steps would you guess is the slowest, and what would you need to see to be sure?
lessons.teach: A trace is the complete record of one request as it moves through a system, made of linked spans. A span is one timed operation inside that request, such as an incoming HTTP call, a database query, or a call to another service. Each span has a name, a start time, an end time, and a parent, which is the span that caused it. The first span with no parent is the root span. Spans started by a parent are its children, and a shared trace ID ties all spans of one request together across services. A trace waterfall draws each span as a horizontal bar on a shared time line, indented under its parent. The bar's left edge shows when it began and its length shows how long it ran. Nesting shows who waited on whom, and offset shows what ran in sequence and what ran in parallel. Worked example: a checkout request is the root span, running from 0 to 2000 ms. An auth child runs 0 to 40 ms. An inventory child runs 50 to 1550 ms, and inside it a database child runs 60 to 1460 ms. A payment child runs 1560 to 1860 ms, after inventory finishes. Following the longest chain from the top, the path is checkout, then inventory, then its database child, so the database query is where most of the time went. Payment is only 300 ms. Common mistake: reading the widest bar at the top level and blaming that service, when the bar is mostly waiting on its children. Another mistake is adding up overlapping parallel spans as if they were sequential. Consequence in a running system: tuning the wrong service costs engineering time and leaves the user-visible delay unchanged. The most useful reading follows the longest chain of nested bars down to the innermost span doing real work rather than waiting on children.

questions.prompt: A thumbnail upload produces a trace. The root span runs from 0 to 900 ms. Its children are validate (0 to 20 ms), fetch-asset (20 to 520 ms), and encode (520 to 880 ms). Fetch-asset has one child, an object-store read running from 30 to 500 ms. Step 1: the root span is 900 ms long. Step 2: the top-level children are validate, fetch-asset, and encode. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the object-store read is the innermost span doing real work on that path, so storage latency is where most of the time went.
choices: Blame encode because its bar is the last one on the timeline and ends closest to the root.
Compare only validate's bar to the root span, since it starts first and is the easiest to read.
Follow the chain into fetch-asset, the child that runs longest, and then look at the children nested under it.
Add the durations of validate, fetch-asset, and encode together to confirm they equal the root span.
questions.why: Step 3 is following the longest chain of nested bars downward, which here means fetch-asset and then its object-store child, rather than summing siblings or picking the last bar.

questions.prompt: In a trace for a ride-booking request, the span for 'send driver push' has a parent span named 'match-driver'. What does that parent link tell you about the push span?
choices: The push span is the root span of the trace, because it is the last operation sent to the phone.
The push span was started by match-driver, which is the span that caused it, so push waited on or was triggered by matching.
The push span and match-driver ran in parallel with no relationship, since they have different names.
The push span belongs to a different trace, because a parent always has its own separate trace ID.
questions.why: A span's parent is the span that caused it, and children share the trace ID with their parent, so the link shows the causal relationship.

questions.prompt: A payments service has two spans in the same request: one runs from 100 ms to 400 ms and another runs from 150 ms to 450 ms. An engineer says the operations took 650 ms in total by adding the two durations. What is the correct reading of their wall-clock time?
choices: About 650 ms, because the two durations are added together.
About 400 ms, the length of the span that ends first.
About 350 ms, the stretch from the earliest start at 100 ms to the latest end at 450 ms.
About 300 ms, the length of the shorter span.
questions.why: The two spans overlap, so they ran in parallel and the elapsed time is from the first start to the last end, not the sum of their lengths.

questions.prompt: A product-page request has a root span from 0 to 1200 ms. Its child 'pricing' runs from 40 to 1150 ms. Pricing has two children: 'rules-engine' from 50 to 110 ms, and 'tax-api' from 120 to 1140 ms. Following the longest chain of nested bars downward, which span is the innermost one doing real work rather than waiting on children?
choices: tax-api, because it is the end of the longest chain from the root and has no children of its own.
The root span, because it is the widest bar on the page and covers the whole request.
pricing, because it is the widest bar under the root and is responsible for most of the time.
rules-engine, because it is the first child of pricing and starts earliest in the trace.
questions.why: The longest chain runs root, then pricing, then tax-api, and tax-api has no children, so it is the innermost span doing the work; rules-engine is on a short side branch.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use a trace waterfall to find out why one API request is slow, and name one thing a waterfall cannot tell you on its own.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would open the trace for one slow request and look at the root span's total duration first. Then I would follow the longest chain of nested bars downward, because a parent bar often just waits for its children. The innermost span on that chain that is doing work is the likely cause. I would also check for overlapping spans, since parallel calls do not add together. The limit is that a waterfall shows timing for the instrumented steps only. It cannot tell me why a database query was slow, such as a missing index or lock contention. For that I would need metrics or logs for that service, correlated by the trace ID.
rubricPoints: A trace is one request made of spans, each with a start, duration, and parent.
Read the nesting and offsets to find the longest chain and the innermost span doing work.
Parallel or overlapping spans should not be added together as sequential time.
A waterfall shows where time goes but not the internal cause, which needs logs or metrics.

suggested.rationale: Deciding which span in a slow request to blame is an exam-style reasoning task that goes beyond reading a single screen.

lessons.plain: When one user request passes through several services, each service writes its own log lines, and it is hard to tell which lines belong to the same request. Correlating means tying them together. A trace ID is a unique label stamped on one request as it travels. If every log line about that request carries the same label in a structured format (named fields you can search, not free text), you can pull up the whole story of one slow or failed request in seconds. It works like a tracking number printed on every box and every scan record. The key idea is that the label must be attached when each log line is written, not guessed afterwards.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer reports that one checkout took 14 seconds. Your web service log says 'payment call slow', and the payment service log says 'retry 3 of 5', but thousands of such lines are written every minute. What single piece of information would let you find only the lines belonging to that one checkout, and where should it come from?
lessons.teach:
A trace is the full record of one request as it moves through a system. A trace is made of spans. A span is one timed step, such as handling an incoming HTTP request, querying a database, or calling another service. Every span in the same trace shares one trace ID, a long random identifier created when the request first enters the system. Each span also has its own span ID, and a child span records its parent's span ID, which lets a tool rebuild the tree of calls.

A structured log entry is written as named fields, usually JSON, instead of a free sentence. Fields such as severity, message, and trace ID can be filtered exactly. Correlation means writing the trace ID into every log entry produced during that request. Instrumentation libraries do this automatically for the active span. OpenTelemetry is the common vendor-neutral set of these libraries. Google Cloud Logging recognizes a dedicated trace field, so the Logs Explorer can link a log line to its trace in Cloud Trace.

It works because the ID is generated once and passed along with every outgoing call, so each service attaches the same value to its own logs. You never need to match timestamps by hand.

Worked example: a request reaches the API and gets trace ID 4bf9. The API writes a log line containing trace 4bf9 and starts a span. It calls the payment service and passes 4bf9 in the request headers. The payment service writes 'card declined' with trace 4bf9. Filtering logs on trace 4bf9 returns those two lines and any others from that request, and the trace view shows the payment span took 11 of the 14 seconds.

Common mistake: writing plain text such as 'checkout 4bf9 failed'. The ID is buried inside a sentence, so it cannot be filtered reliably and may not link to the trace. Another mistake is generating a new ID in each service, which breaks the chain.

Consequence: if one service drops the trace header, its logs fall out of the trace, and the investigation stalls at that hop. Correlation is only as strong as the weakest service that forwards the ID.

questions.prompt: Tandem Rides runs a booking chain. The mobile gateway receives a booking and assigns trace ID 77c2, a long random identifier that marks the whole request. The gateway writes a structured log (named fields, not a free sentence) containing trace 77c2, then calls the pricing service. The pricing service writes its own structured log with trace 77c2 and must then call the driver-matching service. The missing step: before the pricing service calls driver-matching, it must ___ so that the matching service's log lines carry 77c2. Engineers can then filter all logs on 77c2 to investigate one slow booking.
choices: generate a new trace ID so the two calls appear as separate requests
pass 77c2 along in the outgoing request headers
copy the gateway's timestamp into the message text of its own log line
switch its log output from JSON to a plain sentence so the ID is easier to read
questions.why: Passing the existing trace ID in the outgoing headers lets the matching service attach the same value to its own logs, which keeps the chain unbroken.

questions.prompt: A warehouse inventory service handles one stock-count request. A trace is the full record of that request, and a span is one timed step within it. Which identifier do all spans created for that single request share?
choices: The parent span ID recorded by the last database span
The severity field written on each log line
The trace ID, created once when the request first enters the system and passed along to every span
The span ID of the first span the service creates
questions.why: Every span in one trace shares the same trace ID, which is created once at entry and carried through the request.

questions.prompt: A nightly parts-reorder job writes this log line as plain text: 'reorder for SKU 4471 failed, trace 9de0 at supplier call'. An engineer wants every entry from that run. Why is this line weak for correlation?
choices: Google Cloud does not accept SKU numbers inside log messages, so the library drops the line
The line must be written in the same second as the supplier call, and this one is written too late to match
The trace ID sits inside a sentence, so it cannot be filtered exactly and may not link to the trace view
The job should have used a span ID instead of a trace ID, so the line points to the wrong object
questions.why: Structured logs store the trace ID as its own named field that can be filtered exactly, whereas an ID buried in free text cannot be filtered reliably.

questions.prompt: A parts-tracking API forwards requests to a supplier-portal service through a proxy. The proxy strips the trace header from forwarded requests. An engineer filters Logs Explorer on the trace ID from the API's log. What does the engineer see, and where does the investigation stall?
choices: Log lines from every service, because the proxy copies the header back into the response automatically
The trace view shows the supplier-portal timing, but its logs are merged under the API's severity level
Only the API's own log lines; the supplier-portal lines carry a different ID or none, so the chain stalls at the proxy hop
No log lines at all, because a missing header makes the logging library refuse to write entries
questions.why: Correlation depends on each service forwarding the ID, so once the proxy drops the header, the downstream logs fall out of the trace and the search stops at that hop.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why the trace ID should be written into each structured log line at the moment the line is written, instead of matching logs to traces later by timestamp. Name one limit or tradeoff of doing it this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: Writing the trace ID at write time means every log line carries an exact key, so a filter returns precisely the lines from one request, even when thousands of requests overlap in the same second. Matching by timestamp is guesswork, because services have slightly different clocks and busy systems interleave many requests within the same millisecond. The tradeoff is that the ID only exists if every hop forwards it. A service that drops the trace header, or a library that is not instrumented, produces logs with no ID, and those lines fall out of the trace. You also have to keep the logs structured, so the field is searchable, and the instrumentation adds some overhead and setup work across services. So I would verify coverage on each hop before trusting the correlated view.
rubricPoints: The trace ID is a shared key that every span and log line from one request carries.
Logs must be structured so the trace ID is a filterable field, not text inside a sentence.
The ID is created once and forwarded on each outgoing call, so timestamps are not needed.
A service that drops or regenerates the ID breaks correlation for that hop.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a slow-checkout scenario to pick the correct signal and correlating field adds more than reading setup steps.

lessons.plain: Gemini Cloud Assist is Google Cloud's AI helper inside the console. You ask it questions about your system in plain language, and it reads the data for you. A trace is a record of one request as it moves through several services, showing how long each step took. Using the assistant for trace analysis means asking it to read a slow or failing trace, point to the step that takes the most time, and suggest where to look next. It speeds up reading the picture, but you still check its claims against the trace itself before you act on them.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user request takes 2.4 seconds end to end. Its trace shows one long step that covers almost all of that time, with several short steps running inside it. Which part would you investigate first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A trace is a timeline of one request. Each timed piece of work in it is called a span. A span has a start time, an end time, and a name, such as the name of an operation. Spans can nest: a child span sits inside its parent, and together they form a tree. When you draw the spans as horizontal bars against a time axis, the picture is called a waterfall. Cloud Trace is the Google Cloud service that stores and displays traces. Latency means the time a request takes. Trace analysis answers the question: which span on the slowest path is responsible for the time?

Why it works: a parent span's duration includes all of its children, so a long parent bar is a symptom, not a diagnosis. You find the cause by walking down the tree to the deepest slow span that is not waiting on anything else, which is the critical path. Gemini Cloud Assist can summarize a trace and suggest candidates, which saves time on large traces.

Worked example: a checkout request takes 2400 ms. The waterfall shows a root span of 2400 ms. Inside it, an auth check takes 40 ms and an inventory lookup takes 60 ms, run one after the other. A payment span takes 2200 ms, and inside it a database query span takes 2150 ms. Step one: the root is slow, so it is not a clue by itself. Step two: the children add up to about 2300 ms, so the time is in them. Step three: the payment span is the big child, and the database query is almost all of it. The assistant's summary might say the database query inside the payment call is the bottleneck. You confirm by checking that the query span is sequential on the critical path, not running in parallel with other work.

Common mistake: accepting an AI summary without reading the span timings, then blaming the service named at the top of the trace. Consequence: in a running system, rolling back or scaling the wrong service leaves users waiting, and the incident drags on while the real slow query keeps adding delay to every checkout.

An AI summary is a hypothesis. The span durations in the trace are the evidence you act on.

questions.prompt: A search request takes 1500 ms. Its root span is 1500 ms. Inside it, a query parsing span takes 120 ms and a ranking span takes 1260 ms, run one after the other. Inside the ranking span, a cache lookup takes 90 ms and a model scoring call takes 1140 ms, run one after the other. Step one: the root is slow, so it is not a clue by itself. Step two: the children add up to about 1380 ms, so the time is in them. Step three: the ranking span is the big child, and the model scoring call is almost all of it. What is the next step that finishes the diagnosis?
choices: Check that the model scoring call runs one after the other on the critical path, then treat it as the likely cause
Restart the search frontend, since the root span is named after it
Add the 120 ms query parsing span and the 90 ms cache lookup together and treat that sum as the cause
Accept an AI summary's suggestion without reading the span timings
questions.why: The critical path confirmation is the step that turns a suggested candidate into a verified cause, and the model scoring call is the deepest slow span that is not waiting on anything else.

questions.prompt: In Cloud Trace terms, what is a span?
choices: A timed piece of work with a start time, an end time, and a name, which can sit inside a parent span
The full list of every service that a request touched
A count of how many requests arrived in one minute
A single log line that records an error message
questions.why: A span is defined as one timed piece of work with a start, an end, and a name, and spans can nest into a tree.

questions.prompt: A checkout trace totals 3100 ms. The gateway span takes 310 ms. A fraud check span takes 2750 ms and contains a rules-engine span of 2690 ms. An AI summary names the gateway as the problem. What is the best next action?
choices: Roll back the most recent gateway release
Check the rules-engine span's timing and whether it runs on the critical path, since it is the deepest slow span
Ignore the trace because 3100 ms is within the limit
Scale up the gateway service right away
questions.why: The span durations show the time sits deep in the fraud check and rules-engine work, so the gateway named by the summary is a weak candidate that the timings do not support.

questions.prompt: A parent span lasts 800 ms. Its two child spans last 350 ms and 380 ms. What does this tell you?
choices: The parent is the cause, because it is the longest bar in the waterfall
Both children must have run in parallel, so the total should be 380 ms rather than 800 ms
The trace is incomplete and should be discarded
Most of the time sits in the children, so walk into them; the remaining 70 ms is the parent's own unexplained time and a smaller lead
questions.why: A parent's duration includes its children, so the 730 ms of child time is where the investigation should go, with the leftover 70 ms as a secondary lead.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says Gemini Cloud Assist told them the checkout slowdown is in the payment service, so they want to roll back the payment release. Explain to them how you would use the trace to check that claim, and name one limit of relying on the assistant for this.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not roll back yet. First I would open the trace for a slow checkout and look at the waterfall. The root span covers the whole request, so its length alone does not tell us anything. I would walk down the children and find the deepest slow span that sits on the critical path, meaning the work the request is actually waiting on. If the database query inside the payment call accounts for nearly all the time, the assistant's claim holds up in part, but the fix may be in the query, not the release. One limit is that the assistant summarizes what it was shown and can miss parallel spans, sampling gaps, or a slow dependency that is not instrumented. So I would treat its answer as a lead, confirm it with the span durations, and then choose the smallest safe change.
rubricPoints: Explains that a parent span includes its children, so the root's duration alone does not identify the cause.
Describes walking down the span tree to find the slowest span on the critical path.
Says the AI summary is a hypothesis that must be checked against the span timings.
Names a concrete limit, such as missed parallel work, sampling gaps, or uninstrumented dependencies.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style latency situation, choosing between the trace and the assistant's summary, teaches this objective better than a single read.

lessons.plain: When a server, network or disk misbehaves, the first job is to find out which kind of evidence answers your question. Numbers over time, called metrics, show how much of something is used and whether it is trending up or down. Event records, called logs, show what happened at a specific moment, in the words the software or platform wrote. Traces follow one request as it passes between parts of a system and show where the time went. Choosing the right one first saves a lot of searching. This lesson teaches that choice and the Google Cloud tools that show each kind of evidence.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web service starts returning errors to about a fifth of users, and only from one of three zones. Which kind of evidence would you open first, numbers over time, event records, or the path of a single request, and why?
lessons.teach:
Infrastructure issues are problems in the machines, disks, networks and managed platforms that run your application, as opposed to bugs inside the code. Troubleshooting them means turning a vague symptom into a specific place to look. Three signals help. A metric is a numeric measurement sampled over time, such as CPU use, disk fill percentage, or the count of failed responses per zone. Cloud Monitoring stores metrics and Metrics Explorer charts them. A log is a timestamped record of an event, written by software or by the platform. Cloud Logging stores logs and Logs Explorer searches them using the logging query language. A trace is the record of one request across services, split into spans, where each span is one timed step. Cloud Trace shows spans as a waterfall.

Why this works: metrics are cheap to scan and show scope and trend, so they answer where and how big. Logs carry the detail of what happened, so they answer why at a given moment. Traces answer which step of one request was slow.

Worked example: users in one zone get 503 errors. Step 1: a metric of error count split by zone shows zone-b rising while the other zones stay flat, so the problem is scoped. Step 2: a metric of disk usage for the zone-b instances sits at 100 percent, so the suspicion narrows to full disks. Step 3: a log query filtered to those instances and to disk-error text finds the write failures that began at 09:14. Each step used the signal that answered that step's question.

Common mistake: searching logs first for the word error across everything. You drown in noise and may miss that one resource is the cause, which a single metric chart shows at once.

Consequence: a full disk can stop writes while the fleet average CPU looks healthy, so watch per-resource metrics, not only averages.

questions.prompt: A batch video transcoding service runs 12 worker VMs in one europe-west1 zone. Customers report that some uploads never finish. Step 1: a metric of failed jobs split by zone shows europe-west1-c rising while the other zones stay flat, so the problem is scoped to one zone. Step 2: a metric of CPU use per worker in that zone shows three workers pinned at 98 percent while the other nine sit near 30 percent, so the fleet average hides the problem. Step 3 is missing: name the signal and the tool that show which step inside one stalled upload took the time.
choices: A trace of one stalled upload in Cloud Trace, because a trace splits that request into timed spans shown as a waterfall
A second CPU metric chart with a longer time window, because a longer window reveals which step of one upload was slow
A metric of total job count per hour in Cloud Monitoring, because a count of jobs shows how many uploads stalled
A log search across all services for the word timeout, because logs always show which step of one request was slow
questions.why: A trace follows one request across its steps and shows each timed step as a span, so it answers which step of a single stalled upload took the time.

questions.prompt: Which term describes a timestamped record of an event written by software or by the platform, searched in Logs Explorer?
choices: A span
A waterfall
A metric
A log
questions.why: A log is a timestamped record of an event, and Cloud Logging stores logs that Logs Explorer searches.

questions.prompt: A fleet of 40 VMs has an average disk usage of 41 percent. One VM's disk has reached 100 percent and its writes are failing. Which view is most likely to show this problem first?
choices: The fleet average disk usage chart, because an average shows the worst single machine
A trace of a random request, because traces show disk fill levels
A per-VM disk usage metric in Metrics Explorer, because averages can hide one full disk
A search of all logs for the word disk, because the average is always misleading
questions.why: A full disk on one machine can be hidden inside a healthy-looking fleet average, so a per-resource metric is what reveals it.

questions.prompt: During an outage limited to one zone, an engineer starts by running a broad search of all logs for the word error across every service. What is the main risk of starting this way?
choices: Traces will be deleted when a broad log search runs
The engineer will automatically get a certification-level diagnosis from the logs
The search is too noisy and may miss that one resource is the cause, which a single metric split by zone would show at once
Logs cannot be searched by any text at all, so the search returns nothing
questions.why: A broad text search of logs drowns in noise, while a metric split by zone shows the scope of the problem directly.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you decide whether a production infrastructure problem is best investigated with a metric, a log, or a trace, and name one limit of that choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking what question I am answering. If I need to know whether something is unhealthy, how big the problem is, and where it sits, I open a metric in Cloud Monitoring and split it by zone or instance, because one chart shows scope quickly. Once I have a suspect resource, I switch to logs in Logs Explorer to learn what that resource actually reported when it failed. If the question is which step of one slow request took the time, I use a trace in Cloud Trace. The limit is that metrics only show what someone chose to measure, so a fault with no metric can stay invisible until a log or a user report reveals it. Also, broad log searches are slow and costly, so narrowing with a metric first saves time and money.
rubricPoints: A metric answers where and how large a problem is, and shows its trend over time
A log answers what a specific resource reported at a specific moment
A trace answers which step of one request was slow
A limit: metrics only cover what was instrumented, so unmeasured faults can hide

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right signal for a messy infrastructure symptom is an exam-style reasoning task that a short scenario adds the most to.

lessons.plain: A CI/CD pipeline is the automated assembly line that takes a code change, checks it, builds it, and ships it to where users can reach it. CI stands for continuous integration, the habit of merging and testing code often. CD means continuous delivery or deployment, the step of putting the tested result into an environment. When the line stops or slows down, the first question is where and why.
