Troubleshooting it means choosing the right kind of evidence: the exact text a failing step printed, how a number such as run time or failure rate changes over many runs, or the timeline of one run across its stages. This lesson teaches which kind of evidence answers which question.
lessons.guessPrompt: A pipeline that used to finish in six minutes now takes twenty, and nobody changed the code. Before any teaching, which single piece of evidence would you check first to tell whether this is one slow step, a flaky test, or a slow call to an outside service, and why would that piece of evidence be the one to start with?
lessons.teach:
A pipeline run is one execution of the stages you defined, such as fetching source, running tests, building an artifact, and deploying. A step is one unit of work inside a run. Three kinds of observability evidence help you troubleshoot it. A log is a timestamped text record that a step writes, such as its command output or an error message. A metric is a number collected over time, such as run duration, failure rate, or time spent waiting in a queue. A trace is the timeline of one unit of work, broken into spans, where a span is a timed piece of work that can contain other spans. On Google Cloud, Cloud Build keeps the logs of each build step, Cloud Logging is where you search those logs with its query language, Cloud Monitoring holds metrics and dashboards, and Cloud Trace shows spans for services that are instrumented to send them.

The method works because each signal answers a different question. Use a log for what a specific step printed. Use a metric for when something started and how often it happens across many runs. Use a trace for where time went across several calls inside one deploy.

Worked example for the twenty-minute build. First, the run-duration metric across the last thirty runs shows a jump starting on one day, so the change is real and dated. Second, the logs of one slow run show the dependency install step printing a retry warning four times with a long timeout each time, so the cause is inside that step. Third, if the deploy step calls an artifact service, a trace of that deploy shows one call taking most of the time, which tells you where to look next.

A common mistake is reading only the last error line of a red run, or using the average duration, which hides a spike that happens on some runs only. A stalled deploy can leave a service half updated, so before you rerun a failed pipeline, identify which step last succeeded. Log signals answer what happened, metric signals answer how often and since when, and trace signals answer where the time went.

questions.prompt: A pipeline called ledger-api has been failing since run 412. The engineer's notes so far: (1) the failure-rate metric over the last 44 runs shows the jump starting at run 419, so the change is real and dated; (2) the log of failed run 421 shows the database migration step printing 'connection refused' to the database host four times, so the cause sits inside that step. The missing step: the deploy stage may have partly rolled out, so before anyone reruns the pipeline, the engineer must check which step last succeeded, so the rerun does not leave the service half updated. Which check comes next?
choices: Identify which step last succeeded, so the rerun does not repeat or skip a half-finished update to the service
Search Cloud Logging for every warning from the past month and count how many of them mention the database
Read only the last error line of run 455 to confirm that the same failure is still happening today
Compare the average duration of all 44 runs to see whether the pipeline has become generally slower
questions.why: A stalled deploy can leave a service partly updated, so you must find the last successful step before rerunning, and the other choices either reread the same evidence or answer a different question.

questions.prompt: A team asks, for a build pipeline that has run 60 times since Monday: how often has it failed, and since which day? Which kind of observability signal answers this question, and where would they look on Google Cloud?
choices: A single log line from the first failed step, because it is timestamped
A trace in Cloud Trace, because it lists every span across the failed runs
A log query in Cloud Logging that prints the exit code of each run one by one
A metric in Cloud Monitoring, because a metric is a number collected over time such as failure rate
questions.why: A metric is a number collected over time, so a failure rate and its starting date are metric questions, and Cloud Monitoring is where metrics live.

questions.prompt: A build pipeline averages 6 minutes across 50 runs, but 5 of those runs took about 30 minutes each. A colleague says the average looks fine, so nothing needs investigating. What is the best response?
choices: The average is accurate, so the five slow runs are random noise and can be ignored
The average hides the slow runs, so the team should look at the spread of run durations and then inspect the logs of one slow run
Five slow runs out of fifty is too few to matter, so the team should wait for more data
Averages should be replaced by traces, because traces are the only signal that measures duration
questions.why: An average can hide a spike that happens on only some runs, so you look at the spread and then use a log of a slow run to find the cause inside the step.

questions.prompt: A deploy step in a pipeline took 16 minutes, and most of that time was spent in one call to an external artifact service. The team wants to know which call inside the deploy consumed the most time. Which signal should they use?
choices: A metric of average run duration across the whole project for the month
A trace, because a trace shows the timeline of one unit of work broken into timed spans
A count of failed runs per day, because failure counts show where time went
A log of the build step, because logs record how long each call took
questions.why: A trace shows where time went across several calls inside one deploy, so it is the signal that identifies the slow call, while the other signals answer different questions.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a failing or slow CI/CD pipeline needs a log, a metric, or a trace. Name one limit or tradeoff of the signal you would reach for first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the question I am trying to answer. If I need to know what a specific step actually printed, I open that step's log, because only the log has the exact error text and the command output. If I need to know whether a problem is new, how often it happens, or when it started, I look at a metric such as run duration or failure rate, because metrics show patterns across many runs. If I need to know where time went inside one deploy that calls several services, I use a trace. The limit of logs is volume: a verbose build can produce thousands of lines, so I filter by run and step first. The limit of metrics is that they show that something changed but not why, so I always follow a metric with the logs of a slow run.
rubricPoints: Matches the signal to the question: logs for what a step printed, metrics for trends and frequency, traces for where time went across calls
Names the tools or places where each signal lives in the pipeline context
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff of the first signal chosen, such as log volume or metrics hiding cause
Notes that a metric shows that a change happened and a log or trace is needed for the cause

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner repair a failing CI pipeline, which practices locating the failing step and its evidence directly.

lessons.plain: When a live application misbehaves, you need evidence about what it did. Think of a restaurant that has become slow. You can read the order tickets, look at a chart of how many meals leave the kitchen each minute, or follow one order from the door to the table and note where it waited. Those three kinds of evidence are logs, metrics and traces. Logs are written notes about individual events. Metrics are numbers summarized over time. Traces follow one request through every step it passed through. Troubleshooting is largely choosing the right kind of evidence for the question you are asking, then using it to narrow down where the problem lives.
lessons.guessPrompt: Customers say the map page takes several seconds to load since yesterday's release, but the application's error log shows nothing unusual. You have one slow request and a dashboard showing overall response times. Which signal should you open first to find which downstream call is responsible: logs, metrics, or traces? Give a one-line reason.
lessons.teach:
A log is a record of one discrete event, such as a failed request or a warning written by the code, usually with a timestamp and text or structured fields. A metric is a number measured repeatedly over time and stored as a time series, such as request count, error rate, or latency. Latency is how long a request takes. A useful latency metric is a percentile: the 95th-percentile (p95) latency is the time within which 95 percent of requests finish. A trace records the path of a single request through a system. It is made of spans, where each span is one timed step, such as a database call or a call to another service, and spans nest under a parent. A trace ID is a shared identifier stamped on every span and every log line written for one request, which lets you connect a trace to its logs.

Why this works: each signal trades detail for coverage. Metrics are cheap to keep for long periods and answer whether something changed and by how much. Logs hold the specific detail of what happened in one event. Traces show where time went inside one request, which is what a slowness question needs.

Worked example: a map page request takes 4 seconds. Step 1: the p95 latency metric jumped from 300 ms to 4 s just after 09:00, so the problem is real and has a start time. Step 2: open a trace for one slow request. The waterfall view draws each span as a bar on a timeline, and one 3.6-second span for a call to the positions cache stands out while the others take milliseconds. Step 3: search the logs for that trace ID. The cache client logged connection timeouts for the same request, confirming the cause and giving the exact error text.

Common mistake: reading the error log first for a slowness problem. A slow request that succeeds writes no error, so the log looks clean while users wait. Another mistake is trusting an average latency, which can hide the slow tail that real users experience.

In a running system this matters because the metric tells you whether to act, the trace tells you which component to fix, and the log tells you why. Skipping a step usually means guessing.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking API's p95 latency rose from 220 ms to 2.6 s just after 14:10. An engineer opened the trace for one slow booking. The waterfall view shows one 2.1-second span for a call to a seat-hold service, while the other spans take a few milliseconds. The investigation is missing its final step: the engineer needs the exact error the seat-hold client recorded for that same slow booking. What should they do next?
choices: Average the seat-hold span duration over the last 30 days to find the typical wait
Read the error log for all 500 responses in the last hour, since errors are the first thing to check
Restart the booking API so the seat-hold connections reset before checking anything else
Search the logs for the trace ID stamped on that booking's spans, to find the client's error lines for that one request
questions.why: The shared trace ID links the slow span to the specific log lines written for that one request, which gives the exact error text.

questions.prompt: Which signal best answers the question: did the checkout error rate change after yesterday's deploy, and by how much?
choices: A single log line recording one failed checkout
A log search for the word deploy across all services
A metric time series of error rate, compared before and after the deploy
A trace of one checkout request showing its spans
questions.why: A metric is a number tracked over time, so comparing its values before and after the deploy shows both whether it changed and the size of the change.

questions.prompt: A dashboard shows an average request latency of 180 ms for a media upload service, and the team concludes that users are fine. What is the flaw in that reasoning?
choices: Any average over 100 ms proves that at least one request took longer than a second
An average is always lower than the p95, so 180 ms means the p95 is also under 200 ms
The average says nothing about the slow tail: a share of requests can take several seconds while the mean still looks healthy, and a percentile such as p95 exposes that share
Averages cannot be computed from latency measurements, so the 180 ms figure is invalid
questions.why: An average blends fast and slow requests together, so a slow tail can hide inside a healthy-looking mean, whereas a percentile such as p95 reports the value that most requests stay under.

questions.prompt: Users of a search service report that some queries feel slow, but the service's error log has no entries for those queries. Which signal should you open first to find where the time went for one slow query?
choices: A count of log lines per hour, to see whether logging volume went up
The error log, since a request with no error entry has nothing to investigate
A trace of one slow search request, to see the duration of each timed step inside it
A search for the trace ID in the error log, deleted after the first match
questions.why: A trace records the timed steps inside a single request, which is the signal that shows where the time went when a request is slow but not failing.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that when an application gets slow, they always start with the error logs because logs are the most detailed. Explain to them, in your own words, which signal you would start with for a slowness problem and why. Also name one limit or tradeoff of the signal you would not start with.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with metrics, specifically latency percentiles and request rate, because they tell me whether the slowness is real, when it began, and whether it affects all users or only some. Error logs are detailed, but they record events, and a request that is slow yet succeeds writes nothing, so the logs can look clean during exactly this kind of problem. Once metrics show the change and its start time, I would open a trace for one slow request. The trace breaks the time into spans, so I can see which downstream call holds most of it. Then I would use the trace ID to pull only the log lines from that request, which gives the specific error text. The tradeoff of metrics is that they summarize. They show that something is slow but not which request or why. Logs carry that detail, but they are costly to search at scale and easy to misread without a trace to focus them.
rubricPoints: Metrics show whether the slowness is real, when it started, and how widely it spreads.
Traces break one slow request into spans to locate the slow step.
Logs explain why, and are linked to the same request through the trace ID.
A limit: metrics summarize away detail, and successful slow requests write no error logs, so each signal alone can mislead.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right signal for a production scenario is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation, which this objective calls for.

lessons.plain: When a monitoring system is the thing that is broken, you have a problem one level up: the logs, metrics, traces and alerts you rely on stop telling the truth. Maybe a server's logs stop arriving, a graph flatlines when traffic did not, or an alert that should page someone stays silent. Troubleshooting observability itself means asking first whether the signal is missing because the system failed or because the pipe carrying the signal failed. The skill is choosing a check that tells those apart, such as whether the collector is still sending data, before you trust any dashboard again.
lessons.guessPrompt: A CPU chart for one server suddenly shows a flat line at zero for the last hour, but users report the site is slow. Before looking at the server, what is the first thing you would doubt about the chart itself, and why?
lessons.teach:
A telemetry pipeline is the chain that carries observability data from the thing being watched to the place you look at it: an agent or collector on the machine, an ingestion step, storage, then dashboards and alert rules. Each link can fail on its own. The key idea is that silence is ambiguous. A flat line or a missing log could mean the workload is quiet, or that the pipeline stopped delivering. To separate those, check the pipeline's own health signals: the agent's heartbeat or last-seen time for the resource, ingestion or throughput metrics for the log sink or metric pipeline, and the list of exclusion filters and recent configuration changes. An exclusion filter is a rule that drops matching entries before they are stored, so a new one can make healthy traffic vanish from every dashboard.

Worked example. At 14:00 a CPU chart for one VM drops to zero and stays there. Step 1: confirm the VM is running using a source independent of the agent, such as the cloud provider's instance status. It is running. Step 2: check the agent's last-seen time for that VM. It stopped at 13:58. Step 3: check recent changes to the log and metric routing and find an exclusion added at 13:55 that matches this VM's label. The workload was fine; the pipeline was dropping its data.

Common mistake: reading a missing signal as a zero value, or as proof of health. Consequence: an alert based on that metric can never fire because it never sees a breach, so an outage looks like a quiet night.

questions.prompt: At 10:40 a Brightwater Logistics dashboard showing error counts for its order service drops to zero and stays there. Step 1: the load balancer's request count shows about 900 requests per minute still arriving, so the service is receiving traffic. Step 2: the log sink's ingestion-throughput metric shows bytes entering the pipeline falling to zero at 10:37. Step 3 is missing. Which action completes the investigation?
choices: Compare today's error count with the average from the same weekday last month
Mark the incident resolved, since the zero shows the order service is healthy
Raise the alert threshold so the flat line stops firing notifications
Check the exclusion filters and recent routing changes for a rule that matches the order-service logs
questions.why: Traffic still arriving while ingestion drops to zero points to the pipeline discarding the data, so the next step is to look for an exclusion or recent configuration change that would explain it.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is an exclusion filter in a telemetry pipeline?
choices: A rule that copies matching entries into a second storage location for backup
A threshold on a chart that marks values above a limit in red
A check that the agent runs on a machine to confirm the machine is powered on
A rule that drops matching entries before they are stored, so they never reach dashboards
questions.why: The teaching text defines an exclusion filter as a rule that drops matching entries before they are stored, which is the first option.

questions.prompt: A Lumen Freight queue-depth chart has been flat at 0 for two hours. The producer service's own dashboard shows 3,000 messages sent during that window. Which conclusion does the evidence support?
choices: The queue is healthy and the producer is sending nothing
The queue depth metric is valid because the chart shows a clean line
The flat zero is unreliable, and the pipeline's health signals should be checked before trusting it
The producer's dashboard is wrong and should be ignored
questions.why: A missing or flat signal is ambiguous, and the producer's count of 3,000 messages contradicts the zero, so the pipeline's own health signals must be checked before the zero is believed.

questions.prompt: A team at Harbor Credit set an alert to fire when checkout latency is greater than 500 ms. The metric stopped reporting at 08:15 after an agent upgrade, and the alert never fired during a slow afternoon. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The 500 ms threshold was too high for the afternoon load on the checkout service
Traces showed the requests were fast, so the alert was correctly silent
The alert treated the absence of data as a value below 500 ms, so it never saw a breach
The alert was muted by the team during the upgrade window
questions.why: Reading a missing signal as a zero or as a non-breach means an alert based on that metric cannot fire, which is why the slow afternoon went unnoticed.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says our error-rate alert has been silent for two days, so the service must be healthy. Explain to them how you would tell whether the silence means health or a broken observability pipeline, and name one limit of your check.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not accept silence as health yet. An alert that never fires can mean there are no errors, or that the errors never reach the alerting system. First I would check whether the data is arriving at all: the agent or collector's last-seen time for the service, and the ingestion volume for its logs or metric series over those two days. If volume dropped to near zero while traffic was normal, the pipeline is suspect. Next I would check recent changes to exclusion filters, routing rules and the metric names the alert depends on, since a renamed label can silently orphan an alert. One limit of this check is that ingestion can look healthy while the data is wrong, such as a parser that drops a field, so I would also compare against an independent signal like the load balancer's own error count or a synthetic probe.
rubricPoints: Silence can mean healthy or a broken pipeline, so check data arrival first
Look at agent last-seen time and ingestion volume for the affected source
Check recent exclusion filters, routing and renamed labels that can orphan alerts
Name a limit, such as healthy-looking ingestion hiding wrong or dropped fields
Confirm with an independent signal such as a probe or the provider's own error count

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style production situation where a dashboard or alert goes quiet adds the most here, since the core skill is choosing which check separates a broken pipeline from a healthy system.

lessons.plain: When a service feels slow, the first job is to work out where the time goes. Think of a restaurant meal that takes forty minutes. You can ask the manager how long meals took on average this week, which is a summary number over time. You can follow one order through the kitchen stage by stage to see which station held it up, which is a timeline of one request. You can read the ticket for that table to see what happened at each step, which is a detailed event record. Latency troubleshooting means picking the right one of those views for your question, then narrowing down until you find the slow step.
lessons.guessPrompt: A checkout API's average response time stayed at 300 milliseconds after a deploy, but support tickets say some customers wait several seconds. Which single view would you open first to find out whether a few requests are very slow, and why would the average not be enough?
lessons.teach:
Latency is the time a request takes from arrival to reply. A metric is a number recorded repeatedly over time, such as request count or response time, and dashboards plot it. Because a single average can hide a slow minority, engineers use percentiles: the p95 is the value that 95 percent of requests finish under, and the p99 is the value 99 percent finish under. A trace records the path of one request through several services. It is made of spans, where each span is one timed operation with a start, a duration, and a parent span that called it, so the trace view is a waterfall of nested bars. A log is a timestamped event record. Logs become useful for latency when each entry carries the trace ID of the request it belongs to, which lets you jump from one slow trace to the exact log lines it produced.

Worked example: at 09:00 the checkout p99 rises from 300 ms to 4 s while the error rate stays flat. Step 1, the metric shows the problem is slowness, not failure, and grouping by route shows only the position endpoint is affected. Step 2, you open a slow trace for that route; the waterfall shows a 3.9 s API span whose child cache-call span takes 3.7 s, while the database span takes 0.1 s. Step 3, you filter logs by that trace ID and see many cache misses at the same moment, which points to entries expiring together after the deploy.

Common mistake: starting in logs with a text search for the word slow, or judging health by the average. Logs show what happened but not how long each stage took across traffic, and averages let a painful tail hide.

In a running system this matters because a one percent slice of users waiting four seconds is a real incident, even when the dashboard average looks normal. Use metrics to find when and where, traces to find which step, and logs to find why.

questions.prompt: A video service at a different company sees its p95 latency on the upload route rise from 700 ms to 2.6 s at 14:00, while its error rate stays flat. Step 1: a metric grouped by route shows only the upload route is affected. Step 2: you open a slow upload trace, a trace being the recorded path of one request through several services, and its waterfall shows a 2.4 s thumbnail call whose child storage-write span takes 2.3 s. Step 3 is missing. Which action is the correct next step?
choices: Filter the log entries by that slow trace's trace ID and read the lines written during that one request
Add a new metric for total disk usage across the whole fleet before looking at anything else
Search all logs for the word slow across every service and count the matches
Compare the monthly average response time against last quarter to confirm the slowdown is real
questions.why: Logs that carry a trace ID can be filtered to the exact lines produced by the slow request, which explains why the storage write was slow.

questions.prompt: A checkout API reports a mean latency of 180 ms, but its p99 is 3.1 s. Which statement best explains what the mean hides?
choices: The mean counts only failed requests, so it ignores slow successful ones
The p99 measures how many requests arrived, not how long they took
The mean is always higher than the p99, so the p99 must be a measurement error
Some requests are very slow, and an average can hide that slow minority
questions.why: The p99 shows that 1 percent of requests take over 3 s, a slow tail that a single average smooths away.

questions.prompt: A user reports one slow order page. Which signal best shows which internal step of that single request took the time, and which step called which?
choices: An average response time on a dashboard
A metric of CPU usage on the database host
A trace, whose waterfall of nested bars shows each timed step and its parent
A count of error logs for the day
questions.why: A trace records the timed spans of one request and their parent-child nesting, which is exactly the per-step view needed here.

questions.prompt: A team's logs have timestamps but no trace ID, the identifier that marks which request a log line belongs to. A trace shows a 3 s cache span for one request. What is the main limitation they face?
choices: Jump straight from the trace to the exact log lines produced by that request
Match log lines to that request only by timestamp, which is unreliable when many requests overlap
Ignore the logs, since a trace alone is enough to explain why the cache span was slow
Search the logs for the word slow, which will pinpoint the cache span
questions.why: Without a trace ID, log lines cannot be tied to one request with certainty, so matching by timestamp during heavy traffic is guesswork.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a slow API is a capacity problem, a slow code path, or a slow dependency. Name the signal you would open first, the signal you would use next, and one limit of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with a latency metric split by percentile and by route, because that shows when the slowness began and whether it affects everyone or only a tail. If p99 rises while p50 stays flat, the problem is usually a subset of requests, not general overload. Next I open a trace for one slow request. The waterfall shows which span holds most of the time: a long span inside the service suggests a code path problem, and a long child span calling a database or cache suggests a dependency. If the spans look normal but the CPU and queue metrics are saturated, that points to capacity. The limit is that a trace is a sample of requests, so a rare pattern might not be captured, and I would widen the sampling or check the metrics for the affected window before drawing a conclusion.
rubricPoints: Uses a latency metric with percentiles rather than only averages
Uses a trace waterfall to find which span holds the time
Distinguishes capacity saturation from code path and dependency delays
Names a limit such as trace sampling or a narrow time window

suggested.rationale: The mission has the learner diagnose a slow API after a deploy, which practises finding the slow step from latency evidence.

lessons.plain: Application performance monitoring data is the record of how your software behaves while real people use it: how long each request takes, which steps inside a request are slow, how much CPU and memory the code uses, and when it fails. Collecting it means your application, or the platform it runs on, produces these measurements and sends them to a central place where you can look at them. Think of a delivery company that does not just count parcels but timestamps every stop on every route, so when one delivery is late it can see exactly which leg took too long. Without this data, slowness is a rumor. With it, you can point at the step responsible.
lessons.guessPrompt: A checkout page is slow for some customers but fast for others. Which would tell you more about one slow request: a graph of average CPU usage across all servers, or a timing breakdown of each step that one request went through? Say which and why.
lessons.teach:
Application performance monitoring, usually shortened to APM, is the practice of measuring what your software does while it runs. It rests on three kinds of signal. Metrics are numbers sampled over time, such as request count or latency, often summarized as percentiles; a p95 latency of 800 ms means 95 percent of requests finished within that time. Traces follow one request as it crosses services, and each step in that journey is recorded as a span with a start time and a duration. Profiles show where CPU time or memory is spent inside the code. On Google Cloud, metrics and alerting live in Cloud Monitoring, distributed traces in Cloud Trace, and continuous profiling in Cloud Profiler. Application code is usually instrumented with OpenTelemetry, an open standard library that creates spans and metrics, so the data is not tied to a single vendor. The reason this works is that a trace keeps the timing of each step separate, so the slow step stands out instead of being averaged into one dashboard number.

Worked example: a checkout request takes 2400 ms. The root span of the trace lasts 2400 ms. The child span for the payment call lasts 150 ms. The child span for the inventory database query lasts 2100 ms. The engineer opens that span and sees a query scanning the whole table. The data points to the database, not the payment provider.

Common mistake: tracing every request in busy production is expensive, so teams sample. If they keep one request in a thousand at random, a rare slow path may never be captured. Good setups also keep errors and unusually slow requests.

Consequence: without instrumentation, during an incident the team guesses, may fix the wrong service, and the outage lasts longer.

questions.prompt: A ride-hailing app's find-driver request takes 1800 ms. Step 1: the root span of its trace lasts 1800 ms, covering the whole request. Step 2: the child span for the fare service lasts 1200 ms, and the child span for the driver-location lookup lasts 400 ms. Step 3: the engineer sees that the fare service span is the largest slice of the request. Step 4 is missing: the trace shows only how long the fare service span took, not which lines of its code use the CPU time. The engineer needs a tool that breaks down CPU and memory use inside that service. Which tool fills the missing step?
choices: Raising the trace sampling rate to 100 percent so every request is kept
A Cloud Monitoring chart of the p95 latency for the whole app
Cloud Profiler
Adding more driver-location lookup replicas to shorten the 400 ms span
questions.why: Cloud Profiler shows where CPU time and memory go inside the code, which a trace span duration alone cannot show.

questions.prompt: A payments team has a request that passes through four services. They want to know, for each individual request, which service added the most delay. Which signal type answers this?
choices: Profiles, because they show CPU time inside one function
Counts of error responses per minute
Metrics, because a p95 latency number summarizes all requests together
Traces, because each service step is recorded as a span with its own start time and duration
questions.why: A trace follows one request across services and records each step as a timed span, so the slowest step per request is visible.

questions.prompt: A team samples one request in 1000 at random. A rare slow path that happens in about one request in 50,000 is causing complaints. Which statement best describes the problem and the fix?
choices: The fix is to replace OpenTelemetry with a different vendor agent
Random sampling can miss rare slow paths, so keeping errors and unusually slow requests too is the better fix
Sampling one in 1000 means traces are complete for every path, so nothing is missed
Metrics capture every span, so tracing is unnecessary for this problem
questions.why: Random sampling may never capture a rare slow path, and good setups also keep errors and unusually slow requests to catch them.

questions.prompt: A team wants to track the p95 latency of its order API over the last hour and get an alert when it passes 500 ms. Which tool should hold that data and raise the alert?
choices: Cloud Monitoring, which holds metric numbers and alerting rules
Cloud Profiler, which records CPU time inside the code
The OpenTelemetry library, which creates spans and metrics but does not store alerts
Cloud Trace alone, since a single trace shows the 95th percentile of requests
questions.why: Cloud Monitoring stores metrics like percentile latency over time and handles alerting, while OpenTelemetry only creates the data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never worked with monitoring the difference between a metric, a trace and a profile, and name one limit or tradeoff of collecting this data in production.
lessons.modelAnswer: A metric is a number tracked over time, like request count or 95th percentile latency. It tells you that something got slower, and when, but not why. A trace follows a single request across services and records how long each step took, so you can see which call inside that request is the slow one. A profile shows where the code itself spends CPU time or memory, which helps when the slowness is inside one service rather than between services. The main limit is cost and overhead. Tracing every request in busy production is expensive and adds a little latency, so teams sample. Sampling at random can miss rare slow paths, so the sampling rules should keep errors and slow requests too. Metrics are cheap to keep but cannot explain a single request on their own, so you need all three working together.
rubricPoints: Defines metrics as aggregated numbers over time that show that something changed
Defines a trace as one request followed across steps or services, with timed spans
Distinguishes a profile as showing where code spends CPU or memory
Names sampling cost or overhead as a tradeoff and notes that random sampling can miss rare slow requests

suggested.rationale: Choosing between metrics, traces and profiles for a slow-request situation is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario.

lessons.plain: Active Assist is a set of Google Cloud features that studies how your resources actually behave and then suggests improvements. Two kinds of output matter. An insight is an observation, such as a sudden change in how a resource is used, that tells you something is happening. A recommendation is a specific proposed action, such as shrinking an oversized machine or removing a permission nobody uses, along with an estimate of the benefit. It works like a building inspector's report: it points out problems and proposes fixes, but a person still decides which ones to act on and checks the result afterwards.
lessons.guessPrompt: A virtual machine has averaged only 5 percent CPU use for a month. Before you consider shrinking it, what would you want to find out first, and why would that matter?
lessons.teach:
Active Assist is the Google Cloud feature family that analyses usage data for your projects and produces two kinds of output. An insight is an observation about a pattern, for example that a resource's behaviour changed sharply. A recommendation is a concrete proposed change with a stated reason and an estimated impact, such as cost savings or a smaller set of permissions. The engine that produces recommendations is called a recommender. Each recommendation moves through states: active (open and waiting), claimed (someone is working on it), succeeded (applied), failed (applying did not work), or dismissed (someone decided not to act). Recommendations are built from a look-back window of recent usage, which can be days or weeks depending on the type, so they describe the past and not a guaranteed future.

Why it works: the recommender compares what you provisioned with what you actually used, then estimates what a change would save or fix. It cannot see your business calendar, so its advice is a starting point for a decision rather than the decision itself.

Worked example: a Compute Engine virtual machine with 8 vCPUs averages 6 percent CPU over the window. Step 1: the recommender sees the low use and proposes moving the machine to a smaller type, with a savings estimate. Step 2: you check the window for a month-end batch that a long average can hide. Step 3: if the batch exists, you confirm the smaller type handles its peak, perhaps by testing in a staging environment. Step 4: you apply the change, mark it succeeded, and watch the metrics for a week.

Common mistake: applying a recommendation straight from the dashboard because the savings figure looks attractive, without checking for periodic peaks the window missed.

Consequence: in a running system, shrinking a machine that serves a nightly job can make that job miss its deadline, so the change costs more than it saves. Treat each recommendation as evidence to verify before you act on it.

questions.prompt: A team runs a service account that reads from one Cloud Storage bucket once a week. The account was granted the Editor role across the whole project. Active Assist shows a recommendation to narrow the account's permissions, based on a 30-day look-back window that captured four of those weekly runs. Step 1: the recommender sees that the account only ever read objects and proposes a narrower role with a stated reason. Step 2: the team confirms that the weekly job is the account's main purpose and that the 30-day window covered several runs, so the observed pattern is real. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the team applies the narrower role, marks the recommendation succeeded, and checks the next weekly run.
choices: Check whether any other workload also uses this service account before applying the narrower role.
Mark the recommendation dismissed straight away, since any permission change carries risk.
Convert the recommendation into an insight, so that the permission change is no longer proposed.
Extend the look-back window to one year so the recommendation reflects a longer history.
questions.why: Before applying a change, the team must verify that the recommendation's evidence does not miss another user of the account, which is the verification step the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: In Active Assist, what is the difference between an insight and a recommendation?
choices: Insights and recommendations are the same output, but insights are produced only for projects that have billing enabled.
A recommendation is a pattern observed over time, while an insight is an applied change that has already succeeded.
An insight is a concrete change with a savings estimate, and a recommendation is only an observation about usage.
An insight is an observation about a pattern, while a recommendation is a concrete proposed change with a stated reason and estimated impact.
questions.why: The teaching text defines an insight as an observation about a pattern and a recommendation as a concrete proposed change with a reason and an estimated impact.

questions.prompt: A colleague says a recommendation is in the claimed state. What does that tell you?
choices: The recommendation was rejected by a reviewer and will not be revisited.
The recommendation is open and waiting for anyone to act on it.
Someone has started working on the recommendation.
The recommendation has been applied and its result is confirmed.
questions.why: The claimed state means someone is working on the recommendation, as distinct from active (open and waiting), succeeded (applied), and dismissed (someone decided not to act).

questions.prompt: A team applies a recommendation to change a set of resources based only on a savings estimate, and the change later causes a failure at a time of heavy traffic that the usage data did not show. Which explanation best accounts for this?
choices: The recommender's estimate was calculated without any usage data, so the figure was always meaningless.
The recommender cannot produce estimates for resources that run under a managed service.
Recommendations describe past usage over a look-back window and do not guarantee future behaviour, so unchecked periodic peaks can be missed.
The state machine moved the recommendation to failed automatically, which caused the traffic problem.
questions.why: The teaching text explains that recommendations are built from a look-back window, so they describe the past rather than a guaranteed future, and periodic peaks outside that window can be missed.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says Active Assist recommendations are a to-do list we should clear every week. In your own words, explain the difference between an insight and a recommendation, and name one limit that means we should verify a recommendation before applying it.
lessons.modelAnswer: An insight is an observation that something in our usage has changed or looks unusual, such as a resource being used in a new way. A recommendation is a specific proposed action, like resizing a machine or removing an unused permission, with an estimated benefit attached. The recommender that creates them only looks at usage over a fixed look-back window, so it can miss things that happen outside that window, like a quarterly batch job or a seasonal traffic peak. It also has no knowledge of our service-level commitments or upcoming launches. So I would not clear the list blindly. For each item I would check the window against our calendar, test the change in a non-production environment if it affects capacity, apply it with a plan to roll back, and then confirm the metrics afterwards. The list is useful input for decisions, not a set of orders.
rubricPoints: Defines an insight as an observation and a recommendation as a specific proposed action with an estimated impact
Explains that recommendations are based on a look-back window of past usage
Names a concrete limit, such as missed periodic peaks or no knowledge of business context
States that a person should verify, test, and monitor before and after applying a recommendation

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product concepts, states and console or API steps, which a read-through with the official catalogue explains better than a current mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: Observability means watching how a running system behaves, through its logs (text records of events), metrics (numbers sampled over time) and traces (records of one request's path through several services). Storing and querying that data is not free. Cloud providers usually bill by how much data you send in, how long you keep it, and how many metric series you create. Accounting for observability costs means knowing which of those things drives your bill, measuring it, and cutting the waste without blinding yourself when something breaks. Think of it like a security camera system: recording every hallway around the clock costs a lot, so you decide what to keep, for how long, and where to store the footage.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your service writes a debug line for every health check it receives, about 500 times a minute, and the logging bill has tripled this month. Before reading on, what would you change first, and what is the risk of that change?
lessons.teach:
Ingestion means the volume of log data sent into the logging service. Retention means how long stored data is kept before it is deleted. An exclusion filter is a rule that tells the logging service to drop matching entries instead of storing them. A log sink is a routing rule that exports matching logs to another destination, such as a storage bucket or a BigQuery dataset. A metric series is one unique combination of a metric name and its labels; each series you create can add to a monitoring bill. Cardinality is the number of distinct label values; high cardinality means many series.

The cost logic works because most bills scale with volume and time. If you ingest less, you pay less to store and query it. If you keep data shorter, you pay less for storage. If you create fewer unique series, the metric bill stays small.

Worked example: a service emits 200 GiB of logs a month, and 85 percent of that volume is health check lines. Step 1: confirm the volume by looking at the logging usage report. Step 2: write an exclusion filter that matches only the health check request entries. Step 3: apply it and watch ingestion for a day. Step 4: keep the error and warning entries for the full retention period, because they are what you will need in an incident. The ingested volume falls to about 30 GiB and the bill drops with it.

Common mistake: excluding entries that you later need for an audit or an incident investigation. Once dropped, they cannot be recovered. Safer practice is to export the sensitive entries through a sink to cheaper storage before you exclude anything.

Consequence in a running system: a debug flag left on during a 09:00 deploy can flood the log pipeline, raising the bill for the whole month and sometimes delaying the logs your on-call engineer is searching for.

questions.prompt: A payments team's logs total 120 GiB a month, and 70 percent of that volume is heartbeat lines from a sidecar that nobody reads. Their plan has four steps. Step 1: check the logging usage report to confirm the volume. Step 2: write an exclusion filter that matches only the heartbeat entries. Step 3 is missing from the plan. Step 4: keep the payment-failure entries for the full retention period. Which choice correctly fills Step 3, so that audit-relevant entries can still be recovered if needed?
choices: Delete all heartbeat entries from the bucket by hand each week.
Raise the retention period on the heartbeat entries to 365 days.
Turn the sidecar's debug flag off during the deploy window.
Create a log sink that exports the payment audit entries to a storage bucket before the exclusion filter is applied.
questions.why: An exclusion filter drops entries permanently, so exporting the audit entries through a sink to cheaper storage before applying the filter is the safe step that keeps them recoverable.

questions.prompt: Which term describes one unique combination of a metric name and its labels, which each add to a monitoring bill?
choices: Cardinality
Metric series
Ingestion
Log sink
questions.why: A metric series is one unique combination of a metric name and its labels, and each series can add to the monitoring bill, while cardinality is the count of distinct label values.

questions.prompt: A team adds a user_id label to a latency metric, and the service has several million distinct users. What happens to the monitoring bill?
choices: The bill stays flat, because labels are free to add.
The bill falls, because each series is compressed when it has a label.
The bill rises, because the number of series grows with each distinct user_id value.
The bill rises only if the metric is also exported to BigQuery.
questions.why: Each unique combination of metric name and label values is a separate series, so many distinct user_id values create many series and raise the metric bill.

questions.prompt: A company shortens retention on its application logs from 30 days to 7 days. What is the direct effect on cost?
choices: The metric series count falls, because logs turn into metrics.
Storage cost falls, because data is deleted after 7 days instead of 30.
A new exclusion filter starts dropping entries automatically.
Ingestion volume drops, because logs are sent in less often.
questions.why: Retention is how long stored data is kept before deletion, so a shorter retention period means less stored data and a lower storage bill, without changing how much is ingested.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would reduce the logging and monitoring bill for a busy service without losing the information you need during an incident. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by measuring where the bill comes from, because logging cost mostly tracks the volume of data ingested, how long it is kept, and how many metric series exist. Then I would remove the noisy, low-value entries, such as repeated health check lines, with an exclusion filter, and keep errors and warnings at full fidelity. If someone needs older data for audits, I would send it through a log sink to a cheaper storage bucket rather than keeping it in the default store for a long time. The main tradeoff is that excluded entries are gone from the logging service, so a wrong filter can hide the evidence you need during an outage. That is why I would test the filter on a small scope and confirm the error entries still appear afterwards.
rubricPoints: Identifies ingestion volume, retention and metric series count as the main cost drivers
Uses an exclusion filter to drop low-value entries before they are stored
Routes data needed for audit or long-term use through a log sink to cheaper storage
States the tradeoff that excluded logs cannot be recovered and needs careful testing

suggested.rationale: A planned cost model in fictional credits would let the learner see how volume, retention and exclusions change the bill before touching real billing.

lessons.plain: Spot VMs are rented computer servers in Google Cloud that cost much less than normal ones, because Google can take them back whenever it needs the capacity. A VM, or virtual machine, is a computer that runs inside a data center and that you rent by the hour. You get the saving in exchange for a condition: the provider may stop your server with very little warning and makes no promise about how long it will last. That makes Spot VMs a good fit for work that can be stopped, retried or resumed, such as batch jobs, test runs and stateless workers. They are a poor fit for a single database that must never go down. The skill is matching the cheap, interruptible option to the right kind of work.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your nightly batch job takes four hours and can be restarted from the last saved checkpoint. Would you run it on a cheap server that might be taken back at any moment, or on a standard server that is guaranteed to stay up? Why?
lessons.teach:
A Spot VM is a Compute Engine virtual machine sold at a steep discount from the standard on-demand price. The catch is that Google can reclaim, or preempt, it when it needs that capacity back. Preemption means the VM is stopped with a short warning, about thirty seconds, and Spot VMs do not carry the availability promise that standard VMs do. Spot VMs have no fixed maximum lifetime, so they can run for a long time, but how long is never guaranteed.

Why it works: cloud providers keep spare capacity that would otherwise sit idle. Selling that spare capacity cheaply, with the right to take it back, lets the provider fill its machines and lets you pay less. The saving only holds if your work survives being stopped.

Worked example: a batch job processes 10,000 image files and saves progress every 500 files. Step 1: the job starts on a Spot VM. Step 2: after 3,000 files the VM is reclaimed; the shutdown signal arrives and the job has about thirty seconds to save. Step 3: the last checkpoint records 3,000 files done. Step 4: a new Spot VM starts, reads the checkpoint, and resumes at file 3,001 instead of file 1. Only the work since the last save is lost.

Common mistake: putting a single-instance database or a long unsaved computation on Spot VMs and assuming the saving is free. A reclaim then means lost data or a full restart.

Consequence: Spot VMs can sit inside a managed instance group, which recreates reclaimed VMs automatically, so stateless web workers can recover. But if many VMs are reclaimed at once and nothing else absorbs the load, capacity drops and users see slow or failed responses.

questions.prompt: A logging company runs 40 stateless log-parsing workers on Spot VMs, which are discounted VMs that Google can reclaim with about thirty seconds' warning. A managed instance group, meaning a set of identical VMs that the platform keeps at a target count and recreates when one disappears, holds all 40 workers. Step 1: Google reclaims 12 of the 40 workers in the same minute. Step 2: each reclaimed worker receives its shutdown signal and stops. Step 3: the managed instance group notices 12 are missing and starts 12 replacement VMs. Step 4 is missing and must be filled in: what happens to the incoming log load and to users while the replacements are still booting?
choices: Until the replacements finish booting, the 28 surviving workers must absorb the extra load, and if they cannot, responses slow down or fail.
Spot VMs carry the same availability promise as standard VMs, so the 12 reclaimed workers are restored instantly with no capacity dip.
The group pauses the remaining 28 workers so the replacements can take over their share without any load change.
The 12 reclaimed workers keep running on standard VMs at no extra charge, so capacity never drops.
questions.why: Spot VMs carry no availability promise and replacements take time to start, so until they are running the surviving workers carry the load and capacity can drop.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a Spot VM?
choices: A standard VM that Google guarantees to keep running for at least 30 days at a fixed price.
A VM sold at a steep discount from on-demand price that can be stopped with a short warning when Google needs the capacity back.
A VM that is always stopped with a warning before its contents are deleted, so it never loses data.
A VM that runs only during off-peak hours on a fixed schedule and is charged at a flat rate.
questions.why: A Spot VM is a discounted VM that Google may preempt, meaning stop with about thirty seconds' warning, because it carries no availability promise.

questions.prompt: A team wants to cut its cloud bill. It runs two workloads: a stateless API worker fleet behind a managed instance group, and a single-instance primary database that holds the only copy of its orders. Which placement best fits the idea of Spot VMs?
choices: Put the primary database on Spot VMs and keep the API worker fleet on standard VMs.
Put the API worker fleet on Spot VMs and keep the single-instance primary database on standard VMs.
Put neither on Spot VMs, because a managed instance group cannot be used with any discounted VM.
Put both workloads on Spot VMs, because the discount is large enough to cover any reclaim.
questions.why: Stateless workers can be recreated by a managed instance group after a reclaim, while a single-instance database with the only copy of its data would lose that data if reclaimed.

questions.prompt: A batch job on a Spot VM saves its progress every 100 records. The VM is reclaimed after the job has processed 750 records, and the last save recorded 700. How many records of work are lost, and what makes that the answer?
choices: 0 records, because Spot VMs never lose unsaved work when reclaimed.
750 records, because a reclaim always forces the whole job to restart from the beginning.
100 records, because the save interval always sets the loss size.
50 records, because only the work done after the last save at 700 is lost.
questions.why: The loss is the work since the last checkpoint, which is 750 minus 700 equals 50 records, and the checkpoint lets the job resume from 701.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants to move our nightly report generator and our customer-facing API onto Spot VMs to save money. Explain which workload suits Spot VMs, which does not, and what limit they must design around before switching.
lessons.modelAnswer: The nightly report generator is a good candidate, because it is batch work that can be stopped and restarted. Spot VMs are much cheaper, but Google can reclaim them with about thirty seconds' warning, and they carry no availability promise. So before switching, the job must save checkpoints often enough that a reclaim loses little work, and the job runner must restart it on a new VM. The customer-facing API is a poor fit for Spot VMs alone, because a reclaim would drop live requests and capacity could vanish at peak. If we want some saving there, we could run a mix: standard VMs as a base that always serves traffic, with Spot VMs added above that, accepting that those extras can disappear. We should measure the reclaim rate first.
rubricPoints: Spot VMs are much cheaper but Google can reclaim them with short notice.
Good fit: fault-tolerant work that can be stopped and restarted, such as batch jobs.
Poor fit: live, stateful or availability-critical services without a fallback.
Mitigation: checkpoints, retries, and a base of standard capacity.

suggested.rationale: Comparing the discounted price against the cost of lost work and retries in a cost model would let the learner test the tradeoff directly.

lessons.plain: Cloud resources cost money whether or not they do useful work, so optimizing resource usage means paying only for the capacity you actually need, when you need it. It is less about buying cheaper things and more about removing waste: servers sized far bigger than their load, machines running all night for a daytime-only tool, old files kept in expensive storage, and disks or addresses left behind after a project changed. A good engineer measures usage first, then changes the size, schedule, or lifetime of each resource to match real demand.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web service runs on five large servers all year, but its traffic is about ten times higher on weekdays than on weekends and almost nothing overnight. Without looking anything up, name two changes you would make to stop paying for idle capacity, and say what evidence you would check first.
lessons.teach:
Optimizing resource usage means reducing what you pay for and what you waste while keeping the service fast enough for users. Three terms first. Rightsizing means choosing the size of a virtual machine, meaning its CPU and memory, from measured utilization rather than a guess made on day one. Autoscaling means an automatic controller adds or removes instances as load changes, staying between a minimum count and a maximum count that you set. Lifecycle rules are automatic policies on object storage that move data to a cheaper storage class or delete it after a set age.

Why it works: most cloud bills are driven by capacity billed by the hour, whether that capacity is busy or idle. If average CPU over a week is 8 percent, a server twice as large as it needs doubles the spend for no benefit. If load drops by half overnight, a fixed fleet pays for the same overnight hours anyway. Matching capacity to measured demand closes that gap.

Worked example: a reporting API runs on six identical machines. Step 1: over 14 days, peak CPU is 55 percent and overnight CPU is 10 percent. Step 2: the peak fits on four machines at roughly 80 percent, so the fixed count drops from six to four. Step 3: add an autoscaler with a minimum of two and a maximum of five, so overnight load runs on two machines. Step 4: after a week, compare the monthly bill and the 95th-percentile latency. The result is fewer machine hours with the same user-facing speed.

Common mistake: resizing from a single average or from one quiet week. The average hides the peak, and a short sample misses a monthly batch job. Another mistake is setting the autoscaler minimum to zero for a latency-sensitive service, so the first request after a quiet period waits for a new machine to boot.

Consequence in a running system: if the scale-in threshold is too aggressive, the fleet oscillates, adding and removing machines every few minutes, so you pay for boot time and users see errors during each removal.

questions.prompt: A media team keeps application access logs in an object storage bucket that holds 4 TB. Over 60 days of measurement, they find that logs older than 90 days are never read again. Step 1 is that measurement. Step 2: they add a lifecycle rule that moves objects older than 90 days to a cheaper storage class. Step 3 is missing from this summary and is covered in the answer choices. Step 4: the team compares the bucket's bill and the read-time performance of recent logs over a full month against the previous month. Which action best completes Step 3, the step that comes after the rule is in place?
choices: Turn off the rule and stop measuring, because lifecycle rules run on their own and need no further checks.
Delete all logs immediately to save the most money, since the age threshold has already been measured.
Compare the monthly storage bill and the performance of reads against the previous period over a full billing cycle.
Set the rule's minimum age to zero so that new logs move to the cheaper class on the day they are written.
questions.why: After a change, the teaching text says to compare the monthly bill and user-facing performance over a full cycle, so the saving is confirmed rather than assumed.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a lifecycle rule in object storage?
choices: A limit on how many requests per second a single client can send to a bucket.
An automatic policy that moves stored objects to a cheaper storage class or deletes them after a set age.
A report that lists which users have opened each file during the past year.
A scheduled job that restarts virtual machines each night to clear memory.
questions.why: The teaching text defines lifecycle rules as automatic policies that move data to a cheaper class or delete it after a set age.

questions.prompt: A ticket-sorting service runs on eight identical virtual machines. Weekday daytime CPU peaks near 70 percent, but on weekend nights average CPU is about 5 percent and the fixed count of eight keeps running. Which change most directly addresses the cost of those idle overnight hours?
choices: Set the autoscaler minimum to eight so that the fleet never shrinks below its current size.
Add an autoscaler with a minimum of two and a maximum of eight so that overnight load runs on fewer machines.
Set the service to run with zero machines overnight so that no instances are billed during idle hours.
Replace all eight machines with the largest machine type available so that peak load has more headroom.
questions.why: An autoscaler staying between a minimum and maximum count lets the fleet shrink to match low overnight demand while still reaching eight at peak.

questions.prompt: A team sizes a latency-sensitive quote API by setting its autoscaler minimum to zero, so no machines run during quiet periods. What symptom should they expect after a quiet period ends?
choices: The monthly bill will rise sharply because the autoscaler keeps every machine running at full size.
The autoscaler will oscillate, adding and removing machines every few minutes until the load changes.
The first request after the quiet period waits while a new machine boots, which slows that user's response.
Lifecycle rules will delete the quote data because the service has no active instances to hold it.
questions.why: With a minimum of zero there is no warm machine ready, so the first request waits for a new machine to start, which is the failure the teaching text warns about.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who owns the reporting API how you would cut its cloud cost without making users wait longer. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by measuring, not guessing: look at CPU and memory utilization over at least two weeks, including the busiest hour and the overnight low. If the peak only needs four machines at a comfortable utilization, I would reduce the fixed count, then add an autoscaler with a minimum that covers the overnight floor and a maximum that covers the peak. For data written once and rarely read, I would add a lifecycle rule to move it to a cheaper storage class after 30 days. The tradeoff is that autoscaling only helps if the service is stateless and starts quickly. A new instance still takes time to boot, so a sudden spike can see slower responses for a minute or two, and a minimum set too low means that wait happens every morning. I would watch 95th-percentile latency during the first week to confirm the change is safe.
rubricPoints: Measure real utilization over a representative period, including peaks and troughs, before changing sizes
Match fixed capacity to peak demand and let an autoscaler cover the variable part between a set minimum and maximum
Name a concrete tradeoff, such as instance boot time or a too-low minimum causing slow first responses
Verify the change with cost and latency data after rollout

suggested.rationale: Choosing autoscaling minimums, maximums and thresholds against a load curve is the core skill here, and a planned autoscaling engine would let the learner practise it.

lessons.plain: Cloud providers charge for what you use, but some ways of running things cost less. Some discounts apply automatically when a machine runs for most of the month. Others require you to promise a level of use for a year or more in exchange for a lower rate. A third choice concerns the network: the route traffic takes between your application and its users, which affects both speed and the cost of data leaving the cloud. Planning here means matching how steady and predictable your load is to the right discount, and knowing which option trades money for flexibility or speed.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team runs one virtual machine all month and has made no commitment. Would you expect Google Cloud to charge exactly the list price, and why might a team pay less by promising to keep that machine running for a year?
lessons.teach:
A sustained-use discount (SUD) is applied automatically. A virtual machine (VM, a rented computer in the cloud) that runs for a large share of a billing month gets a lower hourly price for that usage. You do not sign anything. However, only certain machine families are eligible, and some newer families, such as E2, generally do not receive it.

A committed-use discount (CUD) is a promise. You agree to use a set amount of resources, such as vCPUs (virtual CPU cores) and memory, for one or three years, and the rate is lower in return. You pay for the commitment whether or not you use it. Usage covered by a commitment is billed at the committed rate and does not also get a sustained-use discount. CUDs suit a steady baseline you can predict, not a workload you may shut down.

Network tiers are a separate choice about how traffic reaches users. Premium Tier carries traffic over Google's own network for most of its path and supports global load balancing. Standard Tier hands traffic to the public internet sooner, costs less for egress (data leaving Google Cloud), and is regional.

Worked example: a service needs four vCPUs every hour of the year. Step 1: without a commitment, it pays on-demand rates, with any eligible sustained-use discount. Step 2: the team buys a one-year CUD for four vCPUs. Step 3: the baseline now bills at the committed rate every hour, busy or idle. Step 4: a burst above four vCPUs is billed at normal rates.

Common mistake: committing to the peak load, which the workload reaches only occasionally. Most months the commitment sits partly unused, and you still pay for it. A related mistake is choosing Standard Tier for a latency-sensitive global service to save on egress, then wondering why distant users are slow.

In a running system, a commitment is a fixed monthly charge that continues after a service is decommissioned or an outage reduces traffic. Choose commitments only for load you expect to keep.

questions.prompt: A retailer runs a product search indexer on N2 VMs that needs 20 vCPUs at all times. Over the past year the lowest steady level has been 16 vCPUs, with extra load during daytime hours. Step 1: the team reviews 12 months of usage and identifies 16 vCPUs as the steady baseline. Step 2: the team buys a one-year committed-use discount for 16 vCPUs. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the 16 committed vCPUs are billed at the committed rate every hour, whether busy or idle.
choices: Leave the extra 4 vCPUs above the commitment at normal rates, with any sustained-use discount their machine family is eligible for.
Cancel the sustained-use discount on the 16 committed vCPUs and pay on-demand rates for the rest of the year.
Buy a three-year commitment for 20 vCPUs so the daytime peak is also covered at the lower rate.
Move the indexer to Standard Tier so the 4 extra vCPUs cost less to run.
questions.why: A commitment covers only the steady baseline, so usage above it is billed at normal rates, and an eligible machine family can still receive a sustained-use discount on that overflow.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes a committed-use discount (CUD)?
choices: It is applied automatically to any VM that runs most of a billing month, with nothing to sign.
It lets you stop paying for a service the moment your traffic drops, without penalty.
It is a promise to use a set amount of resources for one or three years in return for a lower rate, and you pay for it whether or not you use it.
It is a network setting that moves traffic onto Google's own network for most of its path.
questions.why: A CUD is a time-bound commitment to a set amount of resources, billed at a lower rate whether or not the resources are used, which is what option D states in plain terms.

questions.prompt: A team runs a proof-of-concept VM for 9 days each month and plans to delete it in about four months. Which purchasing choice best fits this situation?
choices: Buy a three-year commitment to get the deepest rate on the VM.
Switch the VM to Premium Tier so the discount applies to its network traffic.
Make no commitment and pay on-demand rates, because a commitment would keep charging after the VM is deleted.
Buy a one-year commitment so the hourly rate is lower for the whole period.
questions.why: A commitment is a fixed charge that continues after a service is decommissioned, so for a short-lived workload with no steady baseline, paying on-demand avoids paying for unused capacity.

questions.prompt: A mobile app has users in Asia and Europe and needs fast responses for both. The team moves the app's traffic from Premium Tier to Standard Tier to reduce egress costs. What is the main risk?
choices: Standard Tier stops sustained-use discounts from applying to the VMs serving the app.
Standard Tier forces the app into a committed-use contract that cannot be cancelled.
Standard Tier raises the price of every vCPU the app uses, regardless of network traffic.
Standard Tier is regional and hands traffic to the public internet sooner, so distant users may see slower responses and the app loses global load balancing.
questions.why: Standard Tier is regional and carries traffic over the public internet earlier in its path, which hurts latency for distant users and removes the global load balancing that Premium Tier supports.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how a committed-use discount differs from a sustained-use discount, and name one limit of committing that you would check before buying.
lessons.modelAnswer: A sustained-use discount happens automatically. If a machine family is eligible and a VM runs for much of the month, its hourly price drops, and I do not have to promise anything. A committed-use discount is different: we agree to a fixed amount of vCPUs and memory for one or three years, and the rate is lower in exchange. The tradeoff is that we pay for the commitment whether we use it or not. Before buying one, I would check how steady the load really is over the whole term. If the service might be retired, migrated, or sized down, the commitment becomes wasted spend. I would also check that the committed usage is in the region and machine family I expect, because the discount only covers matching usage. Burst traffic above the commitment is billed normally.
rubricPoints: Sustained-use discounts are automatic and depend on how long a VM runs in the month and on machine family eligibility.
Committed-use discounts require a one-year or three-year promise of resources and are billed whether or not the resources are used.
Committed usage does not also receive a sustained-use discount, and usage above the commitment is billed normally.
Network tier choice trades cost of egress against routing quality and regional or global reach.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly pricing rules, eligibility and product catalogue facts, which are best learned by reading and checking the official pricing terms rather than by a hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: Cloud providers watch how your resources actually behave and then suggest changes: a machine that sits almost idle, a server much bigger than it needs, or an account holding more access than it ever uses. Google Cloud calls these suggestions recommenders. Each suggestion falls into one of five buckets: cost, security, performance, manageability, or reliability. Think of a mechanic who reads your car's logs and says the tyres are underinflated and a spare key is never used, while you still decide what to fix. Nothing changes until a person or a process acts on the suggestion.
lessons.guessPrompt: A virtual machine (a rented server in the cloud) has used almost no processor time for six weeks. Should you delete it right away, and what would you need to know first?
lessons.teach:
A recommender is a service that reads usage data about your cloud resources and produces a suggestion with a stated reason and an estimated effect. In Google Cloud, recommenders are the source of suggestions sorted into categories: cost (spend you could cut), security (access or configuration riskier than needed), performance (a resource too small or too slow for its load), manageability (settings that make operations harder), and reliability (weak points that could cause an outage).

Why it works: the recommender compares what a resource is configured to allow with what it has actually used over a recent window of time. If a virtual machine has averaged almost no CPU or network traffic for weeks, it becomes a candidate for an idle-resource cost suggestion. If an identity (a user or service account, which is an automated identity) holds a broad IAM role (IAM means identity and access management, the rules about who may do what) but has used only two of its permissions, a security recommendation suggests a narrower role. Because the advice rests on history, it is only as good as the data. A job that runs once a month can look idle for most of the window.

Worked example: a team sees a recommendation to remove an idle VM. Step one, open the suggestion and read its category and usage evidence. Step two, check the VM's owner and labels (tags attached to a resource to record its purpose) and ask whether a scheduled job depends on it. Step three, if the VM is confirmed unused, stop it first, which halts compute charges while keeping its disk, and delete it only after a waiting period in case someone needs it.

Common mistake: applying every recommendation automatically. The consequence is that a monthly reporting host gets deleted, and the next month's report fails.

A recommendation is a reasoned hypothesis to verify, not an instruction. Recommenders reduce the search effort, but the owner of the workload still makes the decision.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's security recommendation says a service account (an automated identity used by a program, not a person) holds the Editor role on its billing project, but over the last 90 days it has used only read access to one storage bucket. Work through it. Step one: read the recommendation's security category and the usage evidence, which shows only read permissions were used. Step two: confirm the account's owner and that the nightly invoice job is the only thing that uses this account. Step three: ____ . Which completes the process?
choices: Replace Editor with a narrower role covering only the permissions used, then watch a run or two of the nightly job before removing the old grant.
Leave Editor in place, because a recommendation is only a suggestion and the account should keep whatever it already has.
Delete the service account immediately, since the recommender has flagged it as risky.
Grant the account the Owner role so the nightly job can never fail on a missing permission.
questions.why: The recommendation is a reasoned hypothesis, so the owner narrows the role to the permissions the usage history shows and verifies the job still works before removing the old grant, which avoids both deletion and over-granting.

questions.prompt: A reporting database instance averages 98 percent CPU, and queries queue during the busy hours of each day. Which recommender category is the right fit for this finding?
choices: Cost, because the instance's monthly bill is the main concern.
Manageability, because the instance needs more settings to be tuned by hand.
Performance, because the resource is too small or too slow for the load placed on it.
Reliability, because any slow instance is by definition an outage waiting to happen.
