questions.why: The performance category covers resources that are too small or too slow for their load, which is what the saturated CPU and queueing show.

questions.prompt: A team sees a recommendation to remove a virtual machine that looks idle. The team learns the machine runs a quarterly compliance export, and the recommender's history covered only the last 30 days. What is the main risk of acting on the suggestion without further checks?
choices: The suggestion is always accurate once it has been shown for 30 days, so no check is needed.
Recommenders cannot see quarterly jobs at all, so the machine is hidden from every category.
The suggestion is only in the cost category, so deleting the machine cannot affect anything else.
The window may miss the quarterly run, so the idle reading can be wrong and the owner must confirm the schedule before acting.
questions.why: Recommendations rest on the usage history, and a job that runs rarely can look idle for most of a short window, so the owner must check the schedule before acting.

questions.prompt: A security recommendation says a user account holds a broad IAM role but has used only three of the permissions that role grants. What does the recommendation propose?
choices: Raising the account to the next larger role so that future needs are covered.
Moving the account into the cost category so its spending is reviewed.
A narrower role that covers only the permissions the account has actually used.
Deleting the user's account entirely, because any unused permission is a risk.
questions.why: A security recommendation compares granted access with actual use and suggests a narrower role that keeps the used permissions and drops the rest.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a Google Cloud recommender is and how its categories help you choose what to look at first. Then name one limit of acting on its suggestions without checking.
lessons.modelAnswer: A recommender is a service that looks at how a resource has really been used and suggests a change, sorted into cost, security, performance, manageability or reliability. The categories tell you which kind of problem is being flagged, so you know who should review it. The suggestions are built from history, so the view is only as complete as the data it has seen: a job that runs monthly can look idle for most of the window. That means I would treat each suggestion as a claim to verify. For an idle VM, I would check the owner, the labels and whether any scheduled job depends on it, then stop it before deleting so we can recover if we were wrong. The limit to remember is that a recommender cannot know business intent, so the people who own the workload make the final call.
rubricPoints: Defines a recommender as a service that suggests changes based on observed usage
Names the categories cost, security, performance, manageability and reliability and what each flags
States that suggestions rest on historical data and can miss infrequent workloads
Explains that a suggestion should be verified by the workload owner before action, such as stopping before deleting

suggested.rationale: The objective is mostly a catalogue of recommender categories and how to read them, and no listed mission or planned engine covers recommenders directly.

lessons.plain: Running a workload in the cloud means renting computers, and you pay for what you reserve or use. This objective is about finding where one app's bill is wasted and choosing the matching fix for each of the three main places apps run here: a Kubernetes cluster (GKE), a serverless container service (Cloud Run), and plain virtual machines (Compute Engine). Think of a rented flat: you pay for rooms you reserve, for lights left on, and for the nights no one is home. Knowing which kind of bill you are looking at tells you which lever to pull.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your service gets almost no traffic overnight, yet the bill for those hours is about the same as in the daytime. Name one Cloud Run setting you would check first, and say what you think it does to that overnight cost.
lessons.teach:
A workload is one application or service plus everything it needs to run. Cost optimization for one workload means matching what you pay for to what the workload actually uses. Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) runs containers on a managed cluster of machines. Cloud Run runs containers that start to serve requests and can scale down to zero instances. Compute Engine gives you virtual machines (VMs) that you control directly.

Why it works: cloud bills meter what is reserved or consumed, so cost is roughly the size of the footprint multiplied by how long it exists. On GKE Autopilot you pay for the CPU, memory and storage each pod requests, so a request set too high costs money even when the pod is idle. On Cloud Run the main levers are minimum instances (warm instances kept running even with no traffic), maximum instances (a cap on spend during a surge) and concurrency (how many requests one instance handles at once). On Compute Engine, pick a machine type whose vCPU and memory fit measured load, and stop VMs nothing needs.

Worked example: a Cloud Run service has minimum instances set to 3. From 00:00 to 07:00 it gets no requests. Step 1: three instances stay warm for seven hours and are billed while serving nothing. Step 2: set minimum instances to 0. Step 3: the overnight cost falls to almost nothing. Step 4: the first request after a quiet spell now waits for a cold start, so its latency rises.

Common mistake: setting large requests or machine sizes 'to be safe' and never checking again. Measure real usage first, then size down in steps.

Consequence: in a running system, cutting minimum instances to zero saves money but can break a latency target for the first user after a quiet period, so check that target before you change the setting.

questions.prompt: A Cloud Run service receives about 300 requests per second at peak. Each request takes about 0.2 seconds. The team has set concurrency to 10 requests per instance. Step 1: at peak, about 300 × 0.2 = 60 requests are in progress at once. Step 2: with concurrency 10, about 60 ÷ 10 = 6 instances are needed at peak. Step 3 is missing. Which step completes the plan so that spend is capped during a surge without throttling normal peak traffic?
choices: Set concurrency to 1 so each instance serves one request at a time.
Raise the CPU request on each instance to 6 vCPU.
Set maximum instances to a value above 6 with some headroom, so a surge is capped without starving peak traffic.
Set minimum instances to 6 so six instances are always warm.
questions.why: Maximum instances is the cap on spend during a surge, and setting it a little above the computed 6 keeps peak traffic served while limiting cost.

questions.prompt: On GKE Autopilot, what do you pay for, and how does an idle pod affect the bill?
choices: You pay only for CPU actually used at the moment, so idle pods cost nothing.
You pay a flat fee per cluster regardless of pods, so requests do not affect cost.
You pay for the CPU, memory and storage each pod requests, so an oversized request costs money even when the pod is idle.
You pay for network traffic only, so the size of each pod request has no effect.
questions.why: Autopilot bills the resources each pod requests, so a request set too high raises cost even if the pod does little work.

questions.prompt: A Cloud Run service has minimum instances lowered from 2 to 0 to save money. The service has a strict latency target. What is the main risk to check before making the change?
choices: The first request after a quiet period waits for a cold start, which can push latency above the target.
Requests that arrive during the quiet period are dropped permanently.
Concurrency is reset to 1 for every request, which slows all traffic.
Billing rises because instances must restart every time traffic stops.
questions.why: Scaling to zero saves money, but the first user after a quiet spell must wait for a new instance to start, so the latency target must be checked first.

questions.prompt: A Compute Engine VM has 32 vCPUs and 128 GB of memory, and runs 24 hours a day. Measurement shows a daily batch job peaks at 6 vCPUs and 20 GB, and runs for only two hours. What is the best first action?
choices: Keep the 32 vCPU size and extend the job's timeout instead.
Stop the VM when no job needs it, and move to a machine type that fits the measured 6 vCPU and 20 GB load, changing size in steps.
Add more vCPUs so the batch job finishes faster.
Leave the VM as it is, since a large machine is safer than a small one.
questions.why: Compute Engine cost follows the machine size and how long the VM runs, so stopping idle VMs and matching the type to measured load addresses both.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would lower the monthly bill of one Cloud Run service without hurting its users. Name one tradeoff your change creates.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first find where the money goes. For Cloud Run I check whether minimum instances are above zero, because warm instances cost money even with no traffic. If nights are quiet I would lower minimum instances to zero, and I would review concurrency so one instance can serve more requests before the platform adds another. The tradeoff is cold starts: the first request after a quiet period waits longer. Before changing anything I would check the latency target, and if needed keep one warm instance only during busy hours. I would also set a maximum instance count so a surge cannot create an unbounded bill.
rubricPoints: Identifies which of GKE, Cloud Run or Compute Engine the bill comes from before choosing a lever.
Names a specific lever such as minimum instances, concurrency, pod requests on Autopilot, or machine type.
States that idle warm capacity or oversized requests are paid for even when they are not used.
Names a tradeoff such as cold-start latency or reduced headroom during a surge.
Says to measure real usage and check the latency target before changing settings.

suggested.rationale: A cost model lets the learner see how sizing and idle time change a bill before touching a real service.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Parcels Stands Up Its First Google Cloud Organization
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Parcels is a fictional mid-sized logistics company that has just been given a new Google Cloud organization. An organization is the top node of Google Cloud's resource hierarchy, the tree that holds folders, projects, and resources, and it is where access rules and organization-wide policies start. Your first week as a junior cloud engineer on the platform team is spent helping the lead design the foundation before any application moves in. The company has three product teams: Tracking (a web app for customers), Billing (a payments service that must read data from a shared customer database), and Analytics (a data team that trains machine learning models). Each team will deploy into its own environments: development, staging, and production. The lead asks you to work through three decisions and write up your reasoning. 1. The Tracking and Billing teams both want their own projects, but leadership wants the production projects of all three teams grouped so that one policy can block creation of public storage buckets everywhere in production. Explain where the production projects should sit in the resource hierarchy, which Google Cloud mechanism you would use to apply the shared rule, and why you would not attach that rule to each project one by one. 2. The Billing service in its project must talk privately to the customer database, which lives in a separate shared data project owned by the platform team. Choose between Shared VPC, VPC Network Peering, and Private Service Connect for this connection, and explain the reason in terms of who manages the network and how addresses are shared. 3. New engineers need a consistent workstation with the right command-line tools, a code editor, and the Cloud SDK already installed. Choose between Cloud Workstations and Cloud Shell as the main environment for a full working day, and explain how you would make the setup repeatable for each new hire.

Sub-tasks:
1. Decide where the production projects belong in the resource hierarchy and name the mechanism that applies one shared rule across them.
2. Choose the connectivity option between the Billing project and the shared customer database project and justify it.
3. Choose the main development environment for a full working day and describe how to make the setup repeatable.
subParts: Production project placement and shared rule mechanism
Connectivity choice between Billing and the shared database
Development environment choice and repeatable setup
modelAnswer: Place the production projects for all three teams under a single production folder beneath the organization. A folder is a grouping node in the resource hierarchy that holds projects or other folders and lets you apply the same settings to everything inside it. Apply an organization policy, which is a rule set at the organization, folder, or project level that limits what resources may do, to the production folder. Attach the rule that blocks public access to storage buckets to that folder. Because policies inherit downward, every current and future project created inside the folder receives the rule automatically. Attaching it project by project is a common mistake: a new project created later would be missed until someone remembered to add the rule, and the production controls would quietly have a gap. Consequence: if the rule were missing on one project, a bucket could be made public in production without anyone being alerted to the gap.

Choose Private Service Connect. Shared VPC lets a host project own a network that service projects use, which fits when one central team runs the network and many projects share it, but it means the Billing project would join the platform team's network model. VPC Network Peering connects two separate networks so they can exchange private traffic, but each side keeps its own address and firewall rules, and overlapping address ranges between peered networks cause routing problems. Private Service Connect gives the Billing project a private endpoint, a private address inside its own network, that forwards traffic to the managed or shared service. Each side keeps its own network boundaries, and the connection is one-directional, which limits what the consumer can reach. Worked example: the platform team publishes the customer database through a service attachment, the Billing project creates an endpoint with a private address, and the Billing service sends requests to that address. Common mistake: choosing peering because it sounds simpler, then discovering that the address ranges of the two networks overlap and cannot be reconciled without rebuilding one of them. Consequence: the payment path would fail at connection time in production, which is a serious outage for a payments service.

Choose Cloud Workstations for the full working day. Cloud Workstations is a managed service that runs a configured development environment in Google Cloud, reached through a browser or a supported local editor. You define a workstation configuration, which is a template naming the machine type, the container image that holds the tools, and the editor setup. Cloud Shell is a free, temporary terminal that starts quickly and is well suited to short tasks such as running a single command or checking a resource, but it resets its environment on a schedule and is not designed as a long-term setup for daily coding. To make the setup repeatable, build a custom container image that includes the Cloud SDK, required compilers, linters, and the editor extensions, store it in Artifact Registry (a managed repository for container images and packages), and reference that image in the workstation configuration. Every new hire then gets an identical environment from the same template. Common mistake: installing tools by hand on each workstation, which makes environments drift apart over time. Consequence: a teammate's build can pass locally and fail in the pipeline because a tool version differs.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lantern route planner release
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lantern Logistics is a fictional delivery company that runs a route-planning service called route-planner on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE, a managed way to run containers across a cluster of machines). Its engineers use Cloud Build, a managed service that runs build steps from a configuration file, to turn source code into a container image. The image is stored in Artifact Registry, a managed store for container images and other packages. Cloud Deploy, a managed delivery service, moves a release through a dev, staging, and prod environment in order. The team is changing three things at once: the build will now start automatically on a push to the main branch, the production release must wait for a named person to approve it, and the new version must be rolled out to a small share of traffic first (a canary, meaning a partial release used to check health before a full rollout). The database password for the service is kept in Secret Manager, a managed vault for sensitive values, and the service reads it when it starts. Read the situation and answer the sub-tasks below.

1. Name the trigger that should start the build and explain why a push to main should not also deploy straight to prod. Then name the place where the image is stored and state one audit trail that shows which build produced the image running in prod.

2. The developer proposes writing the database password into the Docker image during the build so the service never needs to call Secret Manager. Say whether this is build-time or runtime secret injection, explain the risk, and say which approach you would choose and how you would limit who can read the secret in each environment.

3. The release manager wants prod to receive 10 percent of traffic for the new version first, with a rollback if error rate rises. Name the deployment strategy, name one success metric the team should watch, and describe what happens to traffic if the metric crosses the threshold.
subParts: Trigger, image storage, and audit trail
Build-time versus runtime secret injection and IAM scope
Canary strategy, success metric, and rollback
modelAnswer: The trigger is a source-change trigger on the main branch, which starts a Cloud Build run. That build should only produce and test an image and hand it to Cloud Deploy as a release candidate. Deploying straight to prod on every push would skip the dev and staging stages and the approval step, so a change could reach customers without a human checkpoint. The image is stored in Artifact Registry, and the image digest (a fixed fingerprint of the exact image contents, unlike a tag that can be moved) should be recorded. A usable audit trail is the Cloud Build history plus Cloud Audit Logs entries that record who approved and which release was rolled out, linked by the digest and release name, so you can trace a running prod pod back to the build that created it.

Injecting a secret at build time means the value is baked into the image layers during the build. Anyone who can pull that image can usually extract the value, and the password stays in the image history even after a later change. Runtime injection means the service fetches the secret from Secret Manager when it starts, so the image contains no secret and the value can be rotated without rebuilding. The team should choose runtime injection. To scope access, give each environment its own secret or project, and grant the GKE workload's service account the secret accessor role only on the secret in its own environment, using IAM (identity and access management, the system that decides who can do what on which resource). The pipeline's build identity should not be able to read the prod password at all. Developers should not hold accessor rights on the prod secret.

A canary is a deployment strategy that sends a small share of live traffic to the new version while the old version keeps serving the rest. Traffic splitting is the mechanism that does this. The team should watch a success metric such as the error rate or the share of requests that finish within a latency target, measured from the service's own telemetry (the logs and metrics it emits). If the metric crosses the agreed threshold during the canary window, the rollout should be halted and traffic should be shifted back to the old version, which is the rollback. The new version should only receive full traffic after the metric stays healthy through the window and the approval step is complete.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Parcels checkout reliability decision
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Parcels is a fictional company that sells shipping labels online. Its checkout API is a service that receives payment requests from the website and returns a success or failure answer. The site reliability team, which is a group that uses software engineering to keep services running, has been asked by product managers to ship a new discount feature quickly. Before deciding how fast to release, the team must agree on how reliable checkout should be. Note that a service level indicator (SLI) is a measurement of one aspect of user experience, such as the share of requests that succeed, and a service level objective (SLO) is an internal target for that measurement over a time window. A service level agreement (SLA) is a promise to customers, usually looser than the SLO, with a penalty if broken. An error budget is the amount of unreliability the SLO allows in a window, calculated as 100 percent minus the SLO target. 'Nines' is shorthand for availability, where 99.9 percent is three nines. Checkout runs in two regions behind a load balancer, which spreads incoming requests across servers. The team's current 30-day window contains 43,200 minutes. Last week a faulty release caused 20 minutes of failed checkouts. A traffic spike later that week tested autoscaling, which is the automatic adding and removing of servers based on load, and the team also keeps a rollback plan, which is returning to the previous working version. Tasks: 1. Define one availability SLI and one latency SLI for checkout in plain terms, then propose an SLO for each with a 30-day window, and explain why the SLA given to customers should be looser than these SLOs. 2. Calculate the total error budget in minutes for a 99.9 percent availability SLO over the 30-day window, subtract the 20 minutes already used, and state what fraction of budget remains and what the team should do with the discount feature release given that remaining amount. 3. During a new incident, one region's error rate jumps sharply right after a release while the other region is healthy. Choose between draining traffic from the bad region, adding capacity, and rolling back the release, justify your choice using the SLO and error budget, and state one risk of the option you did not choose.
subParts: Define SLIs and SLOs and explain why the SLA is looser
Calculate the error budget and recommend a release decision
Choose a mitigation for a regional incident and justify it
modelAnswer: An availability SLI can be the percentage of checkout requests that return a success response, measured as good requests divided by total valid requests. A latency SLI can be the percentage of checkout requests that finish within a set time, such as 800 milliseconds. A reasonable availability SLO is 99.9 percent of requests succeeding over a rolling 30 days, and a latency SLO is 95 percent of requests finishing within 800 milliseconds over the same window. The SLA promised to customers should be looser, for example 99.5 percent, so the team has room to fix problems before a breach triggers a penalty. The gap gives an early warning: missing an internal SLO is a signal to slow down, while breaching the SLA is a contractual failure.

Total error budget equals 0.1 percent of 43,200 minutes, which is 43.2 minutes. Subtracting the 20 minutes already used leaves 23.2 minutes, about 54 percent of the budget remaining. Because more than half remains, the team can proceed with the discount feature, but should release it in small, monitored steps, with a rollback ready, and should pause risky changes if further failures use up the remaining budget. If the budget had been exhausted, the usual decision would be to stop feature releases and focus on reliability work until the window recovers.

The best choice is to drain traffic from the failing region, which means directing new requests away from it to the healthy region, because the release is the likely cause and draining protects users immediately while the other region still meets the SLO. Rolling back the release is also reasonable and may be done next to restore the failing region, but draining is faster to limit customer impact while the rollback proceeds. Adding capacity does not fix a faulty release, because more servers running broken code still fail. A risk of choosing draining alone is that the healthy region may overload if it cannot absorb the full load, so the team should check its autoscaling limits and quotas, which are the caps set on how many servers or resources a project can use, before shifting all traffic.

scenarios.title: Checkout slowdown after a Friday release at Harbor Lantern Goods
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lantern Goods is a fictional online retailer. Its checkout is served by three services: a web front end, a payments service, and an inventory service, all running on Google Cloud. On Friday afternoon, the release team deployed a new version of the payments service. By Saturday morning, customers report that checkout feels slow, and the on-call engineer, Priya, has been asked to work out what is happening. Priya is a beginner on the team, so she is working from the observability tools the company already has. Three signals are available. A metric is a number recorded over time, such as request count or latency, and it tells you how a quantity changes. A log is a timestamped record of a discrete event, such as an error message or a configuration change. A trace is a record of one request as it travels across services, broken into timed pieces called spans, and a trace waterfall is the timeline view that shows where each span starts and stops. Cloud Audit Logs are the platform's own record of who changed what in the cloud project and when. The team uses Metrics Explorer to graph metrics and Logs Explorer to search logs with the logging query language. Priya needs to answer three questions before the Monday review. 1. Which signal and tool should she use first to confirm that checkout latency really rose, and when it started? 2. Once she knows checkout is slow, which signal should she use to find which service inside the request path is adding the time, and how can she link a slow trace to the matching log lines? 3. Her manager wants to know whether anyone changed the payments service configuration or its network settings during the same window, and she needs the right log source for that question. Answer each numbered question for Priya.
subParts: Choose the first signal and tool to confirm that checkout latency rose and when it started.
Identify the signal and tool that show which service in the checkout path adds the delay, and explain how to link a slow trace to its log lines.
Name the log source that records configuration and permission changes in the window, and explain why it is the right source.
modelAnswer: Use a metric, graphed in Metrics Explorer. Latency is a quantity that changes over time, so a metric is the right signal. Priya should pick the checkout request latency metric, use a high percentile such as the 95th or 99th so that slow requests are not hidden by the average, and set the time window to cover Friday afternoon through Saturday morning. The graph shows whether the rise is real and the exact time it began, which can then be compared with the release time. A log search would be slow and noisy for this question because it counts events rather than showing a smooth trend over time.

Use a trace, viewed as a trace waterfall, to see which span takes the extra time. A trace shows one request broken into spans for each service call, so the longest span points to the slow component, such as the payments call. To connect the trace to logs, Priya should copy the trace ID shown on the slow trace and search Logs Explorer for that trace ID, provided the services write structured logs that include the trace field. Matching the trace ID shows the error messages and details written during that exact request, which a metric alone cannot provide.

Priya should use Cloud Audit Logs, specifically the Admin Activity logs, filtered to the payments project and the time window of the release. These logs record administrative changes such as deployments, IAM permission changes, and network configuration edits, along with the identity that made each change. Application logs from the service would not reliably show who changed a setting, and metrics show only numbers. Checking the Admin Activity logs answers the manager's question directly, and the entries can be reviewed without changing anything.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Parcels: Cutting a Rising Cloud Bill Without Slowing the Tracking Page
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Parcels is a fictional logistics company. Its engineering team runs a customer tracking website on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE, a managed service that runs containers across a group of machines called a cluster), a public API on Cloud Run (a service that runs containers and scales them up or down with demand, including to zero when idle), and a nightly report job on Compute Engine virtual machines (VMs, which are rented computers in Google's data centres). Last month the cloud bill rose about 40 percent, while customers complained that the tracking page felt slow at peak times. The finance lead asks Priya, the on-call DevOps engineer, to investigate. Priya finds three things. The nightly report VMs look much larger than the work they do. The logging bill has grown faster than any other line. The slow tracking requests do not match the cluster's CPU graphs, which look fine. Work through Priya's next steps.
1. Name the specific Google Cloud tool that reviews the report VMs for oversizing and suggests changes. Explain in generic terms what the tool does and what Priya should check before applying a suggestion.
2. The nightly report can restart safely if a machine is taken back mid-run, and the tracking website runs all day, every day. Choose a pricing option for each workload and justify each choice.
3. Every service writes debug-level messages, which is driving the logging bill. Name the Google Cloud feature that stops selected log entries from being stored, and explain how it affects cost and what risk it carries.
4. Name the tool that shows where time is spent inside a single slow request across services. Explain how Priya would use it to find the slow step, and why CPU graphs alone did not reveal the problem.
modelAnswer: The tool is Active Assist, specifically the VM rightsizing recommendation produced by the Recommender service. A recommender is a Google Cloud service that studies usage history and proposes changes in categories such as cost, security, performance, manageability and reliability. Rightsizing means changing a VM's machine type so its CPU and memory match what it actually uses. Before applying a suggestion, Priya should check the peak usage window the recommendation was based on, confirm that the nightly job's busiest period is covered, and test the smaller machine type in a non-production copy. The common mistake is applying the suggestion automatically because it looks like a saving, without checking peak load. The consequence is that the nightly report could run out of memory and fail, leaving customers without reports the next morning.

For the nightly report, Priya should use Spot VMs. A Spot VM is spare Google Cloud capacity sold at a steep discount, and Google can reclaim it with very short notice. That works here because the report can restart safely, so a reclaimed machine costs only some re-run time. For the tracking website and API, which run all day, she should use a committed use discount. This is a commitment, usually for one or three years, to a steady baseline amount of vCPU and memory in exchange for a lower rate; the commitment is billed whether or not it is fully used. Sustained use discounts, which apply automatically to some resources that run for a large share of the month, are a fallback when no commitment is made. The common mistake is committing to peak demand instead of the steady baseline, which pays for capacity that sits idle most of the time. Another mistake is putting the report on Spot VMs without retry logic, so a reclaimed machine leaves the report incomplete.

The feature is a log exclusion filter in Cloud Logging. Cloud Logging is the Google Cloud service that collects and stores application logs. An exclusion filter is a rule that matches log entries and drops them before storage, so they are never billed as stored logs. Priya can add a filter that excludes entries with severity DEBUG from the tracking service, and then check the billing report to confirm that log ingestion volume falls. Errors and warnings should still be kept. The common mistake is excluding too broadly, for example dropping all INFO and WARNING messages, which removes the evidence needed during an outage or a security review. The consequence is that when a real incident happens, the team has fewer logs to work from and the investigation takes longer.

The tool is Cloud Trace. Cloud Trace is a distributed tracing service that records how long each step of a request takes, including calls between services, and shows those steps as a timeline. Priya would open a slow tracking request, find the longest step in the timeline, and see whether it is a database call, a call to another service, or work inside the application. CPU graphs did not reveal the problem because a slow request can spend most of its time waiting on something else, such as a database query or a remote call, while the CPU stays mostly idle. The common mistake is looking only at averages from CPU or memory charts. The consequence is that the team might add more machines, which costs money, and the tracking page stays slow because the bottleneck was never the CPU.
